en: Commentary on the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll One, together with the Preface,
composed by the Śramaṇa Baochen of the Eastern Capital during the Song Dynasty.
When Bodhidharma came from the West, he fundamentally did not establish the use of written words;
when the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was entrusted to China in the East, it served as a seal to transmit the Buddha-mind school.
Although this discourse has spread widely throughout the monasteries, practitioners still find it obscure and profound.

There was the venerable master Śikṣānanda, who appeared during the Jiushi era of the Li Tang dynasty; he collated the titles from three previous translations and verified the subtle principles of this single sutra.
Compared to the past, its literary expression is expansive and its meaning is luminous;
it will surely cause those who come after to achieve double the merit without laboring their strength.
At that time, it was hailed as a complete and perfect work, yet no one has been found to provide a commentary or gloss upon it.
I, Baochen, have hastily gathered several commentaries on the ancient texts and rearranged them into this new exposition in seven fascicles.

By mending gaps and filling omissions, verifying facts and setting aside doubts, I have sought to ensure accuracy regarding agriculture and horses; I venture to offer this work as a display of my own pearls.
May those who study the Way exhaustively observe its ultimate realization!
Preface to the Newly Translated Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, composed by the Celestial Script, Golden Wheel, Sagely and Divine Emperor.
I have heard that the summit of Mount Malaya is both most lofty and most majestic;
The city of Laṅkā is truly difficult to approach and difficult to enter.

It is the place where former Buddhas proclaimed the Dharma and the site where past sages practiced their cultivation. Therein resides the lord of the city named Rāvaṇa, who ascends his celestial palace to behold the Honored One’s countenance, offers music to pray for the wondrous Dharma, uses the Maṇi-peak to manifest its arising, and points to the ocean of the *Ratnakūṭa* to clarify its essential principle.

What is called the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* is the profound pivot of the mind-measure (*cittamātra*) of all Buddhas and the wondrous key to the treasury of the principles of all scriptures. It extensively illustrates subtle purports and penetrates the deep meanings: it is neither arising nor ceasing, neither existent nor non-existent; it cuts off the two paths of coming and going and departs from the dual attachments of annihilationism and eternalism, thereby attaining the most supreme and wondrous treasure through the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
Realizing that all phenomena are empty and knowing that external objects are like illusions, he merges the conceptual distinctions of provisional names and equates saṃsāra with nirvāṇa.

As Mahāmati’s questions were first set forth, the intent of the Dharma King was thus revealed: through one hundred and eight points of meaning, he accords with the true mark while transcending the mundane;
through thirty-nine gates, he shatters false views and proclaims the True Dharma.
One understands that names and characteristics are both provisional, thereby dispelling the deluded fetters of false conceptualization;
relying on correct wisdom to realize suchness, one awakens to dependent origination and returns to the wondrous principle.

Once the winds of objective conditions have subsided, the waves of consciousness finally become clear; the three natures are all empty, the two forms of selflessness are both extinguished, one enters the Tathāgata-garbha, and wanders through the gate of liberation.

Tracing the origins of this scripture, it came from the Western Regions; yet when the Yuanjia era was established, the translation by Guṇabhadra had not yet spread widely, as the four-fascicle version translated at the beginning of the Liu Song dynasty was the one available.
Later, during the Yanchang reign period, the ten-fascicle version translated during the Later Wei by Bodhiruci contained many errors in its interpretation.

With sincere devotion, I reflect upon the Buddha’s entrustment, my heart yearning for its perpetuation. In the first year of Jiushi, the year of Gengzi, during the month of Linzhong when the fire deity presides over the calendar, while避暑 (avoiding the heat) at Jifeng and observing the customs by the Ying River, I reissued this sutra within the Sanyang Palace. Having investigated the essential exegesis of three versions, I have completed this definitive teaching in seven fascicles.

The Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa, the Venerable Master Śikṣānanda from the Kingdom of Khotan, the monk Fuli of Dafuxian Monastery, and others—whose fame followed in the footsteps of Dao’an and Huiyuan, whose virtue equaled that of Fotudeng and Huilan—inherited the fragrant path of Nāgārjuna and explored the secret treasury of Aśvaghoṣa. With the fragrance of their precepts mingling with the scent of awakening flowers, and the jewel of their minds becoming as perfectly round as the moon, they were able to fully comprehend the profound and subtle, and to elucidate the most esoteric mysteries. This transcription was completed on the fifteenth day of the first month in the fourth year of the Chang’an era.

Reflecting upon my own meager worth, I find my words fall short of the excellence of refined jade; looking back upon the fourfold eloquence, I am filled with shame, and gazing toward the One Vehicle, I remain utterly unable to fathom it. Yet, unable to refuse the requests of both the monastic and the laity, I have forced myself to compose this literary work. My phrasing is clumsy and my reasoning deviates from the truth, further increasing my sense of shame and trepidation.
I humbly submit that this sutra is subtle and wondrous, the most rare of all; it shatters the darkness of profound ignorance, and the verses that transmit its lamp are inexhaustible;
it expounds upon the merit of continuous flow, and the meanings of its surging springs are endless.
The titles and sequence of the chapters are listed below.
Regarding the title of the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*:

as for the place where the sutra was preached called Laṅkā, this is translated here as "Difficult to Access" (*duranvaya*). It is said to be composed of various jewels, its radiance outshining the sun and moon, and it is the abode of the *yakṣas* who roam through the sky.

This city is situated atop Mount Māra; the mountain is steep and lofty, overlooking the great ocean below, and it has no gates or entrances, so that only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are able to ascend there.
This then manifests the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground, which can only be entered by those who are without mind and without realization.
Looking down upon the great ocean symbolizes that the ocean of the mind is inherently pure, yet it is stirred by the waves of consciousness as it is turned by the winds of external objects.

When one clearly realizes that the objects of perception and the mind are empty, the ocean of consciousness likewise becomes naturally still; as both mind and objects are quiescent, there is nothing that is not illuminated, just as when the great ocean is windless, the sun, moon, and constellations shine forth with brilliant clarity.

This sutra is intended solely for those of superior faculties; it directly teaches that the seed-consciousness and karmic consciousness are the Tathāgatagarbha, distinguishing them from the two vehicles whose practitioners extinguish their consciousnesses and incline toward quiescence.

Furthermore, this is because it differs from those provisional teachings for Bodhisattvas who cultivate emptiness and for whom the cultivation of emptiness is predominant; it directly clarifies that the essential nature of consciousness is entirely true, and thus demonstrates that the essence of consciousness immediately constitutes the functioning of wisdom.
Just as when that great ocean is windless, its reflections become clear, so too is it with the dharma-gate of the ocean-like mind.
As for what is called a "sūtra," in the Sanskrit language it is *sūtra*, which here is translated as "Sūtra of Accordance" (*qìjīng*).
"Harmony" refers to harmony with the Dharma and harmony with the capacity [of the listener].
If one harmonizes solely with the Dharma, then the Dharma does not accord with the capacity;
if one harmonizes solely with the capacity, then the capacity does not reach the Dharma.

"Sūtra" (Jīng) means "constant. Its meaning consists of "pervading," "encompassing," and "gathering. It is called "constant" because it reveals that what was taught by former sages and later sages is all thus.
It is called "pervading" because it maintains the principles of truth without forgetting them.
It is called "encompassing" because it gathers all sentient beings and instructs them.
It further states: "It is like weaving cloth; it is completed by means of the woof, yet its success depends upon the person.
This was translated by the Tripitaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Great Tang Dynasty.

According to the commentary by the monk Zhìyán, a translator at Jìng'ài Temple in the Tang, this sutra is based on the version translated during the Liu Song dynasty, whose introductory preface states: "The Sanskrit texts vary in length, and there are generally three versions: the extensive version consists of one hundred thousand stanzas, the intermediate version consists of thirty-six thousand stanzas, and the abbreviated version consists of four thousand stanzas."
In this land, there have been four translations in total, all of which are abridged versions consisting of four thousand stanzas;
one version was formerly missing.

Among the three extant versions currently held in the Tripitaka, the first was translated by the Tripiṭaka Master Guṇabhadra of India at Cudāmaṇivihāra (Cao Tang Si) in Jinling during the twelfth year of the Yuanjia era of the Liu Song dynasty. It comprises four fascicles, though the text for only one chapter remains incomplete. It is titled *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra* and is contained in the "Shen" (身) case.

Second, the Tripiṭaka Master Bodhiruci of the Later Wei, at the residence of the Prince of Runan in Luoyang and at Jinhua Temple in the capital Ye during the second year of the Yanchang era, supplemented missing passages for a total of three chapters of the sūtra, translating them into ten fascicles divided into eighteen sections, titled the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, contained within the Fa (Fa) case.

Third, at the beginning of the Jiushi era of the Tang dynasty, the Tripiṭaka Master Śikṣānanda of Khotan, the śramaṇa Fuli, and others, having completed the translation of the eighty-fascicle *New Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, observed that the two previously translated versions were cumbersome and abbreviated, and had not yet been fully refined. Intending to polish them further for wider circulation, they subsequently received an imperial decree to translate it once again.

Thereupon, at the Tianzhong Aranya on Mount Song, he collated three versions—the two Chinese texts and one Sanskrit manuscript—compiling them into seven fascicles comprising ten chapters, titled the *Mahāyāna-laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, which is contained in the fourth case.
Therefore, the Imperial Preface states:
"When the Yuanjia era was established as its title, Guṇabhadra’s translations had not yet spread widely;
when the Yanchang era was recorded in its years, Bodhiruci’s interpretations were frequently erroneous."

This present commentary primarily explains the Tang edition; however, it incorporates the titles of the remaining eight chapters translated by Dharmaruci in their respective order within the notes. Thus, the scripture itself consists of eighteen chapters, so that readers may easily understand that while the text has its beginning and end, the underlying principle remains without duality.
Some scholars claim that because the version indicated by Dharmarakṣa consists of only four fascicles, it is easier to master than the seven-fascicle edition;
however, they fail to realize that when the first sutra was initially translated, the language was concise and archaic, and portions of the text were missing from both the beginning and the end.
Even great scholars of profound virtue still lamented the difficulty of its punctuation and reading.

Regarding the prefaces, introductions, and colophons, there are already clear records: during the Yuanfeng era, when Su Dongpo transcribed this four-fascicle version of the sutra for Minister Zhang Wen-ding, he himself wrote a colophon stating:
"The meaning and intent of the *Laṅkāvatāra* are profound and subtle, and its characters are concise and archaic; readers may sometimes be unable to parse the sentences."
The preface written by Jiang Yingshu also states:
"If Zhiqi constantly found the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* difficult to read, then one can imagine how it must have been for others."

This scripture has been collated from three versions to achieve its complete integrity; its phrasing and meaning are now clearly manifest. If you were to open and read it, you would realize that more than half of your understanding has already been attained!
Chapter One: Rāvaṇa King’s Exhortation (1). From this point onward, the meaning of the scriptural text is correctly explained, divided into three parts:
namely, the Introduction, the Main Body, and the Dissemination.
This chapter constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
From the "Chapter on Questions and Answers" through to the "Extensive Verses," comprising seventeen chapters in total, is called the main body of the teaching (*śarīra*).
The final verse is termed the section on dissemination (*pariṇāmana*).
In the original four-fascicle version, this entire chapter of the sutra is missing; there is only a text of more than six lines at the beginning, serving as a brief preface.
As for the term "Rāvaṇa," no standard translation has been seen; he is the King of the Yakṣas.

He exhorted the Tathāgata to enter the mountain of jewels to expound the Dharma of self-realization, and further requested Mahāmati Bodhisattva to serve as the primary questioner; therefore, it is called "exhortation."
Regarding the term "chapter" (*varga*): those items whose meanings and categories are similar are gathered into a single section, hence it is called a chapter.
This sutra consists of a total of four thousand verses and contains eighteen chapters.
This chapter is designated as the first because it initiates the work.
"Thus have I heard" (*evam mayā śrutam*) refers to the essence of the Dharma that was heard; it means that the meaning of this entire sūtra was personally heard by me from the Buddha in the past.
Therefore, the *Buddhabhūmi-śāstra* states: "Those who transmit the Buddha's teachings say, 'Such matters as these I have heard in the past.
This is a general explanation that combines "faith" (*śraddhā*) and "hearing" (*śruta*).
If one explains it by way of analysis, such a person has accomplished faith.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "The Great Ocean of the Buddha-dharma can be entered through faith and crossed through wisdom."
The sutras are neither elaborate nor concise; they cannot be accessed without faith, and thus they are called "Thus" (evam).
Some say: "When the Sages preach the Dharma, they do so only to manifest the Thusness (tathatā); only Thusness is what is 'Thus'."
Furthermore, it is said: "The 'Such' (tathatā) refers to words that accord with principle; the 'Wise' (jñānin) is a title for one who has nothing to contradict.
Now, however, it is said: "'Such' is ultimate emptiness (śūnyatā); 'is' is wondrous existence (prabhāsvara-bhāva)."
Since there is no ultimate truth external [to phenomena], it is empty yet not nihilistic;
since there is no conventional reality external to ultimate truth, it exists yet is not eternal.
This directly refutes provisional and heterodox schools to manifest the Middle Way; therefore, it is said: "Thus."
"I have heard" refers to the accomplishment of hearing.
If one intends to transmit what has been heard to those who have not yet heard it, yet speaks without transmitting it, then the words are established in vain.
It does not depend on the ability to speak, but rather on the ability to transmit; therefore, next, "I have heard" is clarified.
I am Mañjuśrī and Ānanda. Since the "self" is a mere designation for the five aggregates, how can it be called "I"?
There are four kinds of self:

There are four types of self-conception: first, the pervasive conceptualization of ordinary beings; second, the sectarian tenets of non-Buddhists; third, the provisional distinction of guest and host made by the noble ones in accordance with worldly convention; and fourth, the true self of the dharmakāya.
The present case refers to the latter two, and lacks the former two types of self-conception held by ordinary beings and non-Buddhists.
Since there is no self for me, there is likewise no hearing; because all arises from conditions and is empty, conventional designations are not destroyed—this is precisely "hearing without hearing.

If one follows the intent of this sutra, it means that the Bodhisattva who transmits the Dharma, by means of the true self in which self and non-self are non-dual, hears the dharma-gate in which the ultimate and the conventional are unimpeded.
"At one time" (ekasmin samaye) refers to the perfection of time.
"Time" is also a temporal division established conventionally in accordance with the world.
"One" serves to distinguish it from other times; although there are immeasurable occasions when the Tathāgata preached the sūtras, they cannot all be enumerated exhaustively.
To briefly summarize the meaning of "one time" (*ekasmin samaye*): it refers to the auspicious occasion when the Dharma King inaugurated his reign.
"Buddha" signifies the one who has achieved mastery.
In the Sanskrit *buddha*, this is translated as "the Awakened One," referring to one who has perfected awakening for both self and others.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "That which is called 'awakening' refers to the essence of the mind being free from thought.
This state of being free from thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception."
"The single characteristic of the dharma-realm is precisely the Tathāgata’s equal dharma-body.
Thus, non-thought is designated as awakening, which possesses three meanings:
first, self-awakening, which is the realization that one's own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
Second is awakening others, awakening them to the fact that all dharmas are none other than suchness;

third is the perfection of awakening, wherein the principles for oneself and others are complete, which is termed "perfection. Thus, one should know that as long as there is thought, it cannot be called awakening.
The *Awakening of Faith* states: "All sentient beings are not called awakened because, from time immemorial, their thoughts have continued in succession, never being free from discursive thought.
It further states: "If there are sentient beings who can awaken to the state of no-thought, they are thereby oriented toward Buddha-wisdom."
This is the place where [the teaching] was accomplished: within the city of Laṅkā on the peak of Mount Malaya by the shore of the great ocean.
Because the true body (dharmakāya) is neither localized nor non-localized, it is explained next.
The phrase "the summit of Mount Māra on the shore of the great ocean" generally indicates the location where the teaching was given.
This mountain lies within the great ocean and is five hundred yojanas high; none can reach it except by means of supernormal power (*ṛddhi*).
"Lanka" refers specifically to the site where the teaching was delivered; here it is translated as "Difficult to Access.
The meaning is found in the previous title.
Regarding the term "Middle": the Buddha favored the Middle Way; his ascent to the heavens, his descent into the Middle Kingdom, and his passing away at midnight all symbolize the Middle Way.
Now, dwelling within the city, he expounds the Dharma of self-realization, which is the meaning of the Middle Way.
He is accompanied by a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas;
this refers to the perfection of the assembly.
The contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional primarily shatters the cycle of birth and death; this refers first to the listing of the śrāvakas.
The contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness primarily shatters [attachment to] nirvāṇa; this refers subsequently to the listing of the bodhisattvas.
When the two extremes are abandoned, the Middle Way manifests before one.
A great bhikṣu possesses five meanings:
first, the Terrifier of Māras; second, the Mendicant; third, the Destroyer of Evil; fourth, the One of Pure Livelihood; and fifth, the Monk by Name.
A "Mahāsattva" (Great Being) is fully termed *bodhisattva*.
*Bodhi* here means "awakening," which refers to the fruit of Buddhahood sought;
*sattva* here means "sentient being," which refers to the sentient beings to be transformed.
It further states: "These are sentient beings who seek bodhi.
"Together" means at one time and in one place.
This refers to the six meanings being perfectly accomplished and the three doubts being suddenly extinguished.
All those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas have already attained mastery and stand as the foremost;
this praises the virtues of the bodhisattvas.
"Mahā" means great.

The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness—these are the four sublime gateways that encompass all phenomena of both the mundane and supramundane realms.
The following section on the "Correct Teaching" fully elucidates this meaning.
"All have thoroughly attained mastery" means that all bodhisattvas have completely and ultimately mastered this Dharma without obstruction.

"Skillfully knowing that the objects of experience are manifestations of one's own mind" means that the realms of the triple world—both the environment and its inhabitants, as well as the states of delusion and enlightenment, birth and death—are solely manifestations of one's own mind.
The Bodhisattvas are skillfully able to understand this as it truly is, realizing that these objects are not obtained from the outside.

"Playing with the immeasurable powers of sovereign samādhi and supernormal faculties" refers to playing within what is manifested by one's own mind: the immeasurable sovereignty, liberations, samādhis, meditative attainments (*samāpatti*), six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*), and ten powers (*daśabala*).
It is asked: "What is meant by 'wandering in play' (youxi)?

It means that having already attained immeasurable mastery, being both spiritual and supernormal, one forgets the self and acts according to things; with no obstruction between self and other, there is joy everywhere—hence it is called 'wandering in play.'"

"Manifesting various forms according to the minds of sentient beings to subdue them through skillful means" means that, following the minds of sentient beings—that is, within the objective realm manifested by one's own mind—since sentient beings differ, their mentalities and physical forms also vary; accordingly, [the Buddha] manifests in accordance with each type to subdue them through skillful means.

"Those whose heads are consecrated by the hands of all Buddhas" means that they have all reached the culmination of the ten stages (*bhūmi*) and received the empowerment of consecration; this refers to the dignity of their rank.

"They have all come to this assembly from various Buddha-lands, with Mahāmati Bodhisattva as their leader" means that he possesses great spiritual power and virtue, having come from a different region. Because this leading Bodhisattva is endowed with great wisdom, he is called Mahāmati.
The preceding section on the "Preface of Verified Faith through Superior Penetration and Illumination" is concluded.
At that time, the World-Honored One was preaching the Dharma in the palace of the Dragon King Sāgara until the passage "revealing this Dharma.
From here until the end of the chapter, there is a separate clarification of the "Preface of the Arousing of the Resolve."
"Bhagavān" (World-Honored One) refers to one who possesses the aforementioned nine titles, such as Tathāgata, and is thus honored by the world.
"Brahmā" refers to the Brahmā King of the Form Realm.
"Śakra" refers to Śakra-devendra, the lord of the Desire Realm.
"World-Protectors" refers to the Four Heavenly Kings.
"The various devas, nāgas, and so forth" refers to the eight classes of beings, including devas and nāgas.
"Tathāgata" signifies the meaning of the suchness (*tathatā*) of all phenomena.

The term "Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha" refers to *samyaksaṃbodhi*: the wisdom of the equality of one's own mind as it truly is (*yathābhūtajñāna*), which is the sublime contemplation of ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*).
"Equal enlightenment" (*samyaksaṃbodhi*) refers to the wisdom of the measure of one's own mind as it appears (*yāvadbhāvajñāna*), which universally contemplates conventional truth (*saṃvṛtisatya*).

This is what is meant by saying that the Buddhas, the ancestral Buddhas, through their own single thought-moment alone, illuminate the ultimate truth and penetrate the conventional world to achieve unsurpassed enlightenment; therefore, it is said: "In the past, all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas..."
The remaining meanings may be understood from the text as they appear.
At that time, the Yakṣa King Rāvaṇa obtained great benefit throughout the long night.
It is said that the Yakṣa King, through the Buddha’s spiritual power, saw that the waves of the ocean could not manifest images.
Observe this assembly: the Tathāgatagarbha, the consciousness-receptacle, and the ocean of the nature of True Suchness (tathatā) are likewise.
Stirred by the winds of the realm of ignorance, the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise, such that its boundless virtuous functions cannot manifest.
Immediately giving rise to a heart of joy, you should go to invite the Buddha to enter this city and proclaim this matter;

thereby causing the winds of ignorance to cease for all sentient beings, the waves of consciousness to no longer arise, and the ocean of the mind to become clear and still, so that there is no virtue that does not manifest.
Having spoken these words, he immediately went with his retinue to the center and praised the Buddha with this verse:
"The Dharma-treasury of the mind's own nature is selfless and free from the defilement of views."
"Come, with one-pointed mind, listen to the Dharma.
The great blue indra-ratna contains the images of all things, manifesting them in response to whatever is confronted.
All the musical instruments held by these yakṣas and others are made of this very jewel.
Furthermore, they were interspersed with various jewels such as lapis lazuli, wrapped in priceless upper garments;
their sounds were exquisite and their rhythms harmonized in perfect accord.
Within this, three verses are spoken in praise of the Buddha; the first verse consists of three lines which specifically praise the true mind’s own nature as realized—the treasury of all dharmas.

Because it has been fully endowed with immeasurable intrinsic merits since the very beginning, it is free from the dualistic grasping of self and devoid of the defilements of the five views; only a Buddha and a Buddha can realize and know it.

The second section consists of one verse praising and requesting the Buddha to enter the city. The first three lines praise the three bodies (*trikāya*) respectively, while the fourth line constitutes the formal request.
The third section consists of one verse stating that in the past, Buddhas and Bodhisattvas all resided in this city; the World-Honored One should likewise do so, and we pray to hear the Dharma.
At that time, Rāvaṇa, King of Laṅkā, again spoke in verse with a melodic voice:
“World-Honored One, you have dwelt for seven days within the waters of the ocean of Magadha; I pray only that you will compassionately accept me.”

At that time, King Rāvaṇa first praised and invited the Buddha with musical sounds, and now again invites the Buddha by speaking verses in song; this shows that the expression of emotion is the same whether one is sentient or insentient.

Addressing the Buddha by name, he said, "I am Rāvaṇa, the Ten-headed King of Rākṣasas. This refers to the King of Rākṣasas, who represents the sovereign lord of fundamental ignorance within all sentient beings.
The ten heads represent the sharp and dull faculties and the ten afflictions (*anuśaya*); arising from ignorance, they are the foremost of all worldly defilements and afflictions.
"May the Buddha accept me; may he likewise accept all sentient beings, my palaces, my court ladies, and even those who serve my person"—this and more are as clearly explained in the sutra itself.
The general meaning is that it expresses the ability to realize that the true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature.
Since all internal and external defilements and afflictions naturally accord with the perfect and universal awakening of the Tathāgata, it is said that they "serve and receive."
Regarding the terms *dautaka* and *yūṣarata*, I have not seen their correct translations.
*Mahāyāna* is translated here as "Great Vehicle" (*Dacheng*).
At that time, having heard these words and after they had been spoken, the World-Honored One remained silent.
The Buddha spoke to the Yakṣa King, and having consented to accept his invitation, he remained silent.
Then King Rāvaṇa, by means of the wondrous Flower Palace upon which he rode, arrived at the most profound Dharma.
After the Buddha and the various Bodhisattvas had accepted the offerings, they each briefly expounded the essential points of the profound Dharma.
At that time, King Rāvaṇa and his retinue arrived and made this request:
"I now entreat the Great Being to inquire of the World-Honored One regarding all manner of faults."

That king again made offerings to Mahāmati Bodhisattva and requested him on our behalf and for all bodhisattvas to inquire of the Tathāgata regarding the Dharma of the self-realized wisdom, which is free from all faults and leads to entry into the stage of Buddha-wisdom.
At that time, the World-Honored One, by means of his supernormal powers, reached [the mountain] and then vanished from view within the air.

It is said that the Tathāgata, by means of his supernormal powers, again manifested within that mountain the aforementioned infinite, multilayered realms of both the environment and its inhabitants, until finally vanishing from view within the air.

Just as in the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, when Maitreya snapped his fingers, the gates of the pavilion opened; once Sudhana had entered, he saw within that grandly adorned great pavilion countless hundreds of thousands of pavilions, and their vast adornments were likewise so.
Within those inexhaustible hundreds of thousands of towers, each one contained further inexhaustible hundreds of thousands of towers.
Before each tower stood a Maitreya Bodhisattva; before each Maitreya Bodhisattva stood a Sudhana youth; and each Sudhana youth stood with palms joined in reverence before Maitreya.
Even until he arose from samādhi, [the other] suddenly vanished.
These two instances both symbolize the Dharma-realm that transcends the emotions, is free from views, and is vast, sovereign, and unobstructed.

Thus, the Buddhas and sentient beings interpenetrate; pure lands and defiled lands are harmoniously integrated; every phenomenon adorns one another; and every atom universally contains the entire Dharma-realm. They enter into and identify with one another in infinite layers, enabling those who practice awakening to realize and enter the perfect clarity of enlightenment.
King Rāvaṇa saw only himself, from [the moment he thought] up until: "Is it like a whirling wheel of fire or a flame?
Since all phenomena had vanished, King Laṅkā saw only his own body dwelling within his original palace; this clarifies that he did not depart from his current location.
Having engaged in such reflection, one immediately gives rise to investigation and analysis.
One observes all phenomena with discernment: who speaks and who listens?
What kind of thing is this?
Seeking the characteristics of all phenomena, they are found to be utterly unobtainable.
Furthermore, one should reflect that by not giving rise to conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena, one is then able to see.
Again, he further contemplated, observing with right mindfulness, and attained the vision of reality as it is.
He thoroughly understood the nature of all phenomena: there is no agent and no object; there is neither seeing nor hearing. This is called true vision.
At that time, King Laṅkā immediately attained awakening and entered the Tathāgatagarbha, proceeding toward the stage of Buddhahood.

This clarifies that the Yakṣa king, through correct contemplation (*yathābhūta-parīkṣā*), immediately attained awakening, realizing that [all things] are merely one's own mind and abiding in non-conceptual wisdom (*nirvikalpa-jñāna*).

What is called "attaining seeing according to reality and not awakening through another" means that although there are many divergent paths regarding delusion and awakening, there is no separate dharma. When deluded, one takes the objects of the environment to be external things; when awakened, one realizes that the environment is none other than the mind.
Awakening means realizing one's delusion; it does not mean there is a separate awakening that comes from without, which is why it is said, "one does not awaken following another.

To be able to use one’s own wisdom to skillfully observe, thereby forever leaving behind conjecture and false interpretations, means that as for the principle, one awakens suddenly, and upon awakening, [all obstructions] are simultaneously eliminated. If one forms a conceptualized conviction (*adhimukti*), one falls among the various heterodoxies; only by observing with skillful wisdom is there no mind of conceptualized conviction.

Regarding "skillfully attaining mastery over expedient means and knowing the characteristics of progressive advancement through the various stages": this means that once one has realized reality as it is, and further masters skillful expedient means, then from beginning to end throughout the various stages, there will never be any trace of deviousness or deviation.
Therefore, one should delight in distancing oneself from the deluded visions of the mind and consciousness, proceeding directly toward the stage of Buddhahood.
The meaning of the three continuities will be explained extensively below.
Having heard [this] in the midst of space and within the palaces, up until the words: "One should thus perceive all phenomena."
When it was said that the Yakṣa King had attained awakening, the palaces in the void praised and approved this, saying: "One should train in this way; one should view things in this way.
To say "in this way" is a term that accords with reality as it truly is.
This is because he grants that this learning and this view are both in accordance with reality.
The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, perceive all phenomena in exactly the same way.
Previously, the realm of transformation was used as the basis for preaching the Dharma; why, then, is the palace now used as the basis for praise and approval?
Is it not that when one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the palaces and halls of empty space naturally vanish?
How could the phenomenal world of form and emptiness, along with the environment and its inhabitants, remain as they are within the single Dharma-realm? Indeed, they cannot.
"If one holds divergent views, this constitutes the view of nihilism; furthermore, one should not abide even within the six concentrations and so forth.
This clarifies various exhortations to abandon divergent views.
If one holds a view different from this, it is the view of annihilationism;
that is to say, if one deviates from this vision of reality as it is, it constitutes the view of nihilism.

When it says, "You should forever distance yourself from mind (*citta*), intellect (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), and should diligently observe all phenomena," it refers to the Dharma realized within oneself, which is not the domain of mind, intellect, or consciousness; therefore, you should remain far removed from them.
"One who diligently observes" should observe the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) in accordance with reason.
"One who should practice internal cultivation" should engage in secret application and hidden practice.
"Do not be attached to external views" refers to the realms and meanings of the two vehicles and non-Buddhists mentioned below.

Those who hold the various views of the Vedas are the non-Buddhist Brahmins; they revere the four Vedic scriptures spoken by Brahmā, which comprise approximately one hundred thousand verses and are transmitted entirely through oral tradition, not written upon skins or shells.

"Nor should one dwell in the six meditative absorptions (*ṣaḍ-samāpatti*) and so forth" refers to the various speculative views of non-Buddhists, such as the meditative absorptions that suppress afflictions through the six modes of practice involving delight and aversion.

For example, there is a certain non-Buddhist who considers the single realm of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñika*) in the fourth dhyāna to be *nirvāṇa*. He cultivates the attainment of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-samāpatti*) within the desire realm, regarding the lower three dhyānas and the desire realm as suffering, coarse, and obstructive, while regarding the higher non-conceptual heaven as pure, subtle, and detached. Consequently, he attains the lower three dhyānas and the desire realm, wherein his afflictions are suppressed and do not manifest.

Upon the end of life, one is immediately reborn in the fruition of non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñi-vedanīya*), remaining there for five hundred kalpas; thereafter, one falls back and wanders through the cycle of birth and death.
One should not abide in any of these six types of "wrong concentrations" that suppress afflictions through such practices.
"If one can act in this way, it means that one has reached the emptiness of intrinsic nature (*prakṛti-śūnyatā*) as it truly is, free from distracted thoughts and conceptual discrimination.

This means that only by not clinging to the views of the two vehicles or non-Buddhists can one practice according to reality, destroy the evil views of other doctrines, and abandon the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*).
"One who is able to transform the consciousness that is the basis by means of wondrous wisdom" refers to the transformation of the eight consciousnesses into the four wisdoms.
"Entering the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization" means attaining and realizing the same as all Buddhas.
Regarding "one who has skillfully cultivated samādhi and samāpatti": *samādhi* here is translated as "right concentration" (*zhèngdìng*) and also as "right reception" (*zhèngshòu*).
It is called "right concentration" because it is undisturbed, capable of receiving all dharmas, and because it purely maintains discernment.
Furthermore, because there is no object that can be moved, it is called "right concentration" (samyaksamādhi);
because there is no thing that can be received, it is called "right reception" (samyaksamāpatti).
*Samāpatti* is translated here as "equilibrium-attainment" (*dengzhi*).

Because right concentration can give rise to right wisdom, and because it brings all phenomena into a state of meditative equipoise (samādhi) to reach the supreme stage, this dharma should be well-cultivated.

Non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to the view of self and possess the characteristic of a self; furthermore, those who grasp at real *guṇas*—here translated as "functional capacity"—cling to the characteristic of a self and to the four great elements, the aggregates, the elements, and the sense bases as having real functional capacity.
They grasp at and cling to forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles, and mental objects.

Furthermore, those of the two vehicles perceive the twelve links of dependent origination as having real existence; failing to understand their empty nature, they give rise to confused thoughts and conceptual discriminations therein.
Therefore, I exhort you not to give rise to the attachments of external paths or the deluded imaginings of the two vehicles.
"O King of Laṅkā!
When this Dharma is as supreme as it is, and one reflects upon it in this way, that is truly seeing the Buddha."
"What is this so-called 'Dharma'?
It is the abiding of one's own mind in the non-conceptual Dharma.
Only through a sublime and not dull or inferior state can the noble wisdom of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) be accomplished."

Regarding "receiving a superior and wondrous birth among all states of existence," this means that one who is able to realize this sublime Dharma will necessarily receive birth in a superior grade among all states of existence, rather than proceeding toward inferior ones.

Regarding the so-called "shattering the cataracts of ignorance and extinguishing the waves of consciousness": ignorance can obstruct the eye of wisdom, while the waves of karmic consciousness can stir the source of the mind; this Mahāyāna practice is capable of shattering and extinguishing them.

Regarding the two meanings of the nature of consciousness: because non-Buddhists are attached to the view of a self, they are unable to expound within their heterodox doctrines the dharma of the nature of consciousness that is free from such views; thus, it is not the correct meaning of the Dharma.
"Since you previously saw the Buddha and contemplated in this manner, O Yakṣa King, your ability to contemplate this meaning according to reality is indeed the true vision of the Buddha."

The Buddha, knowing that the sentient beings were ready to awaken to the profound Dharma, again manifested his body so that the transformative activities remained as they were, no different from before; these pervaded all things, inexhaustible and infinitely layered.

At that time, King Daśaśīrṣa saw his own body appearing before all the Buddhas; surrounded by yakṣas of great wisdom, he preached the Dharma realized through the noble wisdom of self-awakening, and he also beheld all the Buddha-fields.
Such matters as these were no different from those previously mentioned.

Regarding the statement that the wisdom-eye (prajñā-cakṣus) is not the fleshly eye: because the fleshly eye is obstructed and lacks penetration, it cannot observe universally; therefore, one observes with the wisdom-eye.

Regarding the fact that from each and every pore of the *de* syllable located between his eyebrows, on his thighs, flanks, waist, neck, shoulders, and arms, light is emitted: whenever a Tathāgata emits light, it invariably signifies a Dharma; it is not done in vain.

Now, in this assembly, light is emitted simultaneously from the space between the eyebrows and seven other locations; does this not signify that within the perfect, luminous Middle Way—one which is free from the imagined and dependent natures—all virtues are fully accomplished?

At that time, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas in the void, seeing from afar the Tathāgata seated upon the summit of Mount Laṅkā, which was like the Wondrous High Mountain (Sumeru), laughed with great joy.
This laughter was not without cause.
At that time, the bodhisattvas and the assembly of devas, having arrived at the sight of Rāvaṇa, contemplated the Dharma as it truly is.
Then, the bodhisattvas and the assembly of devas all wondered: "For what cause and condition does the Tathāgata smile with such joy?"
His body emitted radiance, and he entered the bliss of samādhi.
Turning his gaze around, he looked at the Yakṣa King, suspecting that there must be a reason for this.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [said]: "...and none of the various non-Buddhists can fathom it."
Mahāmati, knowing the thoughts of the assembly of bodhisattvas and observing the delusions and attachments of all future sentient beings, asked the Buddha in order to sever their doubts.
The Buddha sighed in admiration, saying, "Excellent!
For the benefit of yourself and others, you have been able to raise this question.
O Yakṣa King, you once asked these two points of meaning from the Buddhas of the past; you wish to ask them now as well, and you shall do so in the future as well."
It is something that cannot be fathomed by those of the Two Vehicles or the non-Buddhists.
Since you have already asked once, you wish to ask again now, and will do so in the future as well.
Regarding these two points, is it truly the case that you do not know?
At that time, the Tathāgata knew that King Laṅkā was someone whom even the gods such as Brahmā and Śakra had never before seen.
Knowing that King Laṅkā wished to pose questions, the Tathāgata told him to ask quickly, desiring to explain [the teachings] so as to fulfill his aspiration.
"Skillfully knowing all the stages" refers to knowing the first stage, up through the Immovable, the Good Intelligence, the Cloud of Dharma, and the Buddha-stage.
"Cultivating remedies and realizing the true meaning" means applying effort and practice within these stages to remedy the obstacles to be countered, thereby avoiding wrong paths.

Regarding "in the palace of the great jewel lotus, the water of samādhi is poured upon his crown": this means that his practice is identical to that of the Buddha; as a prince of the Dharma, he enters the stage of consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
The Buddha further instructed him to give rise to both a single practice of equanimity and immeasurable differentiated practices; he shall certainly attain the realms described above.
These can only be personally realized by you, King of Laṅkā, and cannot be seen by those of the two vehicles, non-Buddhists, Śakra, or Brahmā.
At that time, having received the Buddha’s permission, the King of Laṅkā approached him, saying, "You should question me; I shall explain it for you.

Thus, having been granted leave, the King of Laṅkā immediately prepared his ornaments and offerings—namely, various flowers, incense, banners, streamers, canopies, and necklaces—and adorned himself with these various articles.
The *xiǎn* (canopy) belongs to the category of curtains.

Furthermore, he transformed all musical instruments belonging to the desire realm, as well as those found in the Buddha-fields of the world—including those of the devas, nāgas, and others—to serve as offerings, thereby manifesting his reverence for the Dharma.
Furthermore, various offerings rained down from the midst of the void as they descended from the sky, manifesting his humility and reverence in requesting the Dharma.
When he says, "The Tathāgatas of the past have already taught this for me," he clarifies that the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time share one and the same Dharma.
World-Honored One!

Regarding the two meanings spoken by the manifested Tathāgata, which are not spoken by the fundamental Buddha—namely, that the retribution and manifestation bodies are not the true Buddha, nor are they the speakers of the Dharma—I therefore desire that the World-Honored One, as the fundamental Buddha, explain them for me.
The World-Honored One replied, "I shall explain two meanings for you.
Then the Yakṣa King further elaborated on various points, up to: "Such is the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*); how could it be abandoned?"
"This question correctly concerns the two meanings of the Tathāgata’s dharma and non-dharma: how can these be abandoned?
Previously, one made offerings with ornaments; why now does one adorn the body with ornaments?"
This indicates that he proceeded with the formal etiquette of inquiry, not daring to act with levity.
The remaining meanings are clear from the scriptural text itself.
At that time, the Buddha addressed the King of Laṅkā, saying:
Up to the point where it says, "The external dharmas have such immeasurable distinctions," this correctly answers the preceding question.

The Tathāgata first cited the three analogies of the impermanence of jars and the like, as well as the nature of flames and fire, and the production of sprouts from seeds, in order to clarify the characteristics of the distinction between dharma and adharma, making them easy to understand.
"The internal dharmas are likewise; that is to say, one should know that all conditioned phenomena arising from conditions are merely conceptualizations of characteristics.
This passage cites three internal dharmas to correspond with the preceding metaphors: taking ignorance as the condition corresponds to the metaphor of the jar;
and taking the various consciousnesses [as the condition] corresponds to the metaphor of the nature of fire.
Through the cultivation of contemplative practice, this accords with the analogy of the seed.

However, while a jar takes "fabrication" as its defining characteristic, through the condition of ignorance, it is able to fabricate the various differences among the sense faculties, the body, and the objective world.
Fire takes "transforming through熏 (perfuming)" as its meaning; by means of the various consciousnesses, it is able to perfumingly transform all the distinctions among defiled and pure phenomena.
Seeds take "arising" as their meaning; through the cultivation of contemplative practice, one's own wisdom arises, and one likewise perceives the characteristics of these distinctions.
Such are the teachings and their metaphors; each has its own purpose.
These three dharmas collectively clarify two meanings, for they are all characterized by conceptual differentiation.
"O King of Laṅkā!"
"What is this Dharma?"—as for that which you previously asked, I have already finished explaining it.
The above constitutes the correct response regarding the two meanings of "Dharma" and "non-Dharma," as clarified by the sutra itself.
The *Vajracchedikā-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra-ṭīkā* by Asaṅga states: "Even dharmas should be relinquished because they arise as real characteristics;
how much more so non-dharmas, for it is logically untenable."
They likewise shatter all views of existence and non-existence, causing one to personally realize and enter [the truth].
It is like a great fragrant elephant that breaks its tethering chains and departs with sovereign ease.
Regarding *vipaśyanā*, this is translated as "contemplation" (*guān*); whenever contemplation is undertaken, it must necessarily be practiced in conjunction with tranquility (*śamatha*).

As for tranquility, its Sanskrit term is *śamatha*. While the interpretations of its meaning differ across the various partial and complete teachings, the general sense is that when a single thought accords with principle, gathering distraction back into stillness, it is called "tranquility"; when there is stillness yet constant illumination, it is called "contemplation."
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* combines these two practices into a single gate, such that they mutually support and complete one another without being separated.
If calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) do not coexist, then there will be no way to enter the path to bodhi.

The *Saṃdhinirmocana Sūtra* states: "Sentient beings are bound by signs (*nimitta*) and further bound by coarse heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*); only by diligently cultivating calm abiding (*śamatha*) and insight (*vipaśyanā*) can they attain liberation."
Therefore, Tiantai takes the compassion of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to guide the actions of body, speech, and mind, as well as his vows, constituting the "Practice of Peaceful Bliss.
In all these cases, *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* serve as the means of cultivation (*nispādaka*), while the myriad virtues constitute that which is cultivated (*niṣpādya*).
The *Saṃdhinirmocana*, *Śūraṅgama*, and *Nirvāṇa* sūtras, as well as the *Yogācārabhūmi*, *Mahāyānaśraddhotpāda*, and *Śamathavipaśyanā* śāstras, extensively elucidate its meaning.

“Lokagarbharāja! As for your statement that you have taken the Tathāgatagarbha as your object of perception throughout the past,” the Tathāgata further addressed the Yakṣa King to refute various false conceptualizations, causing him to abandon discursive thought and attain quiescence, thereby giving rise to right view.
"O King of Laṅkā, you say that you have already asked about this matter in the presence of past Tathāgatas, and those Tathāgatas have already explained it to you."
As for your statement that the past is merely conceptual construction and the future is likewise, I am in agreement with you.

Regarding the fact that those Buddha-dharmas are all free from conceptual construction, even for the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain peace and happiness—this clarifies that there is no distinction among the three periods of past, present, and future.

The Tathāgata takes wisdom as his body; he cannot be differentiated by means of the marks of self, person, or sentient being, and so forth. To be free from the differentiation of subject and object—that is, the non-differentiation of the three: mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—is what is meant.
For example, just as sentient beings depicted on a wall have no consciousness or perception, so too are the sentient beings of the world.
There is neither karma nor retribution; all phenomena are likewise thus.
"There is no hearing and no speaking"—this first presents a metaphor, which is subsequently applied to the Dharma.
Furthermore, it says:

"For example, suppose there is a person who sees their own reflection in water or a mirror, sees a shadow in the moonlight or a lamp, or hears an echo in a mountain valley; these all serve as metaphors for sentient beings who, by means of their own minds, grasp at their own minds, giving rise to attachments to material forms within that which is formless."
The same applies to the discrimination between the Dharma and non-Dharma.

If one realizes that these are illusory and brings about a single condition of quiescent extinction, giving rise to self-attesting wisdom that transcends both "is" and "is not," then one unites with the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind of the Tathāgatagarbha as one's object of perception.
How true it is!
Although this chapter is titled "The Introduction to the True Doctrine," it is capable of enabling one to comprehend fundamental ignorance and enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
Chapter Two: Questions and Answers (1–2) *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Chapter Two: Questions and Answers In order to explain this chapter, I shall briefly introduce five sections:

This section consists of five parts: first, the purpose of its introduction; second, the fundamental tenets; third, the resolution of difficulties and objections; fourth, the explanation of the title; and fifth, the commentary on the text.

Regarding the first, the purpose of its introduction: since the introductory section of the preceding chapter has already clarified the causal conditions, it is appropriate for the main body of the teaching to be revealed; therefore, this chapter follows.
Second, regarding the clarification of the fundamental tenets: it means that all sutras each have their own specific tenet.
Therefore, the former masters said:
"In receiving the words, one must understand the tenet."
Now, I shall separately clarify the essential tenets of this sutra.
As for the statement in the "Lower Section" that "all dharmas are unarisen, and one should not establish this as a thesis," these words are intended merely to dispel attachments.
If there is a thesis that is itself without a thesis, then both the thesis and its exposition will be fully elucidated.
The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "There is a dharma capable of giving rise to the faculty of faith in the Mahāyāna; therefore, it should be explained."
"What is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings.
This mind encompasses all mundane and supramundane dharmas; based upon this mind, the meaning of the Mahāyāna is revealed."
Why is this? Because the aspect of the suchness of this mind is the very essence of the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, the aspect of the causes and conditions for the arising and ceasing of this mind can demonstrate the essential nature, characteristics, and functions of the Mahāyāna; it is that upon which all Buddhas have fundamentally ridden, and by means of this Dharma, all Bodhisattvas reach the stage of the Tathāgata.

Therefore, one should know that this self-nature pure, perfectly luminous, and true essence possesses inconceivable virtues and functions, which are primordially complete; it is the fundamental vehicle upon which all Buddhas and sentient beings have always relied.
Furthermore, all beings—whether ordinary or noble—ride upon this Dharma to reach the stage of the Tathāgata; thus, it is their destination.
It is only because sentient beings do not themselves understand how to accord with and enter into it, being defiled by various false imaginings, that they remain muddled and inferior.
Third, resolving the objection:
It is asked,
"Since the Sanskrit original is one and the same, why do the chapter titles translated by the three masters differ in number?"
The answer is:
Tiantai said, "As for 'chapters' (pin), they were either proclaimed by the Buddha himself, arranged by the compilers of the canon, or added through interpretive translation.
He further stated, "In dividing the scriptures into sections and passages, these are all the 'orchids and chrysanthemums' of former sages, each excelling in its own beauty."
Those born later should not engage in disputes or contention; such actions provide no threefold benefit and cause one to lose the single path.
The "threefold benefit" refers to the three *siddhāntas*, beginning with the worldly (*loka*).
The "single path" refers to the *paramārtha-siddhānta*.
Therefore, one should know that whether chapters are combined or separated—whether there is one or many—it is all for the sake of skillful means (*upāya*).

Regarding the fourth point, the explanation of the chapter titles: this opening chapter of the main body of the scripture constitutes the general inquiry and response concerning the overall structure of the entire sutra.

From the initial "Chapter on the Various Consciousnesses" in the *Sarvadharmasamuccaya-parivarta* down to the prohibition against eating meat, there are fourteen chapters in total; these are termed the "Separate Questions and Answers.
This means that Mahāmati first posed one hundred and eight questions, grouped together as a single summary, to inquire collectively of the Tathāgata;
the Tathāgata then addressed each of these inquiries in turn, answering them clause by clause.

Regarding what are called the "sentences of arising" and the "sentences of non-arising," the "sentence of permanence" and the "sentence of impermanence," and so forth up to one hundred and eight sentences—all are answered with the character "non-. This is intended to cause them to abandon discursive thought and enter the gate of the True Suchness of the mind; therefore, it is titled the "Chapter on Questions and Answers."
The following section of the sutra text constitutes the formal commentary.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati approached, bowed with reverence, and spoke in verse:
*Mati*—which here translates as "wisdom."
"To speak of baring the right shoulder and placing the right knee on the ground refers to the ritual of the Western Regions, signifying the bearing of the Buddha-dharma upon one's shoulders.
'The world is free from arising and ceasing, like flowers in the sky; wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.'"
The following eight verses generally extol the virtues of the Buddha.
Regarding the term "the world," it refers to the world of sentient beings.
These verses praise the Buddha for his realization that sentient beings are illusory, like flowers in the sky; therefore, they neither arise nor cease.
That is to say, when the Tathāgata observes with right gnosis, he finds no such sentient being to be either existent or non-existent; therefore, his objectless great compassion arises spontaneously.
If one were to conceive of sentient beings as existing and thereby give rise to compassion, it would be called "compassion born of attachment and views."
"All phenomena are like illusions, far removed from mind and consciousness.
Wisdom perceives neither existence nor non-existence, yet it gives rise to the heart of great compassion.
"All phenomena" refers to the world of the five aggregates.
This refers to all phenomena, namely the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Since phenomena are like illusions, even the mind and consciousness perish; this praises the Tathāgata’s contemplation of phenomena as being like illusions, thereby giving rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
“The world is ever like a dream, far removed from annihilation and permanence; wisdom finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet it gives rise to great compassion.
This summarizes the statement regarding the world of sentient beings and the physical vessel-world.
To falsely conceptualize that form exists, and to claim that the destruction of form is annihilation;
or to falsely conceptualize that consciousness exists, and to claim that consciousness undergoing further rebirth is permanence—
these are what the Buddha knows to be like things seen in a dream, wherein there is neither form nor consciousness upon which one can base such conceptualizations of annihilation or permanence.
This praises the Tathāgata for realizing that the two views are like a dream, thereby perfecting great compassion:
"Knowing that persons and phenomena lack self, and that afflictions and the objects of cognition are eternally pure and signless,
he gives rise to the mind of great compassion."
"Defilements" (kleśa) refer to the obstacle of afflictions (kleśāvaraṇa).
"Knowables" (jñeya) refer to the obstacle to the known (jñeyāvaraṇa).
Through the grasping at a self and phenomena, these two obstacles arise together.
If one realizes the two kinds of emptiness, the obstacles are fundamentally non-existent.
This praises the Tathāgata for attaining the two kinds of emptiness—of persons and phenomena—and for purifying the two obstacles to thereby perfect great compassion.
Question:
Since both person and phenomena are empty and quiescent, and the two obstacles have been fundamentally non-existent from the beginning,
why does the Tathāgata give rise to great compassion?
Answer:
Because sentient beings do not know this principle, they are deluded, inverted, and wander through saṃsāra without end.
To now cause sentient beings to awaken to and enter this Dharma is what constitutes the true arousal of great compassion.
Therefore, the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa* says: "One should preach such a Dharma for the sake of sentient beings.
This is true compassion.
"The Buddha does not abide in nirvāṇa, nor does nirvāṇa abide in the Buddha; they are far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened, whether existent or non-existent."
He speaks of nirvāṇa in contrast to birth and death, and speaks of the Buddha in contrast to sentient beings.
Because the Buddha knows that birth and death are like dreams and lack substantiality, he does not abide in nirvāṇa.
Because he knows that sentient beings are like flowers in the sky and are unreal, he does not abide in Buddhahood.

It is like this: when there is illness, one prescribes medicine; when there is no illness, one cannot prescribe medicine. Therefore it is said: "The Buddha does not abide in nirvana, and nirvana does not abide in the Buddha.
Because there is no Buddha, there is no one who can awaken; because there is no nirvana, there is nothing to be awakened to.

Whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, whether there is nirvana or no nirvana—even all dualistic views such as existence and non-existence—are entirely transcended; therefore, it is said that one is "far removed from the awakened and the object of awakening, whether existent or non-existent."
“The Dharmakāya is like an illusion or a dream; how can it be praised?
Only by knowing that it is without intrinsic nature and without arising does one truly praise the Buddha.

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: “All dharmas are devoid of intrinsic nature. Because they lack intrinsic nature, they are empty; because they are empty, they are signless; because they are signless, they are wishless; because they are wishless, they are unarisen; because they are unarisen, they are unceasing. Therefore, all dharmas are from the beginning quiescent and their self-nature is nirvāṇa, whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, for the nature of dharmas is ever thus.”

3. Chapter on the Collection of All Dharmas (2–5) 1. Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Chapter Three: The Collection of All Dharmas. This chapter is explained through four sections:
first, the purpose; second, the resolution of difficulties; third, the explanation of the title; and fourth, the explanation of the text.

Regarding the intent of this initial section: while the preceding chapter (the "Superior Chapter") concluded with general questions and answers, all subsequent chapters consist of specific questions and answers; therefore, this follows in sequence.
Second, to resolve potential difficulties:
since the one hundred and eight phrases have already been explained in general, why are they each addressed individually in the subsequent chapters?
If the meaning of the words does not go beyond the general [principle], is this not redundant?
Answer:
Only when the general and the specific mutually encompass one another can the views of annihilationism and eternalism be eliminated.
When the ultimate and the conventional are perfectly integrated, the sentiments of rejection and acceptance finally cease.

Regarding the third point, the explanation of the names: the treatise relies on the one mind to open two gates. The preceding chapter has already clarified the gate of the True Suchness of Mind, which universally subsumes all phenomena;
this chapter clarifies the gate of the Arising and Ceasing of Mind, which universally subsumes all phenomena and gives rise to all phenomena, because these two gates are not mutually exclusive.
The treatise states: "Regarding the arising and ceasing of the mind: because it relies upon the *tathāgatagarbha*, there is a mind that arises and ceases.
That which is called the non-arising and non-ceasing [nature] in conjunction with arising and ceasing—neither identical nor different—is termed the *ālayavijñāna*."
This consciousness has two meanings, by which it can encompass all phenomena and give rise to all phenomena.
What are these two meanings?
First, the meaning of awakening; [the second is the meaning of discernment].
Second is the meaning of non-enlightenment (*abodha*).
As for the meaning of enlightenment (*bodha*), it refers to the essence of mind being free from thought.

This state of being free from the marks of thought is equal to the realm of empty space, pervading everywhere without exception; it is the single mark of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), which is the Tathāgata’s equal Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). Based on this Dharma-body, it is termed "original enlightenment" (*mūlabodhi*); and based upon original enlightenment, there exists non-enlightenment.
Thus, one drifts up and down in the sea of suffering through the three subtleties and six coarsenesses.

It is said that there is "initial awakening" (shijue) because of non-awakening; furthermore, it is called "ultimate awakening" (jiujing jue) because one awakens to the source of the mind, whereas it is not ultimate awakening because one does not awaken to the source of the mind.
Therefore, within the ten dharma realms—whether saintly or ordinary, whether cause or fruit, whether the environment or the body, and whether defiled or pure—all are subsumed herein!
Hence, it is titled the "Chapter on the Collection of All Dharmas."
