Because all phenomena arise from conceptual construction and lack intrinsic nature, they transcend verbal expression."
"What is the Great Emptiness of the Ultimate Noble Wisdom?

It is called the Great Emptiness of the Ultimate Noble Wisdom because when the Tathāgata attains the ultimate reality of self-realized noble wisdom, all false conceptualizations, views, and habitual tendencies are entirely abandoned."
"What is mutual emptiness (itaretara-śūnyatā)?
It refers to the absence of 'that' within 'this'; this is called mutual emptiness.
This is termed the emptiness of mutual non-existence.
When that which is here is not there, and that which is there is not here, it is called "empty";
when that which is there is here, and that which is here is there, it is not called "empty.
For example, in the Sāḷha Hall, while elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep are absent, it is not the case that the assembly of bhikṣus is absent.

"Ruruka" is a personal name; his mother was the laywoman Viśākhā, who held the Triple Gem in deep reverence, constructed a vihāra, and established bhikṣus therein, wherein she kept no elephants, horses, or similar animals.
Because elephants and horses are absent, it is said to be empty. "Mahāmati!
This does not mean that the hall lacks the self-nature of a hall, nor does it mean that other places lack elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep."
"If a house and a bhikṣu exist, it is not called empty.
If there are elephants and horses elsewhere, one likewise does not say that the elephants and horses are empty. Mahāmati!"
"Among all dharmas, from their specific and general characteristics up to emptiness, emptiness is the coarsest; you should distance yourself from it.
By saying that this emptiness is the coarsest, it means it is not the true emptiness; therefore, he exhorts one to distance oneself from it.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
That which is 'non-arising' up to the removal of dwelling in samādhi is called non-arising.
This explains non-arising by stating that arising is refuted within the context of causes and conditions; therefore, it is said that things do not arise from themselves.
If one negates arising by asserting non-arising, this is not true non-arising.
Only when one has transcended the eighth stage and above, abiding in the illusion-like samādhi, is it called true non-arising.
“Mahāmati! That which lacks intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva) is so called because it is unarisen; this is what is meant by ‘lacking intrinsic nature.
It is said that all dharmas do not abide for even a single moment, and because they arise with distinct characteristics, they are called lacking intrinsic nature.”
"What is meant by 'the absence of dual characteristics'? Mahāmati!
Just as light and shadow exist only in mutual dependence and cannot be established in isolation, so it is with all things."
He said: "For example, like light and shadow, long and short, black and white—since these all exist only in mutual dependence and lack substantial reality, they cannot be said to be two.
Mahāmati!..."
"It is not that there is a nirvana existing outside of saṃsāra; rather, it is the signless state of selflessness that you should diligently study.
This means that when one realizes that the nature of deluded thoughts is empty, saṃsāra itself becomes nirvana;
whereas if one is deluded regarding the existence of true reality, nirvana itself becomes saṃsāra.
Just as birth-and-death and nirvāṇa are non-dual, so it is for all phenomena by analogy.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I have always taught the Dharma of emptiness, Which is far removed from the extremes of annihilation and permanence. Birth-and-death is like an illusion or a dream, Yet karma is not destroyed."
He said: "The true principle is that birth and death are truly empty, like illusions and dreams.
However, for those who do not attain the understanding of illusions and dreams, the various karmas of birth and death cannot be destroyed."
"Space and nirvāṇa—the cessation of these two is likewise so; the foolish falsely discriminate, while the noble ones are free from existence and non-existence.
By citing the emptiness of the three unconditioned phenomena above, one cannot speak of saṃsāra in contrast to nirvāṇa, nor can one speak of nirvāṇa in contrast to saṃsāra.
Because of the false imaginings of fools, it is said to be dual; because the bodies of the noble ones penetrate and realize reality, they are free from existence and non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying, up to: "All of these are this very meaning."
"The meaning of emptiness and so forth enters universally into all sūtras; there is not a single dharma that does not contain this principle.
Mahāmati! All the sūtras lead one to conceive the notion of water where, in reality, there is no water."
This refers to the convergence of provisional means (*upāya*) back into the ultimate reality (*tattva*).

As for why certain sutras do not speak of emptiness (*śūnyatā*) or non-arising (*anutpāda*), it is because the aspirations of sentient beings are not uniform; therefore, the Tathāgata, in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, provides various different teachings. However, the true reality lies in the awakening of the mind, not in words and phrases.

For example, when a herd of deer is driven by thirst, they perceive a springtime mirage and conceive the idea that it is water; deluded and frantic, they rush toward it, yet that mirage is not actually water.
"What is taught in the various sūtras is likewise thus: one should accord with the meaning and not cling to the words.
This exhorts reliance on the actual meaning rather than attachment to verbal expression.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [said]: "It is like a priceless jewel within a soiled garment.

The *Tathāgatagarbha Sūtra* also says: "Within the various afflictions of greed, hatred, and delusion of all sentient beings, there exists the body of the Tathāgata, eternally unstained and fully endowed with the marks of virtue, no different from my own."
“If non-Buddhists teach that the self is eternal and the agent, does this not make the Tathāgata’s self identical to the self of the non-Buddhists?

This objection challenges the Tathāgata: if he asserts the meaning of the *tathāgatagarbha*, it contradicts the previous teaching that all *sūtras* should speak of emptiness, and would thus be identical to the non-Buddhist teaching of a divine self (*ātman*).
However, their conception of the self has three aspects:
first, its essence is eternal and it is designated as the agent;
second, although it resides within the five aggregates, it is distinct from the guṇas (qualities).
"Third, although it traverses all realms of existence, it is in reality neither born nor extinguished.
Now, when you speak of the meaning of the 'store' (ālaya), is this not the same as the 'self' (ātman) of the non-Buddhists?
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! When I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, it should not be clung to as a self.
What the Tathāgata speaks of is not the same as the *ātman* (self) of the non-Buddhists."
The non-Buddhists speak of a self, likening it to a sesame seed, a grain of wheat, or a thumb, thereby establishing fixed characteristics for it.
The Buddha speaks of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is sometimes called emptiness, sometimes called the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), and even the wishless (apraṇihita).
This is thus of a single essence, yet its names differ according to the objects they respond to; it is not the same as the "self" (ātman) propounded by non-Buddhists.

Because foolish people are terrified by the doctrine of selflessness (*anātman*), the Tathāgata employs skillful means to describe the realm of non-existence as the gateway to the *tathāgatagarbha*, encouraging all bodhisattvas not to equate this with the self-conceptions of non-Buddhists.
“Mahāmati! It is like a potter who, from a single mass of clay, produces various vessels with distinct names and differences according to his needs.

Just as the potter relies on one mass of clay and, through skillful means, fashions various vessels as required, so too does the Tathāgata rely on the single principle of dharma-nairātmya (selflessness of phenomena), employing skillful means according to the capacities of beings to speak either of the *tathāgatagarbha* or of selflessness; thus, there are various different names.”
“Mahāmati! When I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, it is for the purpose of making known the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as being without self.
This clarifies that, in order to abandon false views and realize unsurpassed bodhi, one should know the meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as being without self.
Now, regarding the term "tathāgatagarbha," there are generally three meanings:
first, the sense of being concealed or covered; that is, because the Tathāgata is hidden or covered, it is called a "garbha" (womb/store).
Therefore, the *Tattvārtha-prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* states: "All sentient beings are the Tathāgatagarbha.
The *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata, when not separated from the storehouse of afflictions, is called the Tathāgatagarbha."

2. The meaning of inclusion: This refers to the fact that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body includes all bodily forms and lands, as well as immeasurable merits consisting of the great functions of supernormal powers.
It is also said that it "encompasses" because all sentient beings are contained within the Tathāgatagarbha.
Third, the meaning of "production": since this Dharmakāya contains all virtues, once one realizes and enters into it through thorough understanding, one is able to produce them.

Therefore, the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra* states: "The wisdom of the stages (*bhūmi-jñāna*) can produce the causes and effects of the outflow-free (*anāsrava*), and it can also produce and bring to completion the practices of the human and celestial realms.
Regarding these three meanings, the first pertains to the time of delusion, the latter pertains to the time of awakening, and the middle defines its essential nature.

Therefore, the *Śrīmālā-sūtra* states: "If one has no doubt regarding the Tathāgatagarbha that is enveloped by immeasurable afflictions, one will likewise have no doubt regarding the Dharmakāya, which is the Dharma-treasury free from those immeasurable afflictive envelopments."
"However, while the fruit is manifest and easy to believe in, the cause is hidden and difficult to clarify; thus, those of shallow understanding tend to slight the cause and value the fruit.
I pray that all students will have deep faith in their own minds."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke in verse:
“The continuum of a person, the aggregates, the various conditions, and atoms; the Supreme Lord, the Creator—these are merely the mind’s conceptual constructions.”
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) reckon that it is due to a self-soul (ātman) that the aggregates (skandhas) continue in succession.

Furthermore, they reckon that atoms (paramāṇu) and the like serve as conditions for the arising of phenomena, or they reckon that everything is created by the supreme and wondrous Lord (Īśvara); these are merely the delusive imaginings of the mind-only (cittamātra).
Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Three.
Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Four.
"At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attained the Great Accomplishment of Practice. This follows from the preceding entry.

Because one swiftly attains Bodhi through the three gates of liberation, Mahāmati requests the Tathāgata to explain the methods of practice and the untainted skillful means as they are cultivated by the bodhisattvas.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! When a bodhisattva-mahāsattva reaches this state, they are then called a great practitioner."

The Tathāgata said: "One who possesses the four skillful means is able to accomplish great cultivation. These four names are listed here, and they will be individually investigated and explained below. "Mahāmati!
What is meant by 'observing what is manifested by one's own mind' up to 'thus observing what is manifested by one's own mind'?"

This means that the phenomena of the three realms, including both the environment and its inhabitants, are merely manifestations appearing through the entry of discrimination, which has been permeated by the habitual tendencies of one's own mind.
As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "All dharmas arise from the mind and are produced by deluded thought."
Observing in this manner is called right observation.
"Mahāmati! How does one attain freedom from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing?"
"Upon reaching the transformation of the basis, one attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).

Regarding "being far removed from views of birth": this means that once the stage of effortful practice at the completion of the seventh ground has concluded, one is able to remain free from those views of the characteristics of the two kinds of birth.
Realizing the nature of illusion, one dwells in the eighth stage and comprehends the mind, consciousness, and so forth.

To "attain the body born of mental mastery" refers precisely to the body born of mental mastery that awakens to the self-nature of phenomena through the path of effortless spontaneity (*anābhoga-mārga*).
Mahāmati said:
"World-Honored One!
By what causes and conditions is it called the 'mind-made body' (manomayakāya)?"

Since it was stated above that Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage and beyond transform the consciousness that serves as their basis (*āśraya*), for what reason is it further called the "mind-made body" (*manomaya-kāya*)?
Therefore, he asks: by what causes and conditions is the mind-made body so named?
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! As for the mind-made body (manomayakāya), it reaches the attainment of being far removed from views regarding arising, abiding, and ceasing."
The mind has three meanings, and thus it is taken as a metaphor:

first, swiftness; second, unimpededness; and third, omnipresence. These serve as metaphors for the Bodhisattva who, having attained the illusion-like samādhi, manifests forms throughout the ten directions to transform sentient beings, and likewise possesses these same three meanings.
From the passage beginning with "The mind-made body is also like this" onwards, the application of the dharma to the metaphor can be understood.
"Mahāmati! How does one contemplate that external dharmas lack intrinsic nature?"
"You should thus diligently practice and study.
This clarifies the cultivation of the four practices according to reality, which accomplishes the aforementioned four dharma-gates.
That is to say, by observing the manifestations of one's own mind, one accomplishes the aforementioned gate of the emptiness of all dharmas.
By distancing oneself from views and practices concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing, one accomplishes the aforementioned Dharma-gate of Non-arising.
By skillfully knowing that external phenomena lack intrinsic nature, one accomplishes the aforementioned Dharma-gate of the Absence of Self-nature.
Dedicatedly seeking the practice of personally realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) accomplishes the aforementioned gate of non-duality.

This is called the Bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas, whereby the practitioner attains the great skillful means (*upāya*) as it truly is; therefore, I exhort you to diligently practice and study them.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having reached the point of "not falsely clinging to the gradual or sudden arising of all phenomena," and because he had previously observed that false discrimination gives rise to the triple world through conditions,
Mahāmati raised the characteristics of causes and conditions to inquire further.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! All dharmas arise from causes and conditions; this is called external conditions arising sequentially through successive transformations."
It is said that with the lump of clay as the cause and water, a staff, and so forth as the conditions, the jar is produced as the effect.
Just as this is the case for the cause and effect of the clay jar, the same applies by analogy to the other four cases, such as thread and cloth.
In all cases, the sowing of seeds in curdled milk serves as the cause, while the resulting mat and ivory butter constitute the fruit; the meaning of "condition" (pratyaya) is thus understood.
This is called the dharma of dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda), which necessarily proceeds from cause to effect, arising through successive stages.
This means that that which directly produces [the result] is the cause (*hetu*), while that which indirectly assists is the condition (*pratyaya*).
"Internal" refers to ignorance, craving, karma, and so forth; these are merely conceptual constructions of the foolish.

Regarding internal conditions: because ignorance, craving, karma, and so forth serve as causes and conditions, the aggregates, elements, and sense bases arise within the body; this is termed the "fruit.
This is merely the false discrimination of deluded beings, who each perceive distinct differences.
This is explained in detail in the "Examination of Causes and Conditions" (*Pratyaya-parīkṣā*) chapter of the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*.

Nevertheless, as the external arises from the internal, with the fundamental and the derivative mutually encompassing one another, they constitute a single dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
“Mahāmati! There are six kinds of causes:
namely, the cause of what is to be (bhaviṣyat-hetu) up to the cause of dependence (apekṣā-hetu).”
The preceding general exposition on the internal and external causes and conditions of all phenomena is concluded.
Hereafter follows a specific explanation of the six kinds of causes and four kinds of conditions, all of which are merely conceptual constructions of the deluded.
"Mahāmati! 'The cause of what is to be' (bhaviṣyaddhetu) refers to internal and external phenomena acting as causes to produce effects.

When it is said that the subsequent arising of an effect is called 'what is to be,' this means that by acting as a cause in the present, one obtains the fruit in the future; thus it is termed the 'cause of what is to be.'"
"Connected causes" refers to internal and external phenomena acting as objects of perception to produce resultant aggregates, seeds, and so forth.
This means that once they have functioned as focal objects, internal and external phenomena arise; thus, the cause and effect of the subjective and objective are mutually connected.
The aggregates (skandhas) are the fruit;
the seeds are the cause.
As for "mutual causality," it refers to producing an uninterrupted arising that results in a continuous succession of effects.
It is said that being mutual fruits constitutes their characteristic, while their uninterrupted succession is called their causal characteristic.
The *Abhidharmakośabhāṣya* states: "Co-existent factors are mutual fruits, such as the primary characteristics and the characterized, and the mind and its concomitants."
That is to say, conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa) are [the cause] for conditioned phenomena (saṃskṛta-dharma), and conditioned phenomena are [the cause] for conditioned characteristics;

likewise, the mind (citta) is [the cause] for mental concomitants (caitta-dharma), and mental concomitants are [the cause] for the mind. Because they are mutual effects, these are also called simultaneous causes (sahabhū-hetu).
The efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*) refers to that which produces a result by acting as a sovereign influence (*adhipati*), like a universal monarch (*cakravartin*).

With the exception of its own self-nature, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) have all dharmas as their efficient cause, because they abide without obstruction at the time of [the other's] arising.
For example, when the people of a country perceive that the Wheel-Turning King does not cause them harm, they all say:
"It is because of the Wheel-Turning King that we have attained peace and happiness.
As for the "revealing cause" (*vyañjanahetu*), it refers to that which, upon arising through discrimination, reveals the characteristics of an object, just as a lamp illuminates things.
It is said that once the phenomena of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) have arisen, they are able to manifest the characteristics of objects.
The cause and effect of the subject and object mutually illuminate one another, like a lamp illuminating an object.
Regarding the "contingent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*): it refers to the arising of non-conceptualization when, at the time of cessation, the continuity of characteristics is severed.
"Just as length and shortness, or height and depth, exist in mutual dependence, so too do cause and effect.
When the cause ceases and the effect arises, this is called 'the cessation of continuity at the time of extinction,' wherein one does not perceive the arising of illusory dharmas."
"Mahāmati! This is because the marks of causes sought through the discriminations of foolish people are ultimately unobtainable.
From here on, [the text] refutes the calculation of the six kinds of causal conditions arising from the marks of one's own mind's false imagination.
If one says they arise instantaneously, then there would be no distinction between the agent and the object, or between cause and effect; how, then, could there be the characteristic of a cause?
If they arise gradually, their essential nature and characteristics cannot be found upon investigation; it is like asking how one can be called a father before a son has been born.
It is said that one who has not yet fathered a child cannot be called a father; this single analogy refutes both views simultaneously.
If cause and effect were to arise simultaneously, then father and son would possess identical bodies, making it impossible to distinguish between the superior and the subordinate.
If the cause precedes the effect, then the father comes first and the son later; yet if the son is definitively posterior, from what source does the title "father" derive?
If one challenges [the opponent] with this, both views are utterly lost. The father is a metaphor for the cause, and the son is a metaphor for the effect.

Furthermore, it is said: "Just as one cannot be called a son if there is no father, because the preceding part has already ceased, the subsequent part cannot be designated by that name in succession."
"Those who engage in conceptual construction say that all things which arise through causes and conditions are merely attachments to the characteristics of deluded sentiments.
This statement regarding those who falsely calculate that [things] arise from the four conditions means: that which can directly produce a result is called the *hetu-pratyaya* (causal condition);
that which serves as a basis for mutual dependence is called the *ālambana-pratyaya* (object-condition).
The preceding and succeeding guidance is termed "succession" (*anukrama*);
it is called "predominance" (*adhipati*) because it has the sense of not obstructing arising.
For those who engage in conceptual speculation, the notion that the four conditions cause the phenomena of subject and object to be mutually connected and arise in succession is entirely untenable.
It is solely the measure of mind, due to the characteristics of conceptual construction and attachment.
The extensive meaning of the four conditions is as explained in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*. "Mahāmati!
"Neither the gradual nor the sudden arise at all, up to the arising of views regarding the gradual and the sudden.

In the past, the Buddha used skillful means to teach that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, in order to refute the non-Buddhists' doctrines of spontaneity, causelessness, and false causes.
Furthermore, it is taught that dependent origination is selfless in order to refute the non-Buddhist attachment to a self.
As the following verse states: "In order to negate a creator, the harmony of causes and conditions is taught."
"To preclude the fault of permanence, it is taught that conditions are impermanent.

Now, in this assembly, in order to cause them to abandon the provisional vehicle and realize that all is a manifestation of mind-only, the conclusion of the refutation states: "One should abandon views of sudden or gradual arising within the marks of the conjunction of causes and conditions."
However, in order to refute divergent views, three explanations are presented within the provisional and ultimate teachings:
first, to cause all bodhisattvas to know that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, thereby distinguishing them from the views of non-Buddhists;
second, to know that [phenomena] manifest from the mind, thereby causing them to abandon the views of the two vehicles.
3. Only the mind gives rise to phenomena; this differs from the provisional teachings.
Students should understand this.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"All phenomena are without arising, and likewise without cessation; it is within those various conditions that one discriminates the characteristics of arising and ceasing.

Since all phenomena are without arising, one cannot speak of their cessation; rather, it is only within those unreal conditions that one falsely discriminates the characteristics of arising and ceasing.
"It is not that the conjunction of conditions is denied; such is the process of cessation and renewed arising. It is merely to stop the attachments of the deluded sentiments of the ignorant.

This clarifies that the Buddha does not deny the dharma of arising and ceasing through dependent origination, because the intrinsic nature of dharmas is non-arising; it is solely for the purpose of severing the conceptual attachments of the ignorant, the deluded, and those with false imaginings.

"Whether phenomena exist or do not exist within conditions, they are all devoid of arising; it is through the deluded turning of the mind by habitual tendencies that the three realms of existence appear.

This means that regarding the existence or non-existence of dependent origination, all dharmas are without arising; it is solely because of the deluded turning of one's own mental habitual tendencies that the three realms of existence manifest.
The "three realms of existence" (trai-dhātu) refer to the realm of desire (kāma-dhātu), the realm of form (rūpa-dhātu), and the formless realm (ārūpya-dhātu).
"Originally there is neither arising nor ceasing; yet, having arrived at [this state], one speaks of arising and ceasing."

If one is free from the two kinds of grasping and all false views, then one knows that both the phenomena produced and the causal conditions that produce them are fundamentally non-existent from the very beginning; it is not that one must first investigate them to make them non-existent.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having attained purification regarding the two meanings,
spoke as follows based on what had been said above:
"It is only in accordance with worldly convention that one speaks of arising and ceasing."
Therefore, Mahāmati raised the characteristics of the discrimination of verbal expression and the gateway of mental phenomena to pose his inquiry.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati!..."
"There are four kinds of conventional discourse based on conceptualization; these constitute the four.
The four kinds of conventional discourse are clear from the text and can be understood accordingly.

Furthermore, regarding "discourse like a dream": it is said that when a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage attains the realization of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they reflect upon the stages previously traversed, from the stage of practice through resolute conviction (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) up to the seventh stage. Seeing that the objects experienced therein were not real, they describe all phenomena as being like a dream; therefore, it is called "discourse like a dream."
Mahāmati spoke again:
“World-Honored One, to what place does it go, by what cause does it arise, and how does it originate?
Thus he asked concerning the source from which speech emerges.
He asked, "From what cause do verbal expressions arise?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!"
"It arises from the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, lips, palate, teeth, and tongue.
These various conditions are the sources from which speech issues forth.
Mahāmati spoke again:
“World-Honored One!
Verbal expression arises with conceptualization as its cause, because verbal expression is produced by conceptualization.
This means that those utterances arise based on conceptualization.
"If they were different, conceptualization would not be the cause [of verbal expression]; therefore, they are neither different nor non-different.
If verbal expression were different from conceptualization, verbal expression should not arise dependent upon conceptualization.

If it is claimed that verbal expression and conceptual construction are not distinct, then since conceptual construction does not manifest the object, verbal expression likewise should not manifest the object; yet verbal expression is said to manifest the object. Therefore, both [positions] are untenable.
Mahāmati spoke again:
"World-Honored One, one enters into the ultimate cause through words, yet it is not identical to the words themselves.
Since it is by means of superior verbal expression that meaning can be revealed, Mahāmati asks: Are these words and expressions the primary truth (paramārtha)?"
Is that which has been explained the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
[The interlocutor] again raises the aforementioned mental phenomena of the ultimate truth as a question.
The Buddha then replies:
It is neither language nor that which is expressed by it.

Why is this? The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is the realm of the bliss of samādhi realized through the noble wisdom of self-attestation; one enters it by means of words, yet it is not identical to the words themselves.
Therefore, it is said that killing is like a finger pointing at the moon; once the moon is seen, one realizes that what was pointed out is ultimately not the moon itself.
That which is the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is the realm of internal self-realization by noble wisdom (āryajñāna); when it comes to the ultimate truth, it cannot be displayed.

Language is subject to arising and ceasing, and being fluctuating, it is impermanent; since it arises from a multitude of conditions, it lacks intrinsic nature. How, then, can it manifest the ultimate truth?
"The ultimate truth (paramārtha) is devoid of the characteristics of self and other; it should be understood as that which transcends verbal conceptualization.

To say that the ultimate truth is free from the characteristics of self and other means that conventional discourse, being entangled with the characteristics of existence, is incapable of manifesting it.

Furthermore, the ultimate truth consists solely in the realization of the true mind of self-nature; there is no phenomenon apart from this mind. Since all external phenomena are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature, how could verbal expressions or conceptual constructions ever reveal it?
Therefore, I exhort you to abandon verbal conceptualization and rely upon the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:
"All phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are likewise beyond verbal expression; yet, failing to perceive the meaning of emptiness within emptiness, the foolish wander in saṃsāra."

Because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, there is also no verbal expression; yet, because the foolish and ignorant do not see that expressions are empty and that what is expressed is empty, they transmigrate through birth and death.
"All phenomena are without intrinsic nature and are free from linguistic conceptualization; all existences are like dreams and magical illusions, neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa.
This means that all phenomena and their verbal expressions are unreal, being like dreams and like magical illusions.
For those who are like dreams or magical illusions, how could there be any fixed characteristics of birth-and-death or nirvana?
"It is like a king or a householder who, in order to bring joy to his children, leads them to the Dharma of the personally realized limit of reality."
The first verse presents the analogy, while the subsequent verse applies it to the Dharma.
That is to say, what I have now expounded is the realm of the actual limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of the noble wisdom of self-realization; it is not that which is expressed by verbal discourse.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati reached "the sphere of activity of the noble wisdom of self-realization.

Because Mahāmati had previously stated that the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is that which is attained through the noble wisdom of self-realization and is not a sphere of verbal or conceptual discrimination, he now raised the ultimate truth attained through the noble wisdom of self-realization as the subject of his inquiry.

However, because the ultimate truth (paramārtha) is by nature free from the fourfold views of identity and difference, existence and non-existence, annihilation and permanence, and bothness and neitherness, Mahāmati requested the Dharma that transcends these four extremes.

In this context, three dharmas are taught to clarify the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi), resulting in twelve propositions; based on the text, there are nine, as some are omitted or implied through mutual correspondence.

There are four propositions regarding identity and difference, three regarding existence and non-existence, and two regarding permanence and impermanence; these are thus abbreviated by the compiler of the sūtra.
This is fully as explained in the *Catuḥśāstra-viniścaya*:
"From the distancing of false conceptualizations of self-characteristics up to the fulfillment and perfection of all merits.

This means that it is not only the views of non-Buddhists that are abandoned, but also the attachments to the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases held by those of the two vehicles; thereby causing all bodhisattvas and sentient beings to swiftly realize the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed seed-wisdom (*anuttara-bīja-jñāna*).
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati, excellent!
"Excellent!
[This extends] to all intrinsic natures, such as permanence and impermanence.
Although it was stated above that one is free from existence, non-existence, and so forth, it remains unknown what constitutes existence and non-existence.
Now, I shall precisely elucidate the nature of existence and non-existence.

It is said that ordinary beings, out of ignorance, do not realize that these are manifestations produced by the causes of their own mental constructs and deluded habitual tendencies; instead, they cling to external phenomena as being either existent or nonexistent, giving rise to views such as the four extremes. This is the nature of their false conceptualization regarding existence and nonexistence.
The following twelve similes illustrate that phenomena such as existence and non-existence, or identity and difference, are all unreal and should be abandoned.

[The interlocutor] replies: "I pray that you will explain for me the sphere of practice that is free from identity and difference, existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, and so forth."
“Mahāmati! It is like a herd of deer, driven by thirst, falling into attachments such as the notions of identity and difference.

Just as a deer pursues a mirage, how much more so for the foolish who delight in the objects of desire? To say that ignorant ordinary beings are likewise is to place them on the same level as that herd of deer.”
Perfumed by beginningless conceptual proliferation and discrimination, the three poisons burn the mind; combined with the former, one is oppressed by thirst.
Delighting in the realm of forms, one perceives their arising, abiding, and ceasing; combined with the former, one conceives the notion of water within a mirage during the heat of the season.

Grasping at internal and external phenomena, they fall into attachments such as [the views of] identity or difference; thus, combined with their prior confusion and frantic pursuit, they do not realize that it is not water. "Mahāmati!
Just as with a city of Gandharvas, up to the point of being free from the two natures, one gives rise to the conceptualization of existence.
Regarding the "three types of valid cognition" (pramāṇa):
first is direct perception (pratyakṣa), second is inference (anumāna), and third is authoritative testimony (āptāgama).
"Valid cognition" (*pramāṇa*) is a term established by way of analogy, like using measures such as bushels and pecks to measure objects.

"Direct valid cognition" (*pratyakṣa-pramāṇa*): "direct" (*pratyakṣa*) means manifest; it refers to the clear realization of an object without the mediation of names or words, without a mind of conjecture, directly apprehending the essence of the phenomenon, free from false discrimination, and devoid of error.
Regarding inference (*anumāna*): "inference" means comparing by analogy; that is, because one attains knowledge through comparison and measurement by means of causes and examples.

For instance, seeing smoke from afar, one necessarily knows there is fire; seeing a horn over a wall, one necessarily knows it is an ox. Although these are not seen directly, they are nonetheless not false.
Valid cognition based on authoritative scripture (*āptāgama*) refers to taking the holy teachings of the Tathāgata as the standard.
Thus, the ancient masters said:

"After our Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, one should take the sūtras and śāstras as the measuring line and realized knowledge as the guide, in order to guard against demons and non-Buddhists. This is precisely what that means.
The five-membered syllogism consists of:
first, the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the reason (*hetu*); third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); and fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*).
The first three—the thesis, the reason, and the example—are also called the "three members of inference" (*trirūpa-anumāna*); the example and the application merely serve to establish [the argument].
For instance, as the non-Buddhists falsely speculate, they cling to sound as being eternal.
Within the science of grammar (*śabdavidyā*), they formulate a syllogism as follows:
"Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is certainly eternal" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason is stated as "because it is produced" (*kṛtakatva*), with the concordant example being "like space.
However, since space is not produced, the reason does not apply to the subject; thus, the analogy is inconsistent, and the thesis that sound is permanent is not established.
If, within the Buddha-dharma, sound is impermanent, one establishes the formal argument (*pramāṇa*) as follows:
"Sound" is the subject (*dharmin*); "it is necessarily impermanent" is the thesis (*pakṣa*).
The reason (*hetu*) is: "because it is a product" (*kṛtakatvāt*). The positive example (*sapakṣadṛṣṭānta*) is: "like a jar or a basin."
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Sounds mixed with speech merely rely on names, phrases, and meanings.
How could these be permanent?

The various speculative attachments of the non-Buddhists lead them to claim they surpass others; if one does not refute their attachments by establishing formal arguments (*pramāṇa*) that are dissimilar to theirs, by what means could those attachments be destroyed?
Therefore, the five-membered syllogism taught by the Tathāgata is like using a wedge to extract a wedge, or using sound to stop sound.

It is intended to destroy the heterodox attachments of Māras and outsiders, to establish the fundamental principles of the Buddha-dharma, and to cause all sentient beings to depart from various divergent views—such as those of existence and non-existence—with respect to the realm realized through the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
Fools who are deluded by the teachings still calculate that there is a self-nature, engaging in false conceptualizations and discriminations of oneness and difference, or annihilation and permanence.
"Mahāmati! When practitioners transform their mind, manas, and consciousness, they nevertheless become attached to the notions of a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span."

All practitioners should extinguish mind, intellect, and consciousness; they should depart from the two natures of the grasper and the grasped, enter the stage of the Tathāgata, and give rise to no false conceptualization regarding existence or non-existence.
If one makes calculations of existence or non-existence regarding the realm realized through self-awareness, one again becomes attached to "I" and "mine.
Mahāmati! The specific and general characteristics of all dharmas culminate in the realm of the blissful samādhi of the noble wisdom of personal realization.

As for the "transformed Buddha," it merely accords with the deluded views that arise in ordinary people; through various forms of discourse, it explains specific and general characteristics in order to cause them to understand that phenomena are unreal.
Regarding "not non-Buddha," both the Song and Wei translations read "Dharma-Buddha. "Mahāmati!
It is like the reflection of a tree appearing in water; all conceptual discriminations—such as 'simultaneous' or 'non-simultaneous' and so forth—are likewise [illusory]."
The Tathāgata exhorted them thus:

"Within that which you have realized, you should abandon the evil views and conceptual discriminations of ordinary people and non-Buddhists, such as arising and ceasing, identity and difference, existence and non-existence, annihilation and permanence, and bothness and neitherness."
However, the heterodox views in India are roughly of three types:
first, the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*).
These include those who hold to the aforementioned fourfold conceptualizations, as well as the six teachers and the ninety-six kinds of non-Buddhist sects.
Second, those who affiliate with non-Buddhist paths while remaining within the Buddha-dharma.

Originating from the Vātsīputrīyas and the Vaipulya school, they rely on their own cleverness to read the Buddhist scriptures, yet failing to understand the correct view, they produce their own deluded interpretations.

It is like a cow that drinks water and produces milk, while a snake drinks water and produces poison; those masters who all reject [the doctrine of] non-reception are people of heterodox views attached to the Buddha-dharma.
Third, those who study the Buddha-dharma become followers of external paths.
Clinging to the gates of the Buddhist teachings, they give rise to affliction and vexation, and thus fail to attain realization.
The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one does not obtain the skillful means of Prajñā, entering the Abhidharma leads to falling into existence."
"Entering emptiness leads to falling into non-existence;
entering *kun-lê* (the *kośa*) leads to falling into the view that things both exist and do not exist.

The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "To cling to 'neither existence nor non-existence' is called the discourse of the deluded; those who perversely grasp the True Dharma become, in turn, people of false views."
Furthermore, if all four gates of the Mahāyāna were established as views, then true speech would be false, because it gives rise to the view of speech;
and nirvāṇa would be saṃsāra, because it gives rise to craving and attachment.

To consume much ambrosia (amṛta) is to harm one's life and meet an early death; to lose the gate of skillful means (upāya-mukha) is to fall into perverse attachments, and is therefore termed "internal wrong views.
Thus we know that dharmas have no fixed characteristics; they revolve according to the mind. To cling to them results in error, but to penetrate them is without fault.
As with the Dharma of the four propositions, penetration or obstruction depends on the person.

In terms of the Dharma itself, they are called the "four propositions"; in terms of awakening and entry, they are called the "four gates"; in terms of false conceptualization, they are called the "four attachments"; and in terms of disparagement, they are called the "four slanders."
The four propositions are immovable, yet gain and loss arise from emptiness;
there is not a single dharma that differs, yet ascent and descent differ of their own accord.

If one merely has something to value or rely upon, establishing knowledge and establishing understanding, and does not forget even the slightest point of view, all such things become the ways of external paths. Thus we know that when views exist, one is an ordinary person; when attachment to them perishes, one is a Buddha.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The aggregates of consciousness are fivefold, like reflections of trees upon water; what is perceived is like a dream or an illusion—one should not engage in false discrimination.”
This verse applies the three aforementioned metaphors to the five aggregates; one should not give rise to false conceptualizations regarding them.
"The three realms of existence are like a mirage, a phantom, a dream, and the optical illusion of falling hairs; if one can contemplate them in this way, one will ultimately attain liberation."
The verse cites four metaphors to clarify that the three realms of existence are unreal; one who contemplates in this way will surely attain Bodhi.
"For example, like a mirage in the heat, which moves and deludes the mind, causing even the most foolish person to give rise to attachment."
The first verse above corresponds to the initial parable, and the subsequent verse corresponds to the application of the teaching (*dharma-saṃkrama*).
"Within beginningless saṃsāra, one is entangled and shrouded by attachments."

To summarize the meaning of the twelve similes in the verse: because one is bound and obscured by attachment to a self and phenomena since beginningless time, one must abandon [them] and achieve liberation, just as one uses a wedge to extract a wedge.
The twelve metaphors above are like using a wedge to remove a wedge;

they are like illusions, spells, mechanical devices, floating clouds, dreams, and flashes of lightning. One should contemplate the world as always being thus, thereby forever severing the three continuities.
Furthermore, five similes are presented in verse; by contemplating the world in this way, one can sever the three realms so that they never again continue.
[The similes of] floating clouds and lightning flashes have no further text above.
"In this, there is nothing at all, like a mirage in the sky; knowing all phenomena thus, there is then nothing to be known."
To say that one knows all phenomena to be without intrinsic substance means there is nothing to be known.
"The aggregates are like falling hairs; within them, one falsely discriminates. They are merely provisional designations and names; when sought for their characteristics, they cannot be found."
He said: "The aggregates do not exist; even their provisional designations are empty and lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature.
They are like paintings, falling hair, illusions, dreams, and the city of the Gandharvas—objects of false conceptualization for the utterly foolish."
Furthermore, the seven similes throughout the verses demonstrate that the fourfold views—existence and non-existence, identity and difference, permanence and impermanence—are unreal.
The simile of the painting is absent from the preceding text.
"A clear mirror, pure water, and the eye; even the wondrous mani-jewel are like the son of a barren woman.
This clarifies that although all phenomena appear, they lack any substantial reality.
"Pure Eye" (*viśuddhacakṣus*) and "Son of a Barren Woman" (*vandhyāputra*) do not appear in the preceding text.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the teachings of all Buddhas correspond to the atoms of time and so forth.

It is said that whenever the Buddhas appear in the world and expound the Dharma, they transcend the four propositions and sever the hundred negations; this establishment [of truth] lies beyond the reach of ordinary intellects and even the measures of the sages.

Before the Great Capacity (mahā-yāna) was encountered, all took the Four Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination—realizing cessation, cultivating the path, and attaining liberation from birth and death—as the primary source; these were not shared in their characteristics with the various non-Buddhists who assert a "Supreme Nature" (prakṛti) as being spontaneous.
Although the causes and conditions of the Hīnayāna were initially taught, they already surpassed the profound subtleties of the non-Buddhists. "Mahāmati!
The Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma is like a caravan leader skillfully guiding a multitude."

In order to purify the two types of obscurations—those of afflictions and those of knowledge—he is like a caravan leader who guides merchants, knowing the passages and blockages on the road, the dangers, and the places to rest.

Furthermore, he was skilled in discerning various kinds of jewels; in this way, he was like the Tathāgata who guides sentient beings, severing the two obstacles and causing them to dwell in the place of peace and security within the signless Dharma.
Furthermore, he is skilled in discerning the jewels of the various distinctions among the vehicles and their respective stages.

Regarding the two obstacles of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and cognition (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "The six defiled minds are called the obstacle of affliction, for they can obstruct the fundamental wisdom of *tathatā* (suchness)."
"The meaning of ignorance (*avidyā*) is termed 'obstruction of wisdom' (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), because it can obstruct the innate wisdom regarding worldly activities.
What is the meaning of this?
It is because, by relying on the defiled mind, one is able to see and manifest, falsely grasping at objects, thereby contravening the nature of equality.
Because all dharmas are eternally quiescent and lack any characteristic of arising, and because ignorance fails to realize this and thus falsely opposes the Dharma, one cannot attain it.

This is because one conforms to the world and perceives the various kinds of objects within all realms; this explains the meaning of the two obstacles by means of their mutual dependence as root and branch.
If one explains the two obstacles by means of the two types of grasping, as will be cited later from the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* to explain their meaning:
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
"There are four kinds of dhyāna, culminating in the dhyāna that takes True Suchness as its object, which is the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas.
Because of the two aforementioned obstacles, one is able to obstruct the Noble Path and fail to realize the two fruits of transformation—the Bodhi and Nirvāṇa of a Tathāgata.

All who study the Way should cultivate meditative concentration (dhyāna) to give rise to untainted, wondrous wisdom; only then can they purify those two obstacles. Therefore, the four kinds of dhyāna are explained next.

It is also said that among the six pāramitās, the single practice of meditative concentration (dhyāna) is the most divine and subtle, for it can give rise to the untainted wisdom (anāsrava-jñāna) inherent in one's nature.
All myriad practices and myriad virtues, even up to supernatural powers and radiant light, all emerge from concentration.
Therefore, those who study the three vehicles and seek the noble path must necessarily cultivate dhyāna; thus, the four kinds of dhyāna are explained in detail.
"Mahāmati, what is the dhyāna practiced by fools? [It is] up to this that is called the dhyāna practiced by fools."

Regarding those who practice the contemplations of the two vehicles: they realize the selflessness of persons and perceive that their own and others' aggregates, elements, and bases are all characterized by impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and impurity. By observing these without abandoning them, they attain the first dhyāna, gradually progressing through increasingly superior stages until reaching the samādhi of non-conception and the cessation of feeling and perception.
However, because it does not transcend [conceptual] marks, it is called "the dhyāna practiced by fools.
What is the "dhyāna that contemplates meaning"? It is called the "dhyāna that contemplates meaning" up to this point.
"Meaning" refers to the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena.

From the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the seventh stage, the Bodhisattva contemplates that the dharmas of the two vehicles, external paths, and so forth are all unreal; having realized this, they accord with the correct contemplation of the characteristics and meanings of the stages regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*). Therefore, it is called the "meditation on the contemplation of meaning" (*arthacintā-dhyāna*).
"What is the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object? It is called the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object because it is the realization that these two are non-self;
this is what is meant by 'deluded thought. What is deluded thought?
It refers to the notion that these two [self and phenomena] are non-self; this is deluded thought.
Why is this? Because two kinds of selflessness are taught as remedies for the two kinds of views of self.
Since that which is remedied is not real, the remedy is likewise illusory; therefore, it is said that the two kinds of selflessness are illusory conceptions.

If one knows things as they truly are, with equanimity according to principle, and does not give rise to the deluded thoughts of the two kinds of selflessness, this is called "dhyāna of true suchness as its object" (tathatālambana-dhyāna).
Alternatively, it is called "dhyāna of true suchness through right mindfulness" (samyaksmṛti-tathatā-dhyāna).
"What is the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas?

It is called the dhyāna of all Tathāgatas because it refers to attaining the true Dharma-body of the self-realized noble wisdom of the Tathāgata-stage, which is eternally abiding in quiescence; it causes sentient beings to obtain the three kinds of bliss and to attain the inconceivable matters of the Tathāgata’s wisdom-Dharma-body."
The three kinds of bliss are:
the bliss of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), the bliss of awakening (*bodhi*), and the bliss of nirvāṇa; these are called the Tathāgata’s meditation.

Furthermore, according to former masters, there are generally five kinds of meditation based on the different supports of ordinary beings, non-Buddhists, those of the three vehicles, and those of the one vehicle:
That which involves being mired in heterodox views and practicing while taking delight in higher realms and loathing lower ones is the dhyāna of non-Buddhists;
that which is practiced with right faith in cause and effect, yet still through the mechanism of delighting in and loathing, is the dhyāna of ordinary worldlings;
and that which is practiced after awakening to the principle of the partial truth of self-emptiness is the dhyāna of the Lesser Vehicle.
To practice by awakening to the ultimate truth revealed through the emptiness of both self and phenomena is the Mahayana dhyāna.

If one suddenly awakens to the fact that one’s own mind is originally pure and fundamentally free from afflictions, that the nature of untainted wisdom is inherently complete, and that this mind is ultimately no different from the Buddha, then practicing in reliance upon this is the Dhyāna of the Supreme Vehicle. It is also called the Tathāgata’s Pure Dhyāna, the Samādhi of the Single Practice, and the Samādhi of Suchness. This is the root of all samādhis; if one can cultivate it moment by moment, one will naturally and gradually attain immeasurable hundreds of thousands of various samādhis.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The dhyāna practiced by the ignorant, the dhyāna that contemplates the characteristics of meaning, the dhyāna that takes true suchness as its object, and the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata."
The preceding verse names the four dhyānas.
"When the practitioner is in meditative concentration, they perceive the forms of the sun and moon, the *pātāla* (deep abyss), the fire in the sky, and paintings."
This clarifies the characteristics of the meditation practiced by non-Buddhists and those of the Two Vehicles.

It is said that non-Buddhists, being attached to a self (*ātman*), perceive during meditative contemplation forms resembling the sun and moon, bright, pure, and radiant, or they see red lotuses beneath deep and perilous places.

The followers of the Two Vehicles regard both their own and shared characteristics as substantially existent; they consider the dissolution of the body and the extinction of consciousness to be equivalent to empty space, taking the analogy of a fire extinguished when the fuel is exhausted to be ultimate nirvana.
I fear that the character "hua" (畫) may be an error; the other two versions both read "jin" (盡).
"Such various characteristics fall into the teachings of the non-Buddhists, and likewise fall into the realms of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas."
"The aforementioned signs are the meditative spheres of the non-Buddhists, as well as the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
Abandoning all these, one dwells in the objectless."
The former phrase refers to the dhyāna of contemplating meaning; from here on, it is the dhyāna of clinging to *tathatā*.
"Thus one is able to enter accordingly, and when the true mark of suchness arrives, it touches the crown of this person's head."
This refers to entering the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva asked: "What kind of dharma is called nirvāṇa?"

Because the aforementioned non-Buddhists take the perception of a self (ātman) to be nirvāṇa, while the followers of the Two Vehicles take the extinction of body and cognition—like the extinguishing of fire when the fuel is exhausted—to be nirvāṇa, he asks: "What dharma does the Tathāgata teach as nirvāṇa?"
The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the intrinsic nature of all consciousnesses reaching their limit is precisely the realm of the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*).

To say that when the views and habits of the various consciousnesses have been transformed, it is called *nirvāṇa*, means that the transformation of ignorance (*avidyā*) is itself the manifestation of wisdom (*vidyā*)."

Just as when ice melts it becomes water—which is not some other substance and does not come from elsewhere—it is said that this is the true realm manifested by the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for nirvāṇa,
it is that which is reached through the personally realized wisdom of all noble ones.
This clarifies that the realm of nirvāṇa realized by the Tathāgata is free from the nature of existence, non-existence, permanence, and annihilation.
Why is it not eternal?
It is because it is devoid of the delusive conceptualizations of self-characteristics and common characteristics; therefore, it is not eternal.
Why is it not annihilated?
This means that because it is what has been realized by the Tathāgatas of the three periods of time,
it is not annihilation. Furthermore, Mahāmati,
Great Parinirvāṇa is the ultimate destination to which all practitioners resort.

Because it no longer undergoes the continuity of rebirth, nirvāṇa is deathless; because it is not a conditioned phenomenon subject to arising, abiding, and ceasing, nirvāṇa is indestructible; and because it is neither destructible nor mortal, it is the destination to which practitioners resort.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Because there is neither abandonment nor attainment, and because one reaches the state of being neither identical nor different, it is called Nirvāṇa.
In Nirvāṇa, there are no afflictions to be abandoned and no Bodhi to be attained; therefore, it is neither annihilation nor permanence, neither identity nor difference."
Only that which accords with realization is called the Tathāgata’s nirvāṇa.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas reach that state and therein give rise to the notion of nirvāṇa."

The followers of the Two Vehicles realize that within the aggregates, elements, and sense bases there is no primordial principle (tattva) or self (ātman); they abandon clamor and bustle, extinguish the afflictive obscurations, do not give rise to perversions, and do not initiate future discriminations regarding birth and death; thus, they conceive the notion of nirvāṇa therein.
Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "To merely exhaust birth and death is called liberation; in reality, one has not yet attained all-encompassing liberation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati:
"There are two kinds of self-nature characteristics that arise because one does not realize that [the world] is a manifestation of one's own mind.
Based on the aforementioned transformation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the self-nature of all consciousnesses, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

However, since the intrinsic nature of all consciousnesses is the dharma of ordinary beings, it is clarified that ordinary beings, through their clinging to the intrinsic nature of all consciousnesses, give rise to the characteristics of the two kinds of intrinsic nature.

This means that because the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of beginningless false conceptualization and verbal expression have not been severed, one clings to the notion of an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) in words;

and because one does not know that all phenomena arise from one's own mind, one perceives the existence of all phenomena—such as the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—possessing their own and common characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and thus becomes attached to the intrinsic nature of these dharmas.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
All Buddhas bestow two kinds of empowerment (adhiṣṭhāna) and personally pour water upon their crowns.

Because ordinary beings, based on the aforementioned [delusions], give rise to attachment to the two kinds of marks of self-nature (svabhāva-lakṣaṇa), the Tathāgata, in response to these two kinds of marks of self-nature, empowers all Bodhisattvas with these two kinds of empowerment."
“Mahāmati! This refers to those from the bodhisattva-mahāsattva of the first stage up to the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas.

It means that because the bodhisattva of the first stage receives the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) of the Tathāgata’s spiritual power, he enters the Bodhisattva Mahāyāna Illumination Samādhi (*bodhisattva-mahāyāna-avabhāsa-samādhi*). Having entered it, all Buddhas appear before him and empower his three modes of action (*trikarma*).

Just as it was for Vajragarbha when he dwelt on the first stage within the assembly of the Avataṃsaka Sūtra, so too did the Buddhas bestow empowerment upon all other bodhisattvas who had likewise accomplished the marks of the virtues of the first stage.
“Mahāmati! This bodhisattva-mahāsattva, having received the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*), attains mastery.

Having been initiated into meditative concentration (*samādhi*), because he has accumulated all roots of goodness (*kuśalamūla*) throughout hundreds of thousands of kalpas, he gradually enters the various stages (*bhūmi*) and is able to penetrate the characteristics of that which is to be remedied and its remedy.”
Regarding the attainment of the Stage of the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*), the general meaning of the stages can be briefly summarized in two aspects:
first, the aspect of fruition (*phala-bhāga*), which is inexpressible and accessible only through realization (*pratyātma-vedya*).
Second is the causal portion (*hetubhāga*), which can be explained through provisional discourse regarding practice, realization, abandonment, and verification.
Thus, these ten stages (*bhūmi*) establish the ten stages by cultivating ten superior practices, abandoning ten types of obstacles, and verifying ten aspects of suchness (*tathatā*).
There are two kinds of practice:
first, the general characteristic, which consists in fully cultivating all virtuous practices within each stage;
second, the specific characteristic, which further comprises two types:

First, regarding the ten perfections (*daśapāramitā*): although they are all practiced and cultivated throughout all the stages (*bhūmi*), each stage is specifically said to emphasize one particular perfection. Thus, in the first stage, the perfection of giving (*dāna*) is predominant; in the second stage, the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla*) is predominant; and so on, until in the tenth stage, the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*) is predominant.
Furthermore, one cultivates ten practices, which are now briefly explained in correspondence [with their respective stages].

That is to say, on the first stage, the Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), one cultivates the practice of aspiring joy; by proclaiming the ten great vows, because of the delight in benefiting and gladdening others, one is able to sever the obstacle of the nature of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjanatva-āvaraṇa*) and realize the all-pervading *tathatā*.

This True Suchness (tathatā) is manifested by the two kinds of emptiness; since there is not a single dharma that does not exist within it, one who realizes this is named as having attained the Stage of Joy (pramuditā-bhūmi).

This means that for the first time, one has acquired the nature of a noble being (ārya-gotra), fully realized the two kinds of emptiness, and is able to benefit both oneself and others, thereby giving rise to great joy.

Up to the tenth stage, one practices the conduct of receiving the position, severing the obstacles regarding the lack of mastery over all phenomena, and thereby realizes the *tathatā* (suchness) that serves as the basis for mastery over karma and other such powers.

Because this *tathatā* is universally sovereign over all activities of supernormal powers, dhāraṇīs, and meditative concentrations, one who realizes it is named the Stage of the Dharma Cloud (*dharmameghā bhūmi*).
This means that the great cloud of wisdom contains the waters of manifold virtues, obscuring the coarse and heavy (dauṣṭhulya) like space, and filling the *dharmakāya* which serves as its basis.

Furthermore, these ten stages (*bhūmi*) are common to the three vehicles; although they are identical in the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), the intent here is to clarify their provisional assignment to specific positions.
If categorized according to the three trainings:
the first stage is aspiration, the second stage is ethical discipline, and the third stage is meditative concentration; from the fourth stage upward, all are subsumed under wisdom.
If categorized according to the complete cultivation of practice, each practice is cultivated in unison, and thus all three virtues are universally present.
First is the realization of the Way and its Virtue, because realized wisdom accords with suchness;
second is the teaching of the Way and its Virtue, because it follows the distinctions among virtues;
third is the non-abiding Way and its Virtue, because it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa.

Within a single stage, all the virtues of every stage are fully present because the beginning and the end are perfectly interfused. If one were to follow the distinct stages and levels exclusively, there would be a hierarchy of gradations; yet if one were to remain entirely identical [to the preceding], the progress of cultivation would be lost and one would fall into quiescence. Therefore, while each stage possesses its own virtues and the successive steps appear clearly distinct, through repeated refinement and polishing, the fundamental stage remains unmoved.
About to receive the office of a Buddha, he sat upon the Lotus King Throne, surrounded by his retinue.
His body was adorned with necklaces of various jewels, and the Buddhas of the ten directions all extended their right hands to stroke the crown of the Bodhisattva’s head.

For example, it is like the sovereign Wheel-Turning Sage King and Śakra, Lord of the Devas, who, having received the consecration of the crown prince and been invested with the office, attain sovereignty.
"These bodhisattvas are also like this; they cannot reach [this state] otherwise."
The formal conclusion and demonstration are as can be understood from the text.
If it were not thus, one would be unable to see [the truth].
Furthermore, Mahāmati!
"All Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas attain [these qualities] entirely through the two kinds of sustaining power of the Buddhas.

This is because all who dwell [in these states], acquire the supernormal powers, and skillfully expound the essential points of the Dharma, do so by means of the empowerment of these two kinds of spiritual power.
“Mahāmati! If bodhisattvas were to possess such vast capacities as these,
then ordinary worldlings should also be able to preach the Dharma without relying on the power of sustaining grace (adhiṣṭhāna).”
It is said that ordinary beings cannot do so;

how much less could this be expected of the Buddha? Yet, through the empowerment of great compassion, even all insentient things can still manifest the sound of the Dharma—how much more so those who possess a mind!
This matter is seen as clarified in the *Candraprabha-kumāra-sūtra*, for there is no seeing or hearing that does not yield benefit.
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, [saying] up to: "...and in the distinguished stages, their heads were anointed with water from [the Buddha’s] hand."

The Buddha previously spoke as in the first twelve stages, yet he had not clarified the reason for the special empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*). Therefore, Mahāmati asked: "For what reason does your supernatural power (*ṛddhibala*) specifically empower these two stages?"
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! It is for the purpose of causing them to remain far removed from [such states], even by means of the power of empowerment, that he sustains all bodhisattvas.”
To abandon the two kinds of faults, one must apply effort in the first stage; to attain the two kinds of benefits, one must apply effort in the tenth stage.
To cultivate various roots of goodness while forgetting the bodhicitta is the work of Māra.
This is as explained in the *Avataṃsaka* and the *Mahāsaṃnipāta*. "Mahāmati!
If it were not thus, [the Buddha] would employ the power of empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*) to gather in all bodhisattvas."

It is said that if one does not apply [the practice] at the first stage, one will inevitably fall into the evil views of external paths or the ten realms of the śrāvaka domain; if one does not apply it at this stage, one cannot swiftly attain bodhi.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The World-Honored One’s pure vows possess the power of great empowerment; throughout the stages from the first to the tenth, there are samādhis and empowerments.”
The Bodhisattva accumulates roots of goodness, and through the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s original vows, he responds without thought, like a *maṇi* jewel; therefore, it is called "pure.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [proceeded] to the section on "Explaining that conditioned origination does not have a separate substantial reality."

Because it was stated above that the Buddhas’ teaching of the Dharma takes the truths, dependent origination, cessation, the path, and liberation as its primary focus—and does not share common characteristics with non-Buddhists such as primordial nature (*prakṛti*), the Supreme Lord (*īśvara*), past actions (*pūrvakṛta*), spontaneity (*svabhāva*), time (*kāla*), or atoms (*paramāṇu*)—Mahāmati raised the aforementioned words spoken by the Buddha regarding dependent origination to question the World-Honored One.

As the Buddha taught that dependent origination arises from conditioning (*pratyaya*), and does not arise from the intrinsic nature of the mind itself, so too do the non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena are produced by a supreme Lord (*īśvara*) and other such causes.
Now, the Buddha merely speaks of dependent origination using different names; it is not that there is some separate meaning!
"World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of how, by virtue of an agent, one arrives from original non-existence and is born, and having been born, returns to extinction."
This objection to what the Tathāgata has taught is precisely analogous to that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika).
"As the Buddha has taught, from ignorance as a condition up to [the cessation of suffering], for this reason the non-Buddhists' teaching is superior, not that of the Tathāgata."
It is said that among the twelve links of dependent origination taught by the Tathāgata, ignorance has no cause and does not possess a cause.

Furthermore, it is said that because ignorance exists, formations exist; because formations exist, consciousness exists. This is not a matter of gradual mutual dependence, for such an interpretation would fail to establish the meaning.

Furthermore, it is difficult to maintain that the Tathāgata’s teaching on dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda) is not superior to that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Therefore, one might say that the non-Buddhists’ explanation is superior and not equal to that of the Tathāgata. Why is this?
Because when the non-Buddhists state, "Because this exists, that comes to be," they actually assert that there is no cause.
Why is it that the non-Buddhists surpass the Tathāgata?
It is because they propound such causes as atoms (*paramāṇu*) and the nature of the world (*prakṛti*), which they claim do not arise from other conditions yet are capable of producing other things.
Because the cause is always the cause and not the fruit, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) claim their doctrine is superior.
As the Buddha has taught: contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) is the fruit of ignorance (*avidyā*), whereas the contemplation of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the cause.
In this way, a single dharma would be both cause and effect, resulting in a confusion of causes and conditions.

Ignorance gives rise to volitional formations; volitional formations give rise to old age and death; and old age and death give rise to ignorance. Thus, through such mutual succession, an infinite fallacy would ensue.
Furthermore, regarding the principle that "because this exists, that exists," there is no fixed cause.
By these two points, it is established that the Tathāgata’s teaching is not like that of the non-Buddhists.
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! I have realized that all phenomena are manifestations of mind-only, up to the point that this is not my own teaching.

This means that one realizes all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent and are unarisen, being merely manifestations of mind; therefore, there is no fault regarding the causes and conditions for the teaching of the Dharma.

"If one does not thus understand all phenomena (*dharmas*), but perceives objects as external to the mind and clings to existence and non-existence, then whatever is spoken becomes mere conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, if there are no phenomena, upon what basis do words arise?"

There is the name "causes and conditions for verbal expression," which must necessarily correspond to the phenomena that are the causes and conditions of what is expressed; if the nature of those causes and conditions of what is expressed did not exist, upon what would verbal expression depend to arise?
“Mahāmati! If one were to claim that although all dharmas do not exist, they nevertheless exist as dharmas, then this treatise would be undermined.
It is said that all dharmas are merely verbal designations and possess no real meaning; therefore, the analogies of tortoise hair and rabbit horns are cited.”
This clarifies that even if there were an intrinsic nature to verbal expression, there would still be no intrinsic nature to the phenomena being expressed. "Mahāmati!
It is not the case that all Buddha-fields possess verbal expression."
"Verbal expression is merely a provisional designation!
This further clarifies that the nature of verbal expression is also non-existent.
Thus, the *Awakening of Faith* states: "Because all verbal expressions are mere provisional names without reality, they cannot be apprehended except as they follow deluded thoughts."
"If it were said that there is an intrinsic nature in verbal expression, then all buddha-fields would necessarily possess speech.
However, Mahāmati,
there are some buddha-fields where the Dharma is manifested by a steady gaze, rather than through verbal expression."
The above [passage] refutes the claim that all buddha-fields possess verbal expression for the purpose of manifesting the Dharma; therefore, verbal expression lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
This is because even insects such as flies and ants in this world accomplish their own purposes despite lacking verbal expression.
The Blessed One said: "These verbal designations are merely conventional establishments!
Because these ignorant fools are like insects and ants, I employ verbal expressions to distinguish the characteristics of phenomena."
Therefore, the preceding sutra states: "All verbal expressions arise solely from the hopes and views of the ignorant.
It also says: "Even minute insects have no speech, yet each performs its own task."
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Beginning with space, a rabbit’s horns, and the son of a barren woman—though these do not exist, they are spoken of; the false conceptualization of dharmas is likewise."

"It is said that the three aforementioned things have no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), yet there is only verbal expression; one falsely discriminates all phenomena as being real and substantial, and their intrinsic nature is likewise so.
Within the conjunction of causes and conditions, the deluded falsely claim that things arise; unable to understand them as they truly are, they wander through the three realms of existence."
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-mahāsattva asked, "In what sense was the term 'eternal' spoken?
Thereupon, the Buddha told him that since both speech and that which is spoken are devoid of self-nature, there would be no such thing as the dharma of causes and conditions.

Therefore, Mahāmati cites other sūtras in which the Buddha himself explains that the twelve links of dependent origination—whether a Buddha appears or not—remain eternally constant in their nature and characteristics.
Thus, he asks upon what basis the term "eternal" (nitya) was spoken.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati, it is spoken in reliance upon false dharmas."
The Sage also manifests all delusive phenomena, yet he does not do so erroneously.

This means that he speaks of delusive phenomena as being permanent; for when foolish people perceive these delusive phenomena arising from causes and conditions, they grasp them as real and give rise to views of birth and extinction.
The Tathāgata has said that this is indeed permanent.
