Although those delusive phenomena also appear to the noble ones, they do not give rise to the inverted views of existence or non-existence. "Mahāmati!
"For example, a mirage, a fire-wheel, or falling hair—though these do not exist for one who possesses wisdom, they nonetheless appear.
These seven metaphors clarify that while the objective realm is one, the perceptions of it differ.
“Mahāmati! When false dharmas manifest, they appear in immeasurable varieties, extending to the various understandings of all foolish commoners.
Although those false dharmas manifest with various and immeasurable distinctions, like the moon reflected in water, they are not impermanent.
Why is it not impermanent?
Because false and illusory phenomena transcend both existence and non-existence, they are not impermanent.
How can false views arise from a state that transcends existence and non-existence?
It refers to the various objects of experience of foolish commoners; although these are places devoid of existence and non-existence, they give rise to various false views and understandings.
"Just as the waters of the Ganges are seen by some and not seen by others, so too do the Most Holy Ones remain free from inverted views regarding illusory phenomena."

"Just as the Ganges River appears as fire to hungry ghosts, who perceive fire where there is no fire—this is like seeing others as good people while failing to see them as such—so too do fools perceive falsehood where there is no falsehood; this is like seeing others as sages while failing to see them as such."
Therefore, because all noble ones are entirely free from the inverted views of existence and non-existence regarding false phenomena,
Mahāmati, false phenomena are eternal; thus, the essence of false phenomena is eternal.

This is because all false dharmas are said to be true and eternal, as no various distinct characteristics can be found; it is only through the deluded conceptualization of fools that they speak of there being distinctions.
“Mahāmati! How does one attain the reality of false dharmas such that it reaches the point of being beyond the speech of the noble ones?

That which possesses even a slight degree of conceptualization refers to the arising of the mind and the movement of thought; as soon as there is thought, it deviates from the essence of the Dharma because right mindfulness is lost.”
Having lost right mindfulness, is this not the frivolous conceptualization of a fool! "Mahāmati,
if one discriminates between false dharmas as being either inverted or non-inverted, one remains within the lineage of ordinary beings."

"If foolish people discriminate between the falsely imagined phenomena of dependent origination as either inverted or non-inverted, there consequently arise two kinds of distinctions in their spiritual lineages (*gotra*).

Mahāmati, the lineage of the noble ones (*ārya-gotra*) further consists of three types, namely those who are attached to specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)."
This means that those deluded persons, by observing false dharmas, grasp at their specific and general characteristics and give rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle.
"Mahāmati! What is meant by 'furthermore, there are deluded persons who [seek] to leave behind the clamor of the crowd'?"

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, that śrāvaka who becomes detached from clinging to the falsely perceived dharmas of self-characteristics and common characteristics gives rise to the lineage of the pratyekabuddhayāna."
"What is meant by the wise person’s discernment of delusive phenomena up to the point that no external phenomena exist?
The wise person contemplates the true reality (*dharmatā*) of these delusive phenomena and thoroughly understands both the seer and the seen, for they arise from one's own mind."
There is no external phenomenon characterized by the false conceptualization of existence or non-existence that gives rise to the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle. "Mahāmati!
There are foolish people who, through their discrimination of false phenomena, reach this point and thereby accomplish the nature of the vehicle of birth and death."
This explains the second type of lineage of the foolish.

It is said that all fools, regarding these delusive phenomena, grasp at various things as having intrinsic nature and characteristics; they resolutely cling to the existence of a real self and real dharmas, thereby giving rise to the lineage of the vehicle of birth and death.
“Mahāmati! Within those false dharmas, the various phenomena are neither entities nor non-entities.
To say that these false dharmas are free from existence and free from non-existence is called the lineage of the three vehicles and of ordinary beings.”
“Mahāmati! It is because those noble ones who possess wisdom have completely abandoned all conceptual constructions regarding those very same delusive phenomena.
This reiterates the explanation of the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle, as can be understood from the text itself.
Question:

It was stated above that illusory phenomena (*mṛṣādharma*) are eternal, yet they appear distinct due to conceptual differentiation (*vikalpa*); that is to say, it is precisely *tathatā* which, when conceptually differentiated by ordinary people (*bāla*), is termed "illusory phenomena."

This refers to the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of those very delusive phenomena; thus, it is said that these delusive phenomena themselves are named True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Since delusive phenomena are themselves True Suchness, there are no longer any delusive phenomena remaining—whom could one refer to when discussing "identity"?
The answer is:

It is like pointing to ice and saying it is water, or pointing to water and saying it is ice, to someone who does not recognize water; there are merely names—how could one argue that these two distinct things are identical in nature?

It is also like a single jewel that produces water when facing the moon and fire when facing the sun; when not so directed, there is neither water nor fire. A single entity has never been two, yet there is the distinction between water and fire!

The Dharma-gate of the One Mind is likewise so: when it resides in ordinary beings, True Suchness is called delusive phenomena; when it resides in sages, delusive phenomena are called True Suchness. For one whose sentiments of sagehood and ordinariness are exhausted and whose views of truth and falsehood have perished, who could possibly give it a name?
The Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
“World-Honored One,
are the delusive dharmas you have spoken of existent or non-existent?”

The passage above raises the question of whether the delusive phenomena perceived equally by those of the three vehicles and ordinary beings exist or do not exist, inquiring of the Tathāgata regarding this matter.
The Buddha said:
"Because they are like illusions and lack the characteristic of attachment, [the view that] 'an agent produces [them]' should be regarded as the teaching of the non-Buddhists."
It is said that false dharmas are like illusions, for they cannot be grasped through the conceptualization of existence or non-existence.

If one were to grasp at them as having real intrinsic nature or characteristics, they would become truly existent and unchangeable; consequently, all dependently arisen false dharmas would be identical to the externalists' view that all phenomena arise from existence or non-existence.
Mahāmati spoke again:
“If all false dharmas are identical to illusions, then they should serve as causes for other falsehoods.

If all false dharmas are identical to illusions, then this illusion should serve as the cause for the false dharmas of foolish worldlings, because it must inevitably bring about further retributive fruits in the future.”
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati, it is not because illusory phenomena themselves cease to exist that they are non-conceptual."
Illusion does not act as a cause for delusive confusion, because illusion is unreal and does not give rise to faults or conceptual discrimination.
If it were to give rise to various faults and produce conceptual discrimination, it would then constitute a cause; therefore, it does not act as a cause for other forms of delusion.
“Mahāmati! As for illusory phenomena, they arise from the spells of others and extend even to those who are not noble ones.
This clarifies that false dharmas are like illusions; if one conceives of them with the mind and becomes attached to them, such a person is merely a fool.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The Sage does not perceive false dharmas, nor is there anything real in the interim; because the false is itself the true, the interim is also truly real."
The first two lines state that because the Sages know the essence of delusive confusion to be without reality, they do not perceive delusive phenomena.
The latter two lines mean that by contemplating the true nature of delusive phenomena, delusive confusion is itself the ultimate reality.
"If there were a characteristic of arising that existed apart from delusive phenomena, this would itself still be delusive, like an eye disease that has not yet been cleared away.
Furthermore, Mahāmati!"
Because one perceives that all phenomena are not illusions, it is said that "all phenomena are like illusions.
This means that among all delusive phenomena, there is nothing else that resembles them more than an illusion; therefore, it is said that all phenomena are like illusions.
Mahāmati said:
"World-Honored One!
Is it because of attachment to this that one arrives at these inverted characteristics?"
Since it has been stated that there is nothing resembling [reality] other than illusion, does one say "it is like an illusion" because of clinging to various illusory appearances?
Or does one say "it is like an illusion" because of clinging to inverted characteristics distinct from this [reality]?
"If one relies on the attachment to various illusory appearances up to the perception of various formal characteristics, it is because they are not without cause.

If one calculates that illusory appearances mean all phenomena are like illusions, then other phenomena possessing intrinsic nature would not be like illusions; therefore, it is said that not all phenomena are entirely like illusions.
Why are they not like illusions?
Because the physical forms of men, women, gods, and humans are seen to have causes and are not produced by incantations or spells; therefore, they are not like illusions.
“World-Honored One!
There is absolutely no reason to say that all phenomena are similar to illusions.
This means that there is no distinct cause by which the various characteristics of form are manifested such that they could be said to be like illusions.
Therefore, one cannot say that all phenomena are like an illusion merely because they resemble illusory appearances.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati!..."
Because they do not rely on attachment and are unreal, quickly perishing like lightning, they are said to be "like an illusion.

It is not because the characteristics of an illusion possess various forms and those of humans and devas possess various forms—that these two phenomena are similar—that one says all dharmas are like an illusion.
Because all phenomena are unreal in their very essence, arising and ceasing as swiftly as a flash of lightning, they are said to be like illusions.

"Mahāmati! It is, for example, like a flash of lightning which, having been seen, immediately vanishes; yet people approach it and falsely conceptualize and cling to its various forms and appearances."
"Just as a flash of lightning appears for a mere instant and, having appeared, immediately vanishes— swift and impermanent—
so too, as seen by the world, the conjunction of all phenomena appears based on the false imaginings of one's own mind."
Unable to observe that [phenomena] are unreal and non-existent, they give rise to attachment to the specific and general characteristics of form.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"There is nothing that resembles illusion, nor do any phenomena exist; unreal and as swift as lightning, one should know them to be like illusions."
The first two lines of the verse praise the fact that there is nothing comparable to non-illusion, and thus all phenomena are said to be like illusions;
the latter two lines praise the preceding answer.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva [thought]: "Is it not the case that what has been said contradicts itself from beginning to end?"

Mahāmati said: "Because the Blessed One previously taught that all phenomena are unarisen, and now further states that they are unreal and as swift as lightning, and that all phenomena are like illusions, I say that what the Blessed One has taught earlier and later is mutually contradictory."
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! There is no contradiction, because one perceives that they lack intrinsic nature and are fundamentally unarisen."
"By realizing that all phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind, one knows that birth is fundamentally non-birth.
Thus, Nāgārjuna said:
'All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another; they do not arise from both, nor without a cause; therefore, know them to be unborn.'"
"Viewed in this way, external phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—all lack intrinsic nature; therefore, they are fundamentally unarisen. Mahāmati!

It is in order to distance oneself from the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) doctrine of arising from a cause that [I speak of] non-arising; because it is neither existent nor non-existent, it is called 'unborn'."
The non-Buddhists take the "agent" (kartṛ) to mean the cause of arising, asserting that all phenomena arise from existence or non-existence.
By "existence," they mean the existence of seeds—that is, [entities such as] Īśvara or atoms acting as the productive causes.
It is not that there is no cause or no seed, such that things arise spontaneously like empty space; rather, I do not say they arise from the deluded imaginings of one's own mind.
Therefore, when I speak of all phenomena, I mean that they are not produced without cause or by false causes as the non-Buddhists claim; it is for this reason alone that I call them "unborn."
“Mahāmati! Those who teach all dharmas do so in order to negate the nihilistic view of annihilation.
Thus spoke the Buddha to Mahāmati.

"I teach that all phenomena are neither existent nor non-existent and are unarisen; they arise solely as conditions through the discrimination of one's own mind. This is so that those to be converted may understand that although all phenomena lack a creator, karma does not perish."
Therefore, by embracing the two kinds of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), one refutes those wrong views of annihilationism and conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).

Thus, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* says: "The continuity of birth-and-death arises from internal causes and conditions without depending on external conditions; therefore, there is only consciousness (*vijñapti-mātra*)."
Thus, it is said that the two types of karma—contaminated (*sāsrava*) and uncontaminated (*anāsrava*)—directly induce birth and death (*saṃsāra*).
The conditions (*pratyaya*), namely the two obstacles—the afflictive (*kleśa*) and cognitive (*jñeya*)—assist in inducing birth and death. Why is this so?
There are two kinds of birth and death:

first, birth and death by stages (*prādeśika-utpāda-vyaya*), which refers to the coarse, heterogeneous maturation fruits (*vipāka-phala*) of the three realms produced by various contaminated wholesome and unwholesome karmas, through the auxiliary power of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*). Because the duration of the body and life has fixed limits determined by the force of causes and conditions, it is called "staged."

Second is the inconceivable death and rebirth through transformation (*pariṇāmi-cyuti*). This refers to the subtle, superior fruit of maturation (*vipāka*) induced by uncontaminated karma with conceptual differentiation, which is assisted by the power of the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Because the lifespan and physical existence are transformed through the power of compassion and vows, they lack fixed limits; hence it is called "transformation."
Its wondrous functioning is difficult to fathom; thus it is called "inconceivable.
As the Sūtra says: "There is no self, no agent, and no recipient; even the karma of good and evil does not exist."
"How could this be comparable to the nihilistic doctrine of the evil views!
The above concludes the Tathāgata’s exposition on the non-arising of phenomena.
The subsequent passage explaining that [phenomena] are like illusions correctly answers the two points [raised] and contains no contradiction."

“Mahāmati! From the teaching that the characteristics of all dharmas are like illusions up to the point where all dharmas abide in accordance with reality—what is meant by ‘abiding in accordance with reality’?
It means that because there is no place of abiding, it is called abiding in accordance with reality.”
This is the realm realized through the noble wisdom of self-awakening, the teacherless wisdom, and spontaneous wisdom; it is not awakened to by means of another.
If there were any place of abiding, that would constitute non-abiding.
“Mahāmati! To see all dharmas as they truly are means to be able to thoroughly comprehend that they are manifestations of the mind alone.
Since all dharmas are established from the rootless basis, how could one who does not realize that they are merely their own mind clearly perceive them?”
Therefore, there is no contradiction in what the Tathāgata has taught: that all phenomena are unarisen and like illusions.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke these verses again:

"Because they are unconditioned, they are unarisen; Phenomena encompass birth and death. Thoroughly understanding them as being like illusions and so forth, One does not discriminate among their marks."

Because they are of the nature of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*), they are said to be unarisen; yet, in order to prevent the view of annihilationism, it is taught that the nature of karma encompasses birth and death.

By contemplating all phenomena as having the illusory nature and characteristics of a magical creation, one finds no marks (*nimitta*) to be apprehended; therefore, one remains far removed from the conceptualization of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain that which leads to the awakening of all sentient beings.

Because the Tathāgata, out of compassion for sentient beings, employs various skillful means to provide diverse teachings, he speaks of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables (*nāma-pada-vyañjana-kāya*) so that sentient beings may understand the true meaning within names and phrases, rather than becoming attached to mere verbal expression."

I tell all bodhisattvas: those who can contemplate these signs and penetrate their underlying meaning will swiftly attain bodhi, and furthermore, they will be able to awaken sentient beings through this very means.

Know that dharmas are neither words nor signs, yet they are not apart from words and signs; if there were no words or signs, one would be deluded and inverted, and by clinging to words and signs, one becomes confused about the truth.
Therefore, when the Sages manifest themselves for the benefit of others, establishing signs and instituting teachings, how could it be in vain!
"Mahāmati, 'name-body' (nāmakāya) refers to the establishment of names based on phenomena; up to this point is what is called the 'syllable-body' (vyañjanakāya)."

Just as the designation "jar" or "bowl" is established based on the physical objects of jars and bowls—whereby a single name, two names, or many names express their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva)—this is called a "name-group" (*nāmakāya*).

Regarding "phrase-groups" (*padakāya*) and so forth: it is because of names that phrases are formed, and because of phrases that meaning is revealed. Just as there are jars made of copper, iron, and so forth, phrases have distinct meanings; that is, a single phrase, two phrases, or many phrases that express specific distinctions are called a "phrase-group."
Because these [phonemes] can constitute a name (nāman), they are called "name-bodies" (nāmakāya); that is, one, two, or many phonemes serve as the basis for two types of names.
If one follows the ancient translations and translates *vyañjana* as "flavor" (*rasa*), this refers only to what is manifested, not to that which manifests.
"Body" (*kāya*) has the meaning of an accumulation of many dharmas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati,
"phrase-body" (*padakāya*) refers to the completion of the meaning of a phrase, ranging from the long and short to the high and low.
From this point downward, the distinct meanings are further elucidated.

Regarding the phrase "the body of a sentence (*padakāya*) refers to the completion of the meaning of a sentence": when there is a phoneme (*vyañjana*), there must necessarily be a name (*nāman*), yet it does not necessarily have a sentence;
however, when there is a sentence, there must necessarily be both a name and a phoneme. Therefore, it is said that "the matter of the sentence is complete."

Regarding "name-bodies" (*nāmakāya*): this refers to the various distinct names formed by individual syllables, such as from the letter *a* up to the letter *ha*. For instance, among the fourteen vowels, such as *a* and *ā*, each begins with the short vowel followed by the long one, and the same applies to the high and low tones.
Therefore, the subsequent mention of "letter-bodies" (vyañjana-kāya) refers to long and short, high and low; that is, the modulations of pitch and the variations in length and height of the phonemes.
This is because phrases and sentences must necessarily be established based upon letters.
Commentary on the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Four;
Commentary on the Mahāyāna Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Five:

"Furthermore, regarding the 'body of phrases' (*padakāya*), it is like footprints reaching this point; you should cultivate the characteristics of the bodies of phrases, words, and letters (*nāmakāya*, *vyañjanakāya*)."
"Study. No phenomena in the world transcend the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); this, moreover, clarifies the bodies of names, phrases, and phonemes by way of the five aggregates.
Regarding the phrase "the body of phrases is like a footprint," it means that just as people who have lost an elephant or a horse find them by following their tracks.
Therefore, even those who are obscured regarding the true nature of reality attain awakening through words.
These are the "bodies of names" (*nāmakāya*); because their characteristics are manifested within the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), they are spoken of in terms of their traces.
As for the four aggregates—feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—they lack physical manifestations; therefore, they are explained by means of names.
If one perceives that which is fundamentally quiescent, this is the true reality (*dharmatā*).
Second, the text clearly exhorts one to practice and study:
because the sages of antiquity attained awakening through this, they sacrificed their entire bodies to seek even half a verse.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The distinctions between the body of names, the body of phrases, and the body of syllables—these are what the foolish and ignorant cling to, like an elephant sinking into deep mud.”

The Tathāgata, in order to eliminate the mental afflictions of sentient beings, employs the skillful means of names, phrases, and syllables to teach the Dharma, much like using poison to counteract poison.
If foolish people remain attached to these names and phrases and fail to awaken to the true meaning, they will have no prospect of liberation; they are like a fragrant elephant sinking into the mud.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
In a future age, when someone asks such a question, they will immediately reply: 'This is not a correct question.

This is because, based on the aforementioned characteristics of the bodies of names, phrases, and syllables, it enables all bodhisattvas to comprehend the meaning as it truly is, swiftly attain Bodhi, and reveal it to sentient beings."
Fearing that in future ages those with evil conceptualizations might question the wise using the fourfold logic of identity, difference, both, or neither based on false views, they will respond:
"The meaning I have realized is the true Dharma that transcends the four extremes; your current question is not a valid inquiry."
"To say that 'form is either different from or not different from impermanence' and so forth, up to the point where it is not definitively explained—
this describes the words of those with false wisdom and evil thoughts who engage in vain speculation and irrational questioning."
That is to say, whether form and impermanence, up to wisdom and the wise person, are different or not different.
The wise person should reply:
"Such questions are matters that should not be explained; the Buddha termed them 'unexplained' (avyākṛta) and set them aside."

Because those foolish people lack the wisdom derived from hearing, they do not know what exists or does not exist, nor what is erroneous or correct; therefore, in order to cause them to abandon the fears arising from the false views of nihilism and eternalism, I do not provide a definitive explanation.
The nineteenth fascicle of the *Abhidharmakośa* states:
"The various sūtras speak of fourteen indeterminate [questions]"; this is precisely that meaning, which is also termed the "set-aside answer" (*sthāpanīya-praśna*).
The reason I did not answer was that this constitutes meaningless speech.
To know this does not exempt one from birth and death; to not know it does not obstruct nirvana. "Mahāmati!
"Not answering" refers to such teachings as these, which are termed "indeterminate discourse.

The reason for not providing an answer is the desire to cause non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) to reflect inwardly and achieve self-understanding, thereby enabling them to escape the false views regarding a creator.
Because non-Buddhists conceive of a self as being either identical to or distinct from the aggregates, they debate whether the body and life are one or different;
these are all merely indeterminate and heterodox doctrines! "Mahāmati!..."
"The heterodox teachers, deluded by ignorance, propound the theory of the indeterminate, even claiming that one should desist from teaching until the faculties [of the listener] have matured.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, constantly teaches the Dharma to deliver sentient beings through the four modes of answering questions.

Regarding the "setting aside" (sthāpanīya) of questions, the intention is to defer them to another time; because the faculties of sentient beings are not yet mature, one temporarily sets them aside rather than answering, but this "setting aside" is not taught for those whose faculties are mature.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
For what reason are all dharmas unarisen?
It is for this reason that I say all dharmas are eternal."
It is said that the Tathāgata, for the sake of sentient beings whose faculties are matured, opens the gate of skillful means to reveal the true aspect.
According to their respective types, he may speak of non-arising, non-ceasing, permanence, impermanence, and so forth.
This means that because there is no agent apart from the action and the object of action, it is said that all phenomena are unarisen.
Because they cannot be apprehended through realized wisdom when examining their specific and general characteristics, it is said that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
All phenomena originally come from nowhere, and in departing they go nowhere; therefore, it is said that all phenomena have neither coming nor going.
Since the essence of all phenomena is empty, lacking intrinsic nature or characteristics, and is ungraspable, it is said that all phenomena are not extinguished.
All phenomena arise and immediately perish because their nature is impermanent; thus, it is said that all phenomena are impermanent.

The very arising of the characteristics of all phenomena is non-arising; they are fundamentally without birth or death, and their impermanent nature is itself eternal; thus, it is said that all phenomena are eternal.
This is called the Tathāgata’s skillful teaching of the Dharma, being free from the grasped and the grasper and not giving rise to conceptual discrimination.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“Direct answers, counter-questions, analytical answers, and setting aside—these extend to all that is indeterminate.”
Regarding the four modes of the Tathāgata’s speech:
the first is answering according to the question, which is called "categorical" (ekāṃśa).
For example: [if one asks:]
If asked, "Are all sentient beings subject to birth and death?
one should answer categorically:
"They are all subject to birth and death."
The second refers to when there is an inquirer, one answers by posing a counter-question; this is called "counter-interrogation" (*paripṛcchā*).
The third refers to when the faculties of the inquirer are mature, one provides a detailed analysis.
For example: "When all sentient beings die, do they then take birth again?"
One should distinguish between those with afflictions, who die and are reborn, and those without afflictions, who do not take birth after death.
Fourth, one must set aside the answer in order to subdue non-Buddhists.
It is like asking which comes first, the body or its afflictions, or the chick or the mother hen;
therefore, one remains silent and does not answer.
Just as the Sāṃkhyas reckon existence and the Vaiśeṣikas reckon non-existence, such views of the non-Buddhists regarding existence, non-existence, and so forth, are all undeclared.
"When observed through wisdom, its essential nature cannot be apprehended; because it is inexpressible, it is said to be without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
This clarifies that when right wisdom observes, intrinsic nature is non-existent, thereby encompassing the six preceding sections on the non-arising of all phenomena and so forth.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reached the section on "The Distinctive Characteristics of the Practice of the Srotāpanna.

Because Mahāmati had previously observed that ordinary people give rise to the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle through their discrimination of false dharmas, and because within the Śrāvaka teachings there are four distinct fruits of realization, he raised these four fruits as a question for inquiry.
"Practice" refers to causal practice; it is the causal practice cultivated by one who has attained the stage of Srotāpanna, as they are about to proceed toward the fruit of Arhatship.
Because their faculties are either sharp or dull, there are distinctions among them.
"I and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas shall reach the point where all sentient beings are fully benefited.
As for what is called the "characteristic of skillful means," it refers to the characteristic of the skillful means in the cultivation of the four fruits [of the śrāvaka path].
*Srotāpanna* (須陀洹) is translated here as "Stream-enterer" (*yuliu*).

This refers to one who, from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), cultivates the seven preparatory practices (*saptaprayoga*) and gives rise to the eight patiences (*aṣṭakṣānti*) and eight knowledges (*aṣṭajñāna*). By severing the eighty-eight proclivities (*aṣṭāśīty-anuśaya*) of conceptual delusion within the four truths of the three realms, one is termed a candidate for the first fruit (*prathamaphalapratipannaka*) when the [delusions] up to the eighty-seventh category have been severed; when the eighty-eighth category is exhausted, it is called the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Because one has newly entered the stream of the noble ones (*ārya*), it is named "Stream-enterer."
*Sakṛdāgāmin* (once-returner) is translated here as "one who comes back once.

This refers to the stage after the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*) of the first fruit, wherein one gives rise to nine paths of uninterrupted transition (*ānantaryamārga*) and nine paths of liberation (*vimuktimārga*) to sever the eighty-one grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*) across the nine stages of the three realms (nine times nine equals eighty-one).
Furthermore, the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in a single stage of the desire realm collectively sustain seven births.

Within the body of one who has attained the first fruit (srotāpanna), when the first five grades of the desire realm are completely abandoned, one is termed a candidate for the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmipratipannaka); when the sixth grade is abandoned, one is termed the second fruit (sakṛdāgāmin).

Having passed away from this life, one must once more go to the heavens and once return to the human realm to sever the remaining three grades of afflictions; therefore, it is called "one who goes and returns" (sakṛdāgāmin).

Anāgāmin, here translated as "Non-returner," refers to one who, while already within the state of the second fruit, has abandoned the nine grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation in the desire realm; having exhausted up to the eighth grade, they are termed a candidate for the third fruit (trtīyaphalapratipannaka), and upon exhausting the ninth grade, they are termed the third fruit itself.
Having once gone to the heavens of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), they do not return again to take birth in the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); therefore, they are called "Non-returners" (*anāgāmin*).
The aforementioned three types of fruit-attainers are termed those in training (*śaikṣa*).
There are three translations for "Arhat":
first, "Slayer of Thieves" (Killer of Māras); second, "Non-arising" (Anutpāda); and third, "Worthy of Offerings" (Arhat).

This refers to one within the body of the third fruit who has severed the eighty-one grades of afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation across the eight stages of the two upper realms; having severed up to seventy-one grades, they are called a candidate for the fourth fruit, and when the seventy-second grade is completely severed, they are called the fourth fruit of Arhatship, the stage of No-more-learning (Aśaikṣa).

Therefore, one should simply exhaust all ordinary sentiments and possess no separate "sage-understanding. When Bodhisattvas attain such skillful means, they preach such Śrāvaka-dharmas and such Bodhisattva-dharmas for sentient beings, causing them to realize the selflessness of persons and phenomena, to purify the afflictive and cognitive hindrances, and to ultimately penetrate the characteristics of the various stages until reaching the realm realized by the Tathāgata. Thus they obtain the Dharma-body and the wealth of the Buddha, benefiting beings without end.
Because of these benefits, he requested the Tathāgata to explain the distinctions among the four fruits.
The Buddha said, "Listen attentively!
I shall explain them for you; there are three distinctions, namely: inferior, middling, and superior."
The Master asked:
"Regarding all those who are stream-enterers (srotāpanna) and the practice of the stream-enterer—
now you answer as follows:"
Regarding the various fruits of the Srotāpanna, they are spoken of as mutually illustrative; because their faculties differ—being either sharp or dull—there are three [categories].
"Mahāmati! The inferior [Srotāpanna] attains the highest among all states of existence, while the superior enters nirvāṇa in this very life."
Regarding "one who is reborn seven times": this refers to a single level within the desire realm where the nine grades of innate afflictions collectively moisten seven births.
Specifically, the first grade moistens two births; the next three grades each moisten one birth; the next two grades together moisten one birth; and the final three grades together moisten one birth.

It clarifies that even the most dull-witted *srotāpanna* has not yet severed the afflictions of the desire realm; therefore, they attain *arhatship* after seven往返 (return-and-go) cycles among humans and devas.
This is illustrated by the analogy of a venomous snake biting a person, who dies within seven steps.
Why not four or six?
It is because of the great power [of the path]. Why not eight?
It is because of the power of the poison.
To use an analogy: why does a *srotāpanna* not undergo six more births?
It is because the power of their afflictions (*kleśa*) is strong.
Why do they not undergo eight births?
Because their untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) has reached maturity.
Those of middling capacity may attain the fruit of Arhatship and Nirvana after three or five births.

As for those of superior faculties, they attain the fruit of Arhatship in this very life; they are called "Srotāpannas who attain extinction in the present existence," and it is not said that they pass through the two intermediate fruits.
"Mahāmati! These three types of persons sever the three fetters and attain the fruit of arhatship.
This means that although the *srotāpanna* differs in three ways according to whether their faculties are sharp or dull, they all universally sever the three fetters.
That is to say, clinging to the five aggregates of grasping as "self" or "belonging to self" is called the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); it is one fetter (*saṃyojana*).
To be hesitant and indecisive regarding the principles of the Truths—doubting whether the Buddha or non-Buddhists are correct and not knowing which is the right path—is doubt (*vicikitsā*).
These are two fetters.

That is to say, regarding false views, to follow the irrational ascetic practices and observances of non-Buddhists, and to cling to them as supreme, believing they can bring about purification—this is the third fetter.
Question:
Since one who has already permanently severed all afflictions to be abandoned through the path of seeing attains the fruit of a *srotāpanna*,
why is it said that only these three types of persons sever the three fetters?
Answer:
Because they are comprised of the most preeminent [fetters]. That is to say, these three types of fetters are the most distinguished in obstructing the attainment of liberation. Why is this so?

Due to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), one grasps the five aggregates as "I" and "mine," giving rise to deep attachment and delight; consequently, one does not develop revulsion toward this great mass of suffering, nor does one give rise to the aspiration for supreme liberation.

There may be sentient beings who, although they have already set out toward liberation, nevertheless—due to adherence to rules and observances (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*) and doubt (*vicikitsā*), and because they perversely cling to false paths while doubting the true path—proceed toward a false deliverance and an incorrect deliverance.

Furthermore, these three fetters are the causes for delusion regarding the objects of knowledge, the causes for delusion regarding views, and the causes for delusion regarding the antidotes. As the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "The abandonment of the three fetters is called the fruit of stream-entry;
the attenuation of greed, hatred, and delusion is called the fruit of once-returning;
and the permanent exhaustion of the five lower-tier fetters is called the fruit of non-returning."
The permanent exhaustion of the five fetters conducive to the higher realms is called the fruit of arhatship;
causing all phenomena of origination to become phenomena of cessation is called the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
and the permanent severance of the continuity of all habitual tendencies is called unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
These points all summarize the essentials of the Shared Teaching (Sādhāraṇa-yāna).

Regarding the statement that one attains the higher and further advancement of Arhatship: it means that the fetters (*saṃyojana*) severed by a Srotāpanna are divided into nine grades, and the wisdom capable of severing those fetters is likewise divided into nine grades.
If a beginner’s wisdom is weak, it is called the lowest-of-the-low wisdom; yet it can sever the highest-of-the-high fetters.

The wisdom of one who has practiced for a long time is called "comprehension" (liao) and is termed the highest-of-the-high wisdom; it can sever the lowest-of-the-low fetters and attain the fruit of Arhatship and Nirvana.
“Mahāmati! There are two kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi* (the view of a self-identity), which are abandoned as soon as one realizes the selflessness of persons.

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* states: “Among the ten afflictions—both general and specific—consisting of greed, hatred, delusion, pride, doubt, *satkāyadṛṣṭi*, *antagrāhadṛṣṭi*, *mithyādṛṣṭi*, *dṛṣṭiparāmarśa*, and *śīlavrataparāmarśa*, six are capable of arising both spontaneously (*sahaja*) and through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpita*), because they can arise both through natural spontaneity and through deliberate reflection.”
The four types—doubt, wrong view, and the two types of grasping—arise solely through conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
This is because they can only be produced by means of the influence of evil friends or false teachings, following one's own critical reflection and investigation.
The Sūtra states that there are two kinds of satkāyadṛṣṭi (the view of a self-identity): namely, the innate (*sahaja*) and the conceptually constructed (*vikalpita*).
This is analogous to how various natures of false conceptualization and attachment arise based upon the *paratantrasvabhāva* (dependent nature).

Just as there is that which arises through conceptualization based upon what is co-nascent—namely, the false view of a self-body arising in dependence on the five aggregates—because those conceptualizations are unreal, they are neither existent nor non-existent, yet the foolish grasp at them erroneously.
Just as there is no water in a mirage, yet deer driven by thirst falsely conceive it to be water;
so too this discrimination of the view of a self-body (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), due to a lack of wisdom, has long been associated with the grasping at "I" and "mine."

Although the stream-enterer observes that this person is composed of the five aggregates and that there is no self within them, by means of thorough contemplation, they perceive the non-self of persons;
they immediately relinquish it and sever the conceptualization of the view of a self in the body.
“Mahāmati! When the innate view of self (satkāyadṛṣṭi) reaches the point where craving no longer arises, this is called the characteristic of the view of self.

It means being able to universally contemplate that one’s own body and the bodies of others are equal, and that the aggregates of feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, together with the aggregate of form, exist only as names and lack substantiality, having no characteristic of intrinsic nature.”

Contemplate that the aggregate of form is produced from the four great elements, arising through their mutual dependence; since there is no sovereign within these four great elements, who is able to assemble them to constitute form?

If even the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), which possesses substance, is empty, how much more so the other four aggregates such as sensation (*vedanā*), which lack any material characteristics; are they not, therefore, empty?

Observing in this way, one clearly sees that both existence and non-existence are equally false and unreal; the five aggregates have no essence, and the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) is thereby severed.
Generally, those who possess craving and attachment harbor the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*); since one has abandoned this view of a self-identity, from what could craving arise?
Thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "The cause of all sufferings is rooted in craving."
Because greed does not arise, this is called the characteristic of severing the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). "Mahāmati!
As for the characteristic of doubt, it is because one has clearly perceived the characteristics of the dharmas to be realized; thus it is called the characteristic of doubt."

This means that because one has clearly perceived the characteristics of the four noble truths as they have been realized, one is able to definitively sever the two kinds of false conceptualization regarding the view of a self; thus, doubt has no basis to arise, nor does one conceive of Māras, non-Buddhists, or ordinary worldlings as being Great Teachers.
Arising from pure views is called the characteristic of severing doubt.
"Mahāmati! For what reason does a srotāpanna not grasp at precepts and observances? This is called the characteristic of grasping at precepts and observances."

It is said that the *srotāpanna* does not grasp at the precept of taking future rebirth; observing that wherever there is birth, there is suffering, they do not seek the pleasure of a place of rebirth.

As for those who do grasp, it refers to the foolish who, within the three realms of existence, seek the pleasures of the five desires and practice asceticism with diligence and uphold the precepts, vowing to be born in those places.
This is similar to the case of Nanda, who observed the precepts for the sake of seeking female beauty.

A *srotāpanna* does not grasp at the five sensual pleasures of future rebirths; rather, they seek only the supreme, untainted principle of the Four Noble Truths—the non-conceptual Dharma—and through skillful means, they uphold and practice the right precepts. This is called severing the characteristic of clinging to rules and rituals (*śīlavrataparāmarśa*).
“Mahāmati! Because the *srotāpanna* abandons the three fetters, he reaches this state; therefore, he abandons that craving which is not for *nirvāṇa*.

Ordinary beings are unable to abandon the three fetters and do not realize the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), because due to the view of a self-body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), they cling to this ‘self.’”

One covets fame and profit to bring glory to oneself; one feels anger toward circumstances that conflict with one's desires, fearing they will harm oneself; and through ignorance, one misinterprets reality and engages in irrational calculations.

One fails to realize that the five aggregates are entirely devoid of a self or a master; they are merely the physical form and the deluded mind. Since beginningless time, due to the power of causes and conditions, they arise and perish moment by moment, continuing in an unceasing succession.
Like a trickling stream or a flickering flame, the body and mind are a provisional union that appears to be one and constant.
Ordinary fools do not perceive this and grasp at it as a self, thereby giving rise to all fetters.
The *srotāpanna*, as observed above, perceives that the five aggregates have no master; because they have abandoned the three fetters, they are free from greed, hatred, and delusion.
Ordinary worldlings crave the five desires, while *śrāvakas* crave supramundane *nirvāṇa*; therefore, it is said that there are many kinds of craving.
Because the color of women is the most extreme, it alone is mentioned as that which one must abandon—the entanglement of desire;
yet, because one has attained the bliss of samādhi and right reception (samyaksamādhi), one has not yet been able to sever craving for nirvāṇa.
This is because those who belong to the Bodhisattva vehicle are able to relinquish both of these types of craving.
"Mahāmati! How is it that one who has reached the fruit of a Sakṛdāgāmin attains parinirvāṇa? This is called being a Sakṛdāgāmin.
One who does not understand the characteristics of form gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding form."

The Sakṛdāgāmin contemplates that various forms and appearances arise from false conceptualization; therefore, after coming and going once more between the human and celestial realms, he skillfully cultivates meditative concentration and wisdom, so that the view of self no longer arises. Having reached the ultimate limit of suffering and attained nirvāṇa, he is thus called a Sakṛdāgāmin.
“Mahāmati! What is meant by ‘the fruit of the Āgama reaching the point of no further return,’ which is called Anāgāmin?
Furthermore, Anāgāmin means ‘one who has emerged from the mire of desire,’ for the afflictions of the Desire Realm are like a mire.”
Those who are *anāgāmins* have already transcended the desire realm and are all born in the form realm.

They contemplate that the nature of form throughout the three periods of time is without reality, and they see that wherever there is birth for ordinary beings, there are the faults and evils of various sufferings.

With the non-arising of the habitual tendencies of afflictions and the abandonment of all fetters, they no longer return to take birth in the desire realm, but instead exhaust all outflows within the form realm heavens; therefore, they are called Anāgāmins.
“Mahāmati! An Arhat is so named because they have reached the point where conceptual discrimination is forever exhausted.

It is said that an Arhat practices the four dhyānas and the three samādhis, fully realizes the eight liberations, partially attains the ten powers, and has accomplished the three vidyās and six abhijñās. Because the delusive thoughts that give rise to the various sufferings summoned by afflictions and karmic formations have been eternally extinguished, they are called Arhats.”
Mahāmati said:
"World-Honored One!
There are three kinds of Arhats who manifest birth upon reaching that state."
The *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra-upadeśa* state: "There are four types of śrāvakas:
first, those of determined lineage, also called 'those who incline toward tranquility';
second, those of overweening pride, who are ordinary persons that have attained the fourth dhyāna and claim to be arhats."

Third, those who have once regressed but subsequently give rise again to the great bodhicitta are also called those of indeterminate lineage; they are of the same class as the śrāvakas such as Śāriputra in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* assembly who received their prediction.

Fourth, those who are manifested through transformation rather than being real, referring to the manifestations of Buddhas and bodhisattvas appearing in transformed form to lead actual śrāvakas toward the Mahāyāna.
Regarding the question posed in this sutra, excluding those with overweening pride, there are only three types. To explain which these are:

the Buddha told Mahāmati that those Arhats of fixed nature who have attained quiescence—having severed the afflictions of the four abodes, emerged from the suffering of birth and death, and attained nirvana—are none other than these.

Those who, having regressed, have again resolved upon the mind of great enlightenment; those who, having already generated skillful and vast vows and practices, were matured by Buddhas as their emanations; and those who, for the sake of adorning the Buddha-fields and the assemblies of followers, manifest birth there and act as arhats.
“Mahāmati! Regarding the locus of falsehood, various dharmas are taught so that one may attain the marks of fruition through what is seen as one’s own mind.

This means that for the sake of sentient beings who are subject to false conceptualization, various dharmas are taught; the four fruits realized through the severance of all afflictions, as well as the practices of meditation and the various dhyānas and samādhis known according to reality, are all by nature detached [from inherent existence]. They are merely the marks of fruition attained through what is falsely seen within the measure of one’s own mind!

“Mahāmati! If a srotāpanna were to think such thoughts as ‘...and the various fetters are not severed,’ this clarifies that although one who has attained the first fruit has severed the fetters, he ultimately never gives rise to the thought: ‘I am able to sever the fetters.’”
If one gives rise to such a thought, there would be two faults: namely, falling into the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*) and failing to sever the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), among others.
This applies analogously to the other three fruits as well; thus, in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, the Buddha asked: "Subhūti!..."
"From the stage of srotāpanna up to arhat, can one form the thought: 'I have attained the four fruits beginning with srotāpanna'?
Subhūti replied, "No, indeed not."
“World-Honored One!
To entertain such a thought is itself to be attached to a self, a person, a sentient being, or a life-span.

Although the provisional vehicle is said to be dull and inferior, if one does not abandon coarse and deluded thoughts, one likewise cannot sever birth-and-death within the limits of a segmented existence.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
If one wishes to transcend all meditative absorptions (*dhyāna*), the immeasurables (*apramāṇa*), and so forth, until reaching the state where the mind is not abandoned, one must do so.

To speak of wishing to transcend the various *dhyānas* and four immeasurable minds of the śrāvakas, as well as the four formless attainments (*ārūpyasamāpatti*) and so on, and to obtain the samādhi of the Tathāgata—one should abandon the marks of the false conceptualizations of one's own mind within the triple world."
Mahāmati! For the śrāvakas, the ultimate fruit consists precisely in the attainment of the meditative absorption of the cessation of perception and feeling.
To claim that they transcend the measure of the mind (cittamātra) is not so.
Why is this? Because the mind of false conceptualization has not yet been extinguished.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
“The various dhyānas, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, and the cessation of perception and feeling—none of these can be apprehended apart from mind alone.
By “the various dhyānas” is meant the four dhyānas.
The "immeasurables" (apramāṇa) refer to loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity—the four immeasurable minds for delivering sentient beings.
The "formless samādhis" (ārūpya-samādhi) refer to the four formless absorptions (ārūpya-samāpatti).
The cessation of perception and feeling refers to the four dhyānas and the four formless attainments, wherein both feeling and perception are entirely stilled.
These are all merely the measure of mind; since they do not exist at all, it is said that "mind alone cannot be apprehended."
"The stream-enterer, the once-returner, the non-returner, and the arhat—all such noble ones exist entirely based on the delusion of the mind.

This next passage clarifies that even the four fruits of the path do not depart from the measure of the deluded mind; therefore, it says, "all such noble ones exist entirely based on the delusion of the mind."
The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "Because there is deluded karma, there is deluded perception of saṃsāra; those who weary of saṃsāra perceive nirvāṇa as a delusion.

"The practitioner of dhyāna takes that which is the object of meditation as his focus, severing delusions to perceive the True Truth—all of these are but discursive thoughts; to realize this is liberation."
The first verse clarifies the dharmas to be practiced; the second verse clarifies the person who realizes them.

This third verse clarifies both the object and the subject together, showing that neither is separate from the mind-measure of deluded thought (*vikalpa-citta-mātra*). If one awakens to reality as it is, one speaks of *nirvāṇa* because of the false conceptualization of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). Since the birth and death to be remedied no longer exist, the *nirvāṇa* that remedies them is also discarded; thus, the Bodhisattva attains all-encompassing liberation.

"Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are two kinds of cognitive awareness (*buddhi*): that which reaches up to the grasping of signs through discrimination and attachment, and the wisdom of establishment (*vyavasthāpana-jñāna*).

Because the preceding verse stated that 'thoroughly knowing is liberation,' yet one observes that there is cognitive awareness which does not lead to liberation, these two kinds of cognitive awareness are cited here to distinguish between the superior and the inferior."
That is to say, the wisdom of perfect awakening consists in observing and knowing the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena.

Not knowing that both persons and phenomena are empty of self, one grasps at signs and adheres to them by establishing a self; to understand things in such a way is the wisdom of false awakening, which does not attain liberation.
"The wisdom of observation refers to observing all phenomena; you should train yourself in this way of observing phenomena.
What is the wisdom of grasping signs, conceptualizing, adhering, and establishing? This is called the characteristic of the two kinds of awakened wisdom."

Ordinary worldlings conceive of and cling to the characteristics of a great elemental nature; through false conceptualization and discrimination, they employ the five-membered syllogistic method of thesis, reason, and example to falsely establish what is unreal. This is called the characteristic of the two kinds of awareness: the erroneous and the correct.
The Tathāgata uses a wedge to extract a wedge; as previously explained to refute the calculations of the non-Buddhists, he also teaches the three-membered inference and the five-membered syllogism.
"When a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva knows these characteristics of wisdom, they extend to the illumination of a hundred Buddha-worlds."

If a bodhisattva-mahāsattva realizes that delusion is itself the truth and understands these two aspects of awakened wisdom, they comprehend the emptiness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*) such that a self cannot be found. By means of non-conceptual, signless wisdom (*animitta-jñāna*), they skillfully investigate while in the stage of practice through resolute belief (*adhimukti-caryā-bhūmi*) prior to the [first] ground; thus they enter the first ground, attain one hundred samādhi-doors such as the "Luminosity of the Mahāyāna," and by its superior power see one hundred Buddhas, even to the point of illuminating one hundred Buddha-worlds with light.
Therefore, the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* states: "When a bodhisattva enters the first stage (*bhūmi*), they realize ten hundred gates of clarity (*vidyāmukha*):
first, in a single kṣaṇa, they realize one hundred samādhis;
second, with the pure divine eye, they see one hundred buddha-fields."
Third, by means of the power of supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*), one is able to shake a hundred Buddha-worlds;
fourth, one is able to travel to a hundred Buddha-worlds to teach and transform sentient beings;
fifth, one is able to manifest a hundred types of physical forms from a single body so that sentient beings may see them.
Sixth, he is able to bring to maturity a hundred types of sentient beings to be converted;
seventh, for the sake of benefiting others, he is able to maintain his physical body in the world for a hundred eons;
eighth, he is able to know the events of a hundred eons regarding both the past and the future limits.
Ninth, they are able to enter the gate of illumination of the hundred dharmas through wisdom, penetrating and fully comprehending them;
tenth, they are able to observe the hundred classes of retinues with their bodies, with each successive stage increasing in excellence tenfold.
"One is well able to thoroughly understand the characteristics of the progressively higher stages (uttarottara-bhūmi) up to the supreme bliss of the samādhi of the realm of self-realization.
This refers to the second stage, the Stainless (vimalā), and so on, up to the Tathāgata stage; all of these are the fulfillment of the ten inexhaustible vows within the first stage.
The details are found in such sutras as the *Avataṃsaka*; the remaining meanings are evident from the scriptural text itself.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should thoroughly understand the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the matter derived from them (*bhautika-rūpa*)."

Because the aforementioned non-Buddhists postulate the existence of the nature of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and thereby construct the material forms (*rūpa*) derived from those four great elements, [the Buddha] next exhorts the Bodhisattva to thoroughly understand the great elements and their derivative matter, so that he may realize they lack substantial reality.
"How is this fully understood? Mahāmati!
By reaching and abiding in the state of suchness, one accomplishes the characteristic of non-arising."
Regarding the term "non-arising," there are generally two explanations:
first, non-arising in principle, because the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) is fundamentally unarisen;
second, non-arising in phenomena, because the characteristics of dependent origination are themselves non-arising.

Regarding the statement that "abiding in the state of suchness accomplishes the characteristic of non-arising," this means that by contemplating the three realms as being manifestations of mind alone, one becomes detached from self and what belongs to self, thereby realizing that both principle and phenomena are equally non-arising.
“Mahāmati! How do those great elements (mahābhūta) construct form, up to the arising of form constructed from the great elements?
This passage reveals the false conceptualization of non-Buddhists that the four great elements give rise to derived matter (upādāya-rūpa).

That is to say, through false conceptualization, they reckon that there is a nature of moisture as the water element (*āpas*), which gives rise to the internal and external water realms; internally, this consists of blood, sweat, and flowing fluids, while externally, it consists of rivers, oceans, springs, and sources.

That which possesses the nature of blazing heat and maturation is the fire element; it gives rise to the internal and external realms of fire. Internally, it contains warmth within the body; externally, it incinerates all things.

That which has the nature of movement is the wind element (vāyu-mahābhūta), giving rise to the internal and external wind realms; internally, it is the movement of the breath, and externally, it is the chorus of all myriad sounds.

That which has the nature of being delimited by material form is the earth element (*pṛthivī-mahābhūta*); it gives rise to the internal and external realms of earth. The internal consists of skin, flesh, sinews, and bones; the external consists of plains, marshes, and hills.

Through false conceptualization, they reckon that solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion exist apart from space; due to their adherence to false truths, they fail to understand that the five aggregates are a provisional accumulation lacking inherent nature, and instead claim that derived matter is produced by the great elements. Therefore, the Buddha told the Bodhisattvas that they should thoroughly understand this.
“Mahāmati! Consciousness (vijñāna) is that which, through attachment to various [objects], continues in succession to take birth within other realms of existence.

When it says “consciousness,” it refers to the deluded consciousness (*mṛṣā-vijñāna*) within the aforementioned five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). It is produced by being deluded regarding the true mind (*tathatā-citta*), for it takes attachment to various realms of verbal expression as its immediate cause.
Through the ripening of karma, one undergoes rebirth, with the continuity of existence remaining uninterrupted throughout the various realms of existence.
One should know that both the internal body and external objects—the four great elements and the five aggregates—are merely manifestations of the mind’s own discrimination.

"Mahāmati! The view that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) such as earth and so forth, which are derived form (*upādāya-rūpa*), are caused by [external] great elements is a conceptual construction of the non-Buddhists; it is not my teaching.

It is not that the four great elements act as causes for the great elements; rather, all are manifested by the mind. Therefore, he concludes: 'These characteristics of the great elements and derived form are the deluded conceptual constructions of the non-Buddhists.'"
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
I shall now explain that the essential nature and characteristics of the five aggregates extend even to the non-saints.

From this point onward, he further refutes the view that the five aggregates are all empty and lack the characteristic of self-nature, demonstrating that it is not only the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) and the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are unreal.
"The Noble Ones speak only of that which is like an illusory construction as being the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the aggregates.

This means that although the Noble Ones perceive the five aggregates, they understand them to be unreal and merely conventional designations, being neither identical nor different [from their causes], and being like illusions or dreams.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā* states:
"When a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*), they know form (*rūpa*) as it truly is—like a mass of foam, its nature not being solid;
they know feeling (*vedanā*) as it truly is—like a floating bubble, deceptive, unstable, arising and ceasing with great speed."
One knows perceptions as they truly are, like a mirage: water cannot be found there, yet this perception arises from false craving.
One knows volitional formations as they truly are, like a plantain tree: when peeled layer by layer, no core can be found. One knows consciousness as it truly is, like a magical illusion:
it is provisionally designated through the conjunction of various conditions; though its appearance seems to exist, it lacks reality. Therefore, the five aggregates have no separate existence.

Failing to understand the realm realized by the Tathāgata, one perceives the existence of the aggregates (*skandha*) and, with clinging and discrimination constantly present before one, this is called the characteristic of the intrinsic nature of the falsely imagined aggregates.
“Mahāmati! You should abandon such discrimination until you are like the great earth, universally benefiting all living beings.
That which is called the dharma of tranquility refers to the true nature of all dharmas (*dharmatā*), which from the very beginning has never possessed the characteristic of arising.
The remaining meanings are as stated in the text.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
there are four kinds of nirvāṇa."
The former clarifies awakened wisdom in order to reveal the superiority or inferiority of the virtues of birth;

the latter clarifies nirvana in order to distinguish the correctness or deviance of its manifested virtues. This is what is meant by the two fruits of the transformation of the basis: bodhi and nirvana.
"What are the four? They are:
the self-nature of all dharmas is non-self-nature and is nirvāṇa; up to 'this is not what I have taught.

The non-Buddhists reckon that the essential nature of all dharmas exists and call it 'self-nature'; later, when this is removed and deemed non-existent, they call it 'non-self-nature,' taking the *pradhāna* (the Primordial Essence) as nirvāṇa."

Furthermore, they calculate that the various characteristics of dharmas constitute a manifold nature of characteristics; subsequently, they observe these to be nameless and without nature, taking the *ātman* as *nirvāṇa*.

Moreover, they universally calculate that nature and characteristics are existent, naming them the self-characteristic nature; subsequently, they observe these to be nameless and without nature, taking deluded awakening as *nirvāṇa*.

The first three types correctly represent the calculations of non-Buddhists; furthermore, by severing the flow through the five aggregates and the six destinies, they take the selflessness of persons as *nirvāṇa*, which is the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles.
Because perceiving the existence of the five aggregates is identical to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas),

the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states that those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas who fall into fixed natures all "violate and distance themselves from perfect penetration" and "turn their backs on the city of Nirvāṇa."
"Mahāmati! What I teach is that the cessation of the *vijñapti-mati-vijñāna* (the consciousness of conceptualizing objects) is called *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to the realization of the realm of one's own wisdom, wherein the *ālayavijñāna*, which is the basis of existence, is transformed into Great *Nirvāṇa*."
It further states:

"When the habitual tendencies of the self-nature of all consciousnesses—the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*)—along with their views and habits, have been transformed, I and the Buddhas call this 'Nirvāṇa.
This, moreover, speaks exclusively of the cessation of the consciousness that discriminates the objects of knowledge as being named Nirvāṇa."
Setting aside the distinction between general and specific designations, all desire the simultaneous extinction of the seeds and active manifestations of the various consciousnesses.
This can be seen from the subsequent question and answer.
Mahāmati said:
“World-Honored One!
Is it not that you establish eight kinds of consciousness, such that up to the seventh consciousness arises?
The Tathāgata said:
"The cessation of discriminating consciousness is called nirvana.
Mahāmati, suspecting that this differed from what was previously taught, asked:
"Have you not established eight kinds of consciousness?"
Yet you speak alone of the extinction of the *manas* consciousness, as if the other seven consciousnesses do not all likewise cease.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati:

“Because that *manas* consciousness permeates the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), it gives rise to delusion and creates karma, serving as the cause for the various consciousnesses, and because it takes objective realms as its conditions.”
"The other seven kinds of consciousness arise based upon it.
If the mental consciousness ceases, then the other consciousnesses do not arise.
"Mahāmati! [the Buddha said.]
"The mental consciousness discriminates objects and proceeds through deliberation; it has no separate substantial entity or characteristic.

This means that when the six consciousnesses perceive objects and give rise to conceptual attachment, they produce the three types of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which perfume and increase the *ālaya-vijñāna*. Consequently, the seventh consciousness, *manas*, functions in conjunction with them, grasping at "self" and "what belongs to self," constantly and critically deliberating as it continues in a stream; it has no separate substantial entity or characteristic.
"Because the ālayavijñāna serves as both cause and object-condition, the collection of mental states arises; they, in turn, become causes for one another.

Furthermore, because the root-consciousness (mūlavijñāna) serves as the cause and transforms to produce the sense-faculties, the body, seeds, and the receptacle world as its objects, it is said that "the various collections of mind arise through attachment to objects manifested within one's own mind. This refers to the arising of the manifest from seeds and the production of seeds from the manifest. Since the manifest and the seeds lack intrinsic nature, they are like reeds leaning against one another; thus, it is said they "mutually serve as causes for one another."
"Mahāmati! Just as the waves of the ocean arise due to intentional effort, when the *manovijñāna* ceases, the seven consciousnesses also cease.
Just as waves in the sea push and pull one another, they also arise from one another in succession."

Forms, sounds, odors, tastes, and tangibles are the winds of objective realms manifested by one's own mind; that they stir the various consciousnesses, causing them to arise and perish from moment to moment, is likewise so.
Therefore, it is said that when the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) ceases, the remaining seven consciousnesses also cease.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I do not [establish] by means of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor by means of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

This verse refutes the four kinds of nirvāṇa asserted by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). That is to say, I do not establish the extinction of characteristics through intrinsic nature; they take such things as the *pradhāna* (the primal principle) to be nirvāṇa.
"When the consciousness that discriminates objects ceases, this is called Nirvana.
This verse means that the cessation of the consciousness that perceives objects through false views is the Nirvana of the Tathāgata.

"The mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) is the cause of the mind (*citta*); the mind is the object-field of the intellect (*manas*). Because of these causes and their objective conditions (*ālambana*), all consciousnesses arise in dependence upon them."
The verse above explains that the eight consciousnesses serve as mutual causes for one another:
"Just as when a great torrent ceases, the waves no longer arise; so too, when the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) is extinguished, the various [sensory] consciousnesses do not arise."

"Just as when a stream is exhausted there are no waves, this serves as an analogy for the cessation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), whereby the remaining seven consciousnesses also do not arise.
This verse combines the preceding metaphor with its application to the Dharma.
Question:

It was stated previously that the various non-Buddhists claim that when the consciousness that grasps the continuity of objective realms ceases, it is the beginningless, continuous consciousness itself that ceases.

It was also stated that the śrāvakas falsely conceptualize the cessation of future sense faculties and objects as nirvana; since the faculties and objects have ceased, consciousness likewise does not arise.
Now, when it is said that such mental consciousness ceases and various cognitions do not arise, how does this differ from the views of those non-Buddhists and the followers of the Two Vehicles?
Answer:

The non-Buddhists perceive that at the destruction of the body and the end of life, the six consciousnesses no longer grasp objects; yet they do not realize that this is merely because false conditions have ceased. They falsely reckon that the cessation of the continuous stream of the six consciousnesses means the cessation of the beginningless, continuous consciousness itself, thereby falling into the nihilistic view of annihilationism.

Although for those of the Two Vehicles the faculties and objects will cease in the future, and the continuity of the six consciousnesses merely ceases in its active manifestation (*samudācāra*), their seeds of habituation (*vāsanā*) have not yet actually ceased.

This refers to the fact that when the various habitual tendencies of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) within the *ālayavijñāna* are eternally extinguished through continuous cultivation, the remaining seven consciousnesses also follow in being extinguished; therefore, they are not the same.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati,
I shall now explain how one reaches the state of no longer grasping at the characteristics of false conceptualization.
Based on the previous statement that the cessation of the *vijñapti-mātra* consciousness through the discrimination of false imaginings is called Nirvāṇa."

Now, this precisely clarifies the general characteristics of the various distinctions among delusive conceptualizing consciousnesses, enabling all bodhisattvas to understand their unreality, transcend all delusions to reach the realm of the Tathāgata, realize that the various views of non-Buddhist teachings do not arise, abandon the discrimination of subject and object, and no longer engage in false imaginings regarding dependent origination.
"Mahāmati! What are the characteristics of the differentiation of the falsely imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), up to the characteristics of the differentiation of the falsely imagined nature?
[The text] enumerates twelve types of false discrimination; their meanings are explained as follows.
"What is meant by 'discrimination of verbal expression' (abhilāpa-vikalpa)?
It refers to the discrimination of verbal expression that clings to various sounds and phrases as having an intrinsic nature; this is the discrimination of verbal expression.
"What is meant by 'conceptualization of what is expressed' (abhilāpa-vikalpa)?
It refers to the conceptualization of what is expressed as being the five dharmas and the three natures; this is called the conceptualization of what is expressed."

"What is the discrimination of characteristics? It refers to the conceptualization that the four great elements possess specific characteristics; this is called the discrimination of characteristics. What is the discrimination of objects?
[It refers to the conceptualization of the objects of the senses]; this is called the discrimination of objects."
To calculate wealth and profit with stinginess, greed, and attachment is called discrimination regarding objects.
What is discrimination regarding intrinsic nature? ... [up to] ... this is called discrimination regarding intrinsic nature.

Just as one calculates that there are the natures of the four great elements—stating that the nature of earth is solidity, the nature of water is moisture, the nature of fire is heat, and the nature of wind is motion—and even extending this to the ultimate and conventional truths, each having its own distinct intrinsic nature; this is called "discrimination of intrinsic nature."
"What is 'discrimination based on causes' (hetu-vikalpa)?
It refers to the arising of the characteristics of causes and conditions through the discrimination of existence and non-existence;
this is called discrimination based on causes."
"What is conceptualization through views? It refers to the conceptualization that arises from views; this is called conceptualization through views.

Based on this [notion of] existence and non-existence, one gives rise to the fourfold logical positions (catuṣkoṭi); this is called conceptualization through views. What is conceptualization through principles?
It refers to the conceptualization that arises from principles; this is called conceptualization through principles."
"To conceive of 'self' and 'what belongs to self' within the five aggregates and to speak of false dharmas—this is called discrimination by principle.
What is discrimination by birth? ... up to ... this is called discrimination by birth."
"To reckon that dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, invariably arise from conditions is called the discrimination of arising.
What is the discrimination of non-arising... [up to] ...this is called the discrimination of non-arising."
