"The designation 'self' is a conventional fiction, yet in reality it cannot be found, even when examined by a practitioner.

This clarifies that the three realms are provisional, and that both the self and all phenomena lack any substantial reality. It speaks of four kinds of equality: the equality of impermanence regarding the characteristics of conditioned phenomena;

the equality of suffering regarding the causes of outflows (āsrava); the equality of emptiness and unreality regarding all produced phenomena; and the equality of non-self—these are the four equalities.
All practitioners should constantly and diligently observe:
"To be free from all views, as well as the discrimination of subject and object, where there is neither attainment nor arising—this I call the measure of mind (cittamātra)."

It is said that the practitioner contemplates the fourfold equality, thereby being able to leave behind all views and the dualistic discrimination of subject and object; this state of non-arising and non-attainment is spoken of in mutual dependence and is likewise the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).
"It is neither existent nor non-existent, being free from both existence and non-existence; likewise, the mind is also free [from them]. This, I declare, is the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*).

This means that while one is free from the four extremes of existence and non-existence, even such freedom from the mind must itself be transcended; yet, one has still not surpassed the measure of the mind.
"Tathatā, emptiness, the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), nirvāṇa, and the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu); the various kinds of mind-made bodies—I declare these to be the measure of the mind (cittamātra).

This means that tathatā is spoken of in contrast to change, emptiness in contrast to existence, the limit of reality in contrast to delusion, nirvāṇa in contrast to birth-and-death (saṃsāra), the dharma-realm in contrast to the six destinies, and the mind-made body in contrast to the five aggregates (pañcaskandha). All of these are therapeutic gateways (pratipakṣa-dharmamukha). If one seeks after words and grasps at them with the notion of attainment, all such things are merely the measure of the mind.
Therefore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā Sūtra* states: "If there were even a single dharma that transcended nirvāṇa, I would likewise say it is like an illusion or a dream.
Because nirvāṇa is without marks (*animitta*), if one grasps at marks, this is merely the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) and not true nirvāṇa.
"Bound by the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization, the various [phenomena] arise from the mind"—up to "I declare this to be the measure of the mind.
These words refer to the six realms of birth and death, as well as the environments and inhabitants; they constitute the conventional measure of the mind of false conceptualization.

As Mahāmati has said, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is likewise free from the means of cognition (*pramāṇa*), such as the sense organs, as well as from propositions (*pakṣa*), reasons (*hetu*), and examples (*dṛṣṭānta*); it is called the measure of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-pramāṇa*) because it is taught in contrast to the mind-measure (*citta-mātra*) of conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).
The supreme ultimate measure (*paramārtha-pramāṇa*) is likewise taught as an antidote [to all conceptualization].

Thus, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "When falsehood is spoken, the various truths are revealed; yet falsehood and truth are both equally false. Since it is neither true nor not true, how can there be that which sees and that which is seen?"
All of these are intended to sever the emotional views that posit oppositions between the ultimate and the conventional, so as to enable one to realize and enter into reality as it is.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva asked: "What is meant by 'speech'?"
"What is meant by 'the meaning'?

Because it was previously stated that one attains liberation through knowing things as they truly are, [the Buddha] raised the point that a bodhisattva should rely on the meaning and not cling to verbal expressions, and thus asked: "What is speech, and what is the meaning?"
The Buddha said:
“Listen attentively!
I shall explain for you: when one speaks in mutual dialogue with another, this is called speech.”

It is said that with the habitual tendencies of conceptual proliferation as the cause and the throat, tongue, palate, and so forth as the conditions, various sounds, letters, and discourses are produced; therefore, it is called speech.
"What is meant by 'meaning' (artha)?
It refers to the various modes of practice undertaken by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva; this is called 'meaning.

This clarifies the ultimate reality: the Great Bodhisattva, through right mindfulness, observes within a state of tranquility, perceives the emptiness of both persons and phenomena, and proceeds toward the city of Nirvāṇa—the realm of self-awakening."

Because it extinguishes all delusive habitual tendencies, practices the superior progressive stages of the grounds, and reaches the realized Dharma of the Tathāgata ground, it is called "meaning" (*artha*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati:
"Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas reach the state of entering the personally realized realm that transcends verbal expression.

This clarifies that those Bodhisattvas who are skilled in the meaning of words understand that things are neither identical nor different; they are like a lamp illuminating forms, yet the forms are not the lamp.
This means that although one perceives form by means of a lamp, one cannot say they are different; yet since form is not the lamp, one cannot say they are one.

By this analogy, although one enters into the meaning by means of words, the meaning is not the words, and thus one cannot say they are one. Therefore, it is said that by means of words—like a lamp—one enters into the realization of the ultimate reality which is beyond verbal expression.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
If there are those who, regarding non-arising and non-ceasing—up to this point—hold such views, they are the ignorant, not the noble ones.

This clarifies that if, within the various phenomena of defilement and purity such as non-arising and non-ceasing, one grasps the meaning according to the words and reckons that the verbal expression and the meaning are identical, this is called "establishment" (*samāropa*).
To maintain that the verbal expression differs from its meaning is called "denigration.
To say that this arises because one gives rise to conceptual discrimination based on their difference is an explanation that establishes the notion of difference.
For example, to take the various illusory phenomena perceived as being real is the false and deluded view of a fool, not that of a noble one.
This concludes the first section on the refutation of conceptual construction.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If one grasps at the meaning according to the words and establishes [views] regarding all phenomena, because of that establishment, one will fall into hell after death."

It is said that foolish worldlings grasp at the literal meaning of words to establish various phenomena; by reckoning that phenomena exist, they fail to escape the evil realms, and the same applies to those who engage in slander.
"Within the aggregates there is no self, yet the non-aggregates are not the self; it is not as they conceptualize, nor is it that [the self] does not exist at all."
Just as there is no self within the aggregates, so too there is no referent within verbal expression.
Just as the aggregates are not themselves the self, so too verbal expression is not itself the referent.
The meaning of reality is not established by the false conceptualizations of those fools, nor is it the case that ignorance is devoid of existence and non-existence.
"If all things possessed an intrinsic nature as the foolish discriminate them, then everyone should perceive reality exactly as they see it."

If, as those foolish people discriminate and perceive, all words and their referents possessed an intrinsic nature, then all ordinary fools would be people who see the ultimate truth and should be called noble ones (*ārya*).
"All phenomena, whether defiled or pure, are entirely devoid of intrinsic nature; they do not exist in the manner that they are perceived by others, yet they are not non-existent either.

Because those deluded worldlings are unable to perceive the ultimate truth, all phenomena such as the defiled and the pure perceived by the ignorant lack self-nature; therefore, it is said that they do not exist in the manner perceived by them, yet they are not non-existent either.
That is to say, the true meaning does not involve existence or non-existence; it is that which can be realized only by the noble ones through their own self-awakened holy wisdom.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall lead you to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment."

The Tathāgata, based on the preceding section concerning the characteristics of the proper discourse of a bodhisattva, intends to clarify that the one who knows the words is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while the one who knows the meaning is wisdom (*jñāna*); therefore, he next [explains] the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness.
“Mahāmati! There are three kinds of knowledge, ranging from worldly knowledge up to the knowledge that calculates the existence and non-existence of phenomena.
As for the statement regarding “clinging to existence and non-existence,” this refers to the knowledge of the mundane, emotional views held by ordinary people and non-Buddhists.
"What is supramundane wisdom?
It refers to all those of the two vehicles who are attached to the specific and general characteristics [of phenomena].

Because those of the two vehicles are fixated on the specific and general characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases, they do not realize the emptiness of dharmas; they practice to sever birth and death and aspire for nirvana—this is supramundane wisdom."
"What is meant by 'supreme supramundane wisdom that leads to the realization of the selflessness of phenomena (dharmanairātmya) and entry into the stage of the Tathāgata'?

This clarifies the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*): by contemplating all phenomena—whether characterized as specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—as fundamentally neither arising nor ceasing, and being free from both existence and non-existence; by realizing the two kinds of selflessness, namely that of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*) and phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), one attains the stage of the Tathāgata. This is called supreme supramundane wisdom.
“Mahāmati! Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom: the wisdom that knows arising and ceasing, and the wisdom that knows non-arising and non-ceasing.
This clarifies that the Tathāgata possesses a single wisdom which manifests differently according to the objects it encounters.

This means that it guides those of the two vehicles to know the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), leads ordinary beings to know arising and ceasing, and enables bodhisattvas to know non-arising and non-ceasing; therefore, it is further said to be of three kinds.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
Arising and ceasing are consciousness; that which is free from characteristics and signlessness, as well as the absence of causes for existence and non-existence, is wisdom.
To say that arising and ceasing, falling into existence and non-existence, and the causes of existence and non-existence are all consciousness;
That which is without arising or ceasing, and is free from existence, non-existence, and causes, is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
That which possesses the characteristic of accumulation is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which reaches the state of not clinging to objective spheres is wisdom.

“The characteristic of arising into actual manifestation from the accumulation of seeds is consciousness (*vijñāna*); furthermore, the characteristic of perfuming and accumulating the seeds of all phenomena is called consciousness.
That which arises through the correspondence of the threefold conjunction is consciousness, up to the characteristic of non-apprehension, which is wisdom (*jñāna*).”

"When the self, the faculties, and the objects—these three factors—conjoin and correspond, consciousness arises. It does not arise by depending on conditions nor originate through external objects; its unimpeded correspondence and its nature of spontaneous spiritual understanding is called wisdom."
"The realm experienced by the realization of one's own noble wisdom (pratyātma-āryajñāna) is like the moon in water, neither entering nor exiting.
This means that through the awakening of one's own noble wisdom, one realizes that all realms are without reality, being like the moon in water; therefore, there is no entering or exiting.

It is further said that the nature of wisdom is fundamentally luminous and is certainly not subject to arising and ceasing; it is only because one departs from delusion that it is called "arising," and because one is shrouded by delusion that it is called "ceasing.
It is like the moon appearing when water is clear and its reflection sinking when water is turbid, yet the nature of the moon remains ever thus, fundamentally without coming or going.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Gathering karmic actions constitutes the mind; observing phenomena constitutes wisdom. Through insight, one can realize the signless, establishing sovereign majesty and radiance."
The accumulation of karmic seeds as the cause of birth and death is called consciousness (*citta-vijñāna*).
To observe all phenomena as being like dreams, illusions, or reflections, and not to create various karmas under the influence of afflictions, is called wisdom (*jñāna*).
To be able to realize the signless, pure, and wondrous *dharmakāya*, possessing majestic light and sovereign mastery—this is called wisdom (*prajñā*).
"The mind is bound by its objects; cognition and conceptualization give rise to knowledge (*jñāna*); regarding the signless and the preeminent, wisdom arises therein."
To say that one is bound by dream-like and illusionary realms refers to the mind of false conceptualization (*vikalpa-citta*).
To realize that various unreal realms arise from false conceptualization is called wisdom; this is the eighth stage, the Stage of No-Characteristics (*animitta-bhūmi*).
Furthermore, regarding the superior stage, it is the stage of the Tathāgata.
It is said that the Buddha-wisdom arises from the eighth stage, the stage of the Tathāgata:
"When mind, mentation, and consciousness are free from all conceptual discrimination, one attains the non-conceptual Dharma; such a son of the Buddha is not a śrāvaka."
"Mind" refers to the eighth storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*); "intellect" refers to the seventh consciousness; and "consciousnesses" refers to the preceding six consciousnesses.

Therefore, the following verse says: "The storehouse consciousness is called mind; that whose nature is deliberation is called intellect; that which can discern the characteristics of various objects is therefore called consciousness."
It is said that because the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) and the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṭtivijñāna*) are illusory, one no longer engages in conceptual discrimination.
"Son of the Buddha" refers to a bodhisattva; it means that one who has attained the state where there is no false conceptualization or discrimination of phenomena is a bodhisattva, not a śrāvaka.
"The sublime patience of quiescence, the Tathāgata’s pure wisdom, arises from the supreme meaning of Bodhi and is far removed from all conditioned activities.

The *Renyōkyō* (Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra) states that there are five patiences—namely, the patience of subduing (*kṣānti*), the patience of faith (*adhimukti*), the patience of conformity (*anuloma*), the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika*), and the patience of quiescence (*śānti*)—each of which has lower, middle, and superior grades.

Before the stages (bhūmi), one merely attains the three grades of the patience of subduing (kṣānti); in the nine stages, these are respectively assigned to the next three types of patience; in the tenth stage, Equal Enlightenment (samyaksambodhi), and Buddhahood, one attains the patience of quiescent extinction (śānti-kṣānti). Therefore, it is called the "excellent patience of quiescent extinction," which is the pure wisdom of the Tathāgata.
The pure wisdom of the Buddha’s patience arises from the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) and is entirely free from the spheres of activity of the deluded mind and consciousness.
"I possess three kinds of wisdom; the noble ones can clearly illuminate them, discerning all characteristics and revealing all phenomena."

The Tathāgata teaches the Dharma according to the capacities of beings through three kinds of wisdom; as a sage who illuminates and knows, he discerns that all marks are unreal, and reveals everything so that all may awaken to the true Dharma.
"My wisdom is free from all marks because it transcends the two vehicles and reaches the thorough realization that all is but mind-only.

This means that the followers of the two vehicles, weary of birth and death and seeking nirvana, reckon that there are the five aggregates and other such dharmas, failing to realize that these are merely the measure of mind-only.

The Buddha’s wisdom is pure; knowing that the characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*) are unreal is called "penetrating the measure of the mind" (*cittamātra*).
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are nine kinds of views regarding transformation among the non-Buddhists.

Based on the characteristics of superior wisdom and cognition, the knowledge of non-Buddhists perceives arising and ceasing; therefore, next, the nine kinds of arising, ceasing, and transformation according to non-Buddhists are clarified—namely, either the object transforms and the mind changes, or the mind transforms and the object changes.
"What is called the theory of transformation of form, transformation of characteristics, up to the transformation of arising and non-arising?
Based on differences in the primary and secondary forms, it is called 'transformation of form';
based on the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the five aggregates, which do not remain for even a single moment, it is called 'transformation of characteristics'."
To claim that phenomena arise from no cause or from false causes is called the transformation of causes;
for the mind to give rise to objects such that subject and object correspond is called the transformation of correspondence;
and to hold views regarding the four extremes of existence and non-existence is called the transformation of views.
To say that produced phenomena arise from the Primal Essence (avyakta), the Lord (īśvara), and so forth, is called the transformation of arising;
the cessation of all conditioned phenomena is called the transformation of substance;
and the conditions that can manifest the fruit are called the transformation of the clear manifestation of conditions.
Due to the differentiation of phenomena produced by conditions, it is called the transformation of manifest production.
Based on these nine kinds of transformations, the various non-Buddhists give rise to views of existence and non-existence, and thus produce their theories of transformation.
"Regarding the transformation of form herein, it refers to the perception of distinct differences in form; that all phenomena undergo transformation is likewise so.

To clarify this transformation of form: it is like fashioning various vessels and garments from gold, whereby there are diverse and differing shapes, which are said to undergo transformation, yet the nature of the gold itself does not change.
The transformation of all phenomena is likewise.
The wondrously luminous true essence is eternally abiding and unchanging, yet ordinary people and non-Buddhists have no knowledge of it.
One should know that the various attachments and conceptualizations of all other non-Buddhists regarding all such transformations are exactly like this.

Regarding all other non-Buddhists, up to their clear understanding of transformations and their various attachments, none of these are either identical or different; they are merely products of false imagination, and thus all such transformations are likewise [unreal].
"It is, for example, like milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth, which ripen until they are seen by one's own mind as having no external objects.
The non-Buddhists falsely speculate that all natures undergo transformation, being neither identical nor different, just as milk, curd, wine, fruit, and so forth ripen.

Because one obtains curd from milk, one cannot say they are different; because their flavor and aroma differ, one cannot say they are the same. In reality, they do not exist [as separate entities], for there is no dharma that undergoes transformation.
The existence or non-existence of phenomena is a false manifestation of one's own mind, for external natures lack reality.
Thus, all such [assertions] by deluded ordinary beings are like speaking of birth and death in relation to the son of a barren woman.
"These fetters are all merely the habitual tendencies of the false imaginings of fools, who speak of transformation as if it were real.

They are like seeing forms in a dream or a phantom, or like a stone woman giving birth to a child; since these phenomena do not exist from the beginning, how can one discuss their arising, ceasing, or transformation?"
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:

“The transformation of shape, location, and time, as well as the primary elements and the sense faculties, arise gradually in the intermediate state; such conceptualization is not the wisdom of the enlightened.”

The non-Buddhists say that form, location, time, the four great elements, and the seeds bring about the transformation of the sense faculties; the followers of the Two Vehicles reckon that there is an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) through which one gradually continues into the birth-state. All such views are merely false imaginings.
“The Buddhas do not discriminate between dependent origination and the world; rather, the world of conditions is like a city of Gandharvas.

The Buddha knows that phenomena arising from causes and conditions are unborn, and does not, as those with false imaginings do, discriminate and calculate that there is a transformation of various worldly phenomena within causes and conditions.

However, that which arises from conditions in the world is like a city of Gandharvas, being fundamentally unreal. Thus, one knows that when illuminated by wisdom, worldly phenomena themselves become Buddha-dharma; therefore, there is no discrimination.
Because of emotional attachment, one takes the Buddha-dharma and turns it into worldly dharma; thus, the treatise discusses transformation.
The single mind is truly unmoving, yet dualistic views naturally create distinctions; within the same single Dharma, separate understandings of ordinary person and sage arise.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva arrived at the "Profound and Secret Meaning and the Characteristics of Understanding its Meaning.

Based on the preceding verse regarding the primary elements and the sense organs arising in gradual succession, Mahāmati stated that this is precisely the meaning of attachment to the profound and secret.
Since there is deep-seated attachment, there must also be its abandonment;
for it is through the liberation from deep-seated attachment that one attains emancipation.
Thus, taking up the meaning of "deep-seated attachment," he asks by way of contrasting it with the characteristics of the state of liberation.
One version reads: "The meaning of the continuity of all phenomena and the meaning of liberation.
[May it] cause me and all bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to reach non-attachment to verbal expression and to transform the basis of reliance.
There is no object of thought or benefit, being like the sun, moon, maṇi jewel, water, fire, and so forth.
The remaining meanings are self-evident from the sūtra itself.
To say that one knows secret attachments and liberation to be without reality provides such a benefit; therefore, one should make this request.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!
I shall explain for you [the stages] up to the firm attachment to the desire for existence and non-existence."
This clarifies that all phenomena are illusory and devoid of intrinsic substance, and thus cannot be expressed in words.
It is only through the skillful means of the sages, intended to guide and lead sentient beings so that they may realize their unreality, that various verbal expressions are employed.
Ordinary, ignorant people do not understand this; they cling to verbal expressions and grasp at their meanings, adhering to what is profound and secret.

These include attachment to signs, up to and including attachment to the three vehicles and the one vehicle. Such secret attachments are immeasurable in number; they are all the self-deluded grasping of ordinary, ignorant beings of external paths, who entangle themselves as a silkworm makes its cocoon. Using these attachments to teach others is to entangle them; thus, they cling to existence and non-existence with firm and dense desire, remaining unaware of it themselves.
“Mahāmati! Within this, there is truly neither the mark of secrecy nor the mark of non-secrecy, because when one seeks its essential nature, it cannot be apprehended.
The preceding passage was a statement of [erroneous] calculation; this section correctly elucidates the true meaning of all phenomena.

Therefore, it is said that herein there truly exist neither secret nor non-secret characteristics; for if they were definitively present, the great bodhisattvas would be unable to perceive all phenomena as quiescent and free from conceptual differentiation.

If all non-Buddhists and ordinary worldlings can understand that what is seen is but the mind and that external objects fundamentally do not exist—all being equally signless—and if they accord with this by observing it, seeing the quiescence of all phenomena whether existent or non-existent, then there will be neither the characteristic of secret bondage nor the characteristic of non-secret bondage.

However, this is not only that there is originally no bondage, but also no liberation; it is only those who do not awaken to the true meaning of all phenomena who falsely perceive bondage and liberation. Why is this so?

There is neither bondage nor liberation; this means that all phenomena—whether the mental states of ordinary beings or the measures of the sages, whether existent or non-existent—are entirely illusory, for their substantial essence cannot be found when sought.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
For ignorant ordinary beings, when they reach this state, there is no longer any distinction between the secret and the non-secret.

It is said that because the three poisons and craving arise to produce the retribution of wealth and pleasure, and because these coexist with greed and delight, the continuity of birth and death within the three realms remains uninterrupted."
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
If one clings [to this], then all the subtle bonds will not arise at all.
It is said that when the mind is bound, all bonds arise together with the afflictions (kleśa); therefore, it is said that the subtle bonds of the various consciousnesses arise in succession."
When the mind is liberated, all is liberated; as it accords with the true nature (dharmatā), it is said that all subtle fetters are entirely non-arising. No method for transcendence surpasses this.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Unreal and false discrimination is called the 'secret sign. If one can know it as it truly is, all nets of secrecy will be severed."
"Because of unreal conceptualization, there is said to be a secret binding; if one realizes the truth, even liberation does not exist—how then could a secret net exist?
The ignorant and foolish cannot realize this; they grasp at meanings according to words, like a silkworm in its cocoon, binding itself through its own conceptualizations."
It is said that ordinary beings do not know that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature; instead, they grasp at meanings according to words, and thus become bound by their own deluded imaginings.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati [said]: "This is merely false conceptualization."

Based on what was said above, regarding all phenomena (*dharma*), there are immeasurable instances of deep-seated attachment; these are all merely the conceptual constructions and attachments of the ignorant, wherein neither bondage nor liberation exists.
Mahāmati, intending to raise objections and provide a detailed analysis, first restates the question for fear that [the interlocutor] might fall into the view of nihilism (*śūnyatā-dṛṣṭi*).

"As the World-Honored One has said, 'one discriminates all dharmas by means of various minds'" refers to the aforementioned words of the Buddha regarding the characteristics of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) and so forth, which secretly imply the existence of immeasurable varieties; these are all texts concerning the self-discrimination of the ignorant and foolish.

Regarding the statement that "all phenomena have no intrinsic nature," this restates the Buddha’s previous teaching that when one seeks the essential substance of all phenomena, it cannot be found; this is merely a product of false conceptualization.
The Buddha reiterated what he had said above: "In this, there is neither bondage nor liberation; it is only those who do not understand reality who perceive bondage and liberation. [Vimalakīrti said:
"World-Honored One!
If all dharmas are merely false conceptualizations and do not exist, then would not all dharmas—both defiled and pure—be utterly destroyed?"
This clarifies the formal presentation of the critique regarding the established tenet.

If you say that there are merely false discriminations that calculate various bonds and liberations while, in reality, no phenomena exist at all, then there would be neither the afflictions of sentient beings' defilement nor the pure nirvana of the sages; would this not mean that the Tathāgata has utterly destroyed all phenomena and fallen into the view of nihilistic emptiness?
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! It is so, it is so.
Up to this point, there is only the false attachment to the absence of intrinsic nature and characteristics."
In the Great Wisdom Inquiry above, there are two kinds of objections:
first, the objection that if the Tathāgata says there is neither bondage nor liberation, then all phenomena would lack both defilement and purity;
second, the objection that the Tathāgata falls into the error of viewing emptiness as a substantial view.
The Buddha spoke thus, confirming the questions raised.

First, he answered the preceding objection, stating that according to the true principle, there are in fact no sentient beings, no afflictions, and likewise no pure nirvana; these are merely false conceptual attachments, for from the beginning, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and characteristics.
"However, all noble ones (ārya) know and see the intrinsic nature (svabhāva) of phenomena as it truly is through their noble eye of wisdom.
This answers the subsequent objection.

It means: "I do not fall into the view of emptiness; all noble ones possess the true intrinsic nature of phenomena, which is known only by the noble ones through noble wisdom and seen by the eye of wisdom; thus, I do not fall into the view of emptiness."

Thus we know that having already dispelled the notion of existence by means of emptiness, [the text] now further reveals fragments of the truth; it is simply by being free from emotional attachments that the true nature manifests of itself, and is therefore called "knowing and seeing according to reality."
Mahāmati said:

"If the various sages do not reach the same level as the conceptual discriminations of ordinary fools," [this implies that] based on the Buddha's previous statement that all phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*),
one does not fall into the view of nihilistic emptiness (*śūnyatādṛṣṭi*).
Mahāmati, wishing again to raise an objection for further discernment, restates his question as follows:

"If all the noble ones can know through noble wisdom and see through the eye of insight that there exists a true intrinsic nature of phenomena—which is not something that can be known or seen by the physical eyes of ordinary people, and which differs from the false conceptualizations of the ignorant—[then how is this so?]"
Therefore, Mahāmati, following upon these tracks, gave rise to doubt and presented five kinds of difficulties, hoping for the Tathāgata’s resolution:
"How is it that ordinary, ignorant people can become free from discrimination, yet are unable to awaken to and comprehend the dharmas of the noble ones?"
This is the first difficulty: that ordinary beings and sages are distinct.
Since non-Buddhists and foolish worldlings do not perceive the true *dharmatā* of the sages, how could they rely upon the truth to abandon the false?
Therefore it is said: "Because they are unable to realize the dharmas of the noble ones as they truly are.
"World-Honored One!
That is not a perverted view; it is the holy vision that remains far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence."
The second is the objection regarding neither inversion nor non-inversion.
It is said that one cannot even say that those fools are either inverted or not inverted.
Why is it neither inversion nor non-inversion?

Since ordinary beings and sages are each distinct, and because fools do not perceive the true Dharma of the sages—which is free from existence and non-existence—if they were to see the Dharma perceived by the sages yet still engage in worldly, deluded activities, they could then be said to be inverted.
Because they are fundamentally unreal, one cannot say they are either inverted or non-inverted.

Furthermore, the Noble Ones do not attain [realization] in the manner of the conceptual discriminations of ordinary beings, for [these states] are not the objective characteristics of the domain of their own practice.
The third section clarifies the difficulty regarding the fact that the sages are not the same as ordinary people in their inverted views.

It states that the various sages do not share with ordinary people the false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) characterized by the apprehension of signs; this clarifies that such signs are not the objective sphere traversed by the sages' own wisdom. Therefore, they do not attain things in the manner of ordinary people.
If one practices within the sphere of one's own [conceptual] domain, that is not "non-attainment," and such a person is likewise equal to an ordinary being.
This is because they perceive the existence of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena, thereby falling into the view of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
This constitutes a formal objection.

It states that when those noble ones act within their own sphere of experience, there likewise exist the true nature and characteristics (*dharmatā-lakṣaṇa*) of phenomena; yet these manifest in the same manner as the falsely imagined and grasped natures of the ignorant. Furthermore, because the reasons why the true nature of phenomena is neither a cause nor a condition are not explained, [the noble ones] fall into the same views regarding the nature and characteristics of phenomena as the false attachments of the ignorant.
This means that even the noble ones are likewise inverted, just like ordinary people.
"World-Honored One!
Since their other realms of experience are not the same as this, who is capable of thoroughly understanding the nature and characteristics of phenomena?"
This is a re-explanation for the sake of clarification.

As for the "remaining realms," these refer to the realms of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) within the three worlds; since the ways in which the ordinary deviate from the Noble Path are infinite, the same applies to how the Noble differ from the ordinary.
Whether noble ones or ordinary beings, who among them can truly understand the reality of the characteristics of phenomena as they actually are?
"World-Honored One!
The nature and characteristics of all phenomena do not arise through conceptual discrimination; when one reaches the perceived characteristics of phenomena, such phenomena do not exist."
The fourth [point] clarifies the objection that the realm of ordinary beings is not false.
It states that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena exist inherently; they do not come into being through conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*).
How then can the Buddha say that all phenomena exist because of conceptual discrimination?
World-Honored One!

The characteristics of the discriminating mind and the characteristics of the objects of all dharmas are two distinct marks; since their causes are not similar, how can it be that all dharmas exist by virtue of discrimination?

Furthermore, for what reason do you say that although ordinary, ignorant people discriminate among all phenomena (*dharma*), the nature of these phenomena does not exist in such a way? And why do you say that, in order to cause sentient beings to abandon discrimination, it is taught that the characteristics of phenomena as they appear through discrimination have no such reality?
This clarifies that the realm perceived by ordinary beings is real and not illusory; it is established as such because it does not arise from conceptual discrimination. [The interlocutor asks:
"World-Honored One!
For what reason do you cause all sentient beings to arrive at and speak of the nature of noble wisdom?"
The fifth [section] clarifies the difficulty regarding the noble ones falling into the view of existence.

It asks: for what reason does the Buddha cause those ordinary beings to abandon the views of existence and non-existence, yet [cause them] to cling to the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*)—the sphere of noble wisdom—and thus fall into the view of existence?

Why is it that you do not speak of the empty Tathāgatagarbha—the dharma of quiescence that is beyond the sphere of mental activity—but instead speak of the reality of the self-nature as the object of noble wisdom?
This falls into the view of existence (*bhavadrṣṭi*).
Furthermore, when the Buddha stated above that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is not like this through conceptual differentiation, this falls into the view of non-existence (*abhāvadrṣṭi*).
Thus, it is difficult to say that even the Sage falls into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
The Buddha said,
"Mahāmati! It is not that I do not speak of reaching the state that is free from all attachments to existence and non-existence."

The Tathāgata clearly explains through skillful means that while there is the true intrinsic nature of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), this very nature is such that no characteristic of reality can be apprehended; it transcends the measures of ordinary and noble beings, being accessible only through realization and correspondence. This constitutes the comprehensive answer to the five preceding difficulties.
Therefore, I told Mahāmati:
"It is not that I do not speak of the dharma of emptiness—tranquil, beyond the reach of the intellect, and transcending all views—which would cause one to fall into the view of existence.
Why does it not cause one to fall into the view of existence?"
I have already explained the true dharma realized by noble wisdom, for it does not contradict the fact that the self-nature of phenomena is empty of intrinsic reality.

Because sentient beings have lacked awakening since beginningless time, they cling to the notions of existence and non-existence. Therefore, regarding the dharma of suchness-emptiness, I speak of it through the reality of noble wisdom as being "not empty" in its suchness, so that upon hearing this teaching, they will not give rise to fear of annihilationism or eternalism, and may likewise realize the true dharma I have realized—freeing themselves from the marks of delusive conceptualization and entering the true nature of consciousness-only.

Knowing that what is perceived is distinct from no external dharmas, one realizes the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—attains the seal of the Dharma as it truly is, and comprehends the realm of the sages; thus, one becomes free from all attachments to existence and non-existence, to ordinary sentiments, and to the measures of the sages.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!

Because the Bodhisattva-mahāsattva has reached the point where the characteristics of the arising of those tenets and reasons [are understood], it is said that the true intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena is fundamentally unarisen; thus, one should not further establish a tenet of 'non-arising'."
The text consists of six sections intended to refute and establish the emotional attachments to tenets.
First, the refutation that phenomena are fundamentally unarisen:
the statement that "a bodhisattva should not establish that all phenomena are entirely unarisen" is a general heading that serves as an exhortation.
Why is it that one should not establish the thesis of non-arising?

It is because all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent, and because the characteristics of arising associated with that thesis and its reasons are themselves fundamentally non-existent; therefore, the thesis of non-arising cannot be established.
"Furthermore, Mahāmati!
All phenomena are unborn, because their own tenets depend upon something else for their arising.
This refutes the doctrine of dependent arising through two causes.
If you, O Wise One, establish the thesis that "there is no arising," you thereby undermine the very meaning of non-arising yourself.
Furthermore, why does this undermine the meaning of non-arising?
It is because the thesis of "non-arising" that you establish must depend upon the phenomenon of arising as its basis.
Regarding the doctrine of non-arising: if one explains non-arising as being produced from another, this would destroy the very meaning of non-arising.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "If a phenomenon is established in dependence, that phenomenon in turn becomes dependent."
"Furthermore, that thesis itself enters into the category of all phenomena, because the characteristic of non-arising is also non-arising.
This third critique is identical to the refutation applied to all phenomena.
Moreover, that thesis of non-arising itself falls within the enumeration of all phenomena.
"All dharmas" refers to phenomena such as those mundane and supramundane, produced and unproduced, existent and non-existent, identical and different, permanent and impermanent, and so forth.
If one establishes the thesis of "non-arising," it is immediately included within the enumeration of all dharmas.
It is said that all phenomena have the characteristic of non-arising; since they are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning, they do not depend upon being established.
Furthermore, because those [phenomena] are composed of various parts according to their respective schools, even the characteristics of existence and non-existence are ultimately unarisen.
The four members and five members constitute the fallacy of falling into the extremes of existence and non-existence.
Furthermore, since they establish the thesis of non-arising by means of the five members—namely, the reason, the example, the application, and the conclusion—it should not be so established.

Furthermore, regarding that thesis of non-arising (*anutpāda*), it cannot be established as being either identical to or different from existence or non-existence; thus, this thesis itself enters into the enumeration of all phenomena (*sarvadharma*).
Since the intrinsic nature and characteristics of existence and non-existence are fundamentally non-arisen, where could a thesis of non-arising be established?

"Therefore, from 'all phenomena are unarisen' up to 'because of the distinct characteristics of reciprocal causes,' this constitutes the fifth refutation based on the many faults in establishing a thesis.
Thus, if one establishes the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen, one immediately destroys the very meaning of non-arising."
The conclusion urges that one should not establish a thesis in this manner, for a five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) incurs many fallacies.

Regarding the statement that the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the reason (*hetu*) is fundamentally non-arising, to further establish "non-arising" as the thesis (*pakṣa*) is called a "successive reason" (*pāramparyahetu*).
Regarding "because of their differing characteristics": the intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena is non-arising, which differs from the thesis of [mere] non-arising.
Just as they are non-arising, so too are all phenomena empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
The refutation by way of mutual comparison follows the same principle.

As it has been stated that "if non-arising is thus," so too it should be understood that one ought not to establish a thesis regarding the emptiness and lack of intrinsic nature of all phenomena; this is likewise the case.
“Mahāmati! Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas who fall into such [views] will give rise to alarm and fear, thereby distancing themselves from the Mahāyāna.
This first passage generally refutes the improper establishment of a thesis.
This Bodhisattva should explain that all dharmas are identical in essence to illusions and dreams, and by nature free from existence and non-existence.
Because they appear like illusions and dreams, their arising does not constitute true arising;
because illusions and dreams do not truly appear, their non-arising does not constitute true non-arising.

Since the establishment [of reality] does not depend on the formulation of a thesis, one cannot speak of arising or non-arising; therefore it is said that they are like illusions and dreams, because they are seen or not seen.

For all phenomena are merely the marks of deluded and false conceptualization; if one speaks of arising or non-arising, foolish ordinary beings will mostly fall into the extremes of existence and non-existence, thereby giving rise to fear.
If, however, one says they are like illusions and dreams, these two attachments are naturally dispelled.

To synthesize what was previously stated: there is a true intrinsic nature that is free from both existence and non-existence; one should enter into realization in this manner, for this is to be in accord with the Mahāyāna.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"No intrinsic nature, no discourse, No phenomena, no basis— The foolish and ignorant engage in false discrimination, Their evil perceptions like a corpse."

It is said that all phenomena (dharmas) lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature and are beyond verbal expression; whether as phenomena or principles, both the dependent mind and its objective basis are entirely non-existent.
These are merely the false imaginings and evil conceptions of the foolish, who possess no life of wisdom and are like corpses.

In the verse above, the Seal of the Tathāgata describes the difficulties raised; first, it answers the preceding question by stating that the nature of all phenomena does not exist in such a way, for these are merely false conceptualizations and the like.
"All phenomena are unarisen, as established by the non-Buddhists; for whatever arising they possess is not established by conditions."
This clarifies that the nature and characteristics of all phenomena are fundamentally unarisen.

The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), failing to understand this, conceive of false dharmas and establish the existence of arising; yet what they establish as "arising" is not said to be produced by causes and conditions, but is conceived as arising from a primal self (puruṣa) or primordial matter (prakṛti).
If one can awaken to the fact that all phenomena arise from conditions and thus lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then because they lack intrinsic nature, they are unborn.
"All phenomena are unborn; the wise do not conceptualize them. Because your school [asserts] arising as its cause, this realization of yours is thereby destroyed."
The "wise one" is so called because they know that the essence of all phenomena is non-arising, and thus do not engage in the conceptual discrimination of existence or non-existence.
If the thesis of non-arising were established by relying on phenomena that arise from others, such a false cognition would destroy the original meaning of non-arising.
These two verses summarize the preceding point that one should not establish a thesis regarding the non-arising of all phenomena:
"Just as those with cataracts in their eyes falsely perceive a net of hairs through deluded thought, so too are all phenomena falsely discriminated by the ignorant."
This means that those who, through false imagination and discrimination, reckon that all phenomena exist are like those with cataracts who see floating hairs or falling strands of hair.
"The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; there is no real essence to phenomena," until one reaches the state of non-discriminative wandering.
Regarding the existence or non-existence of the three realms and all phenomena of birth and death, they possess only provisional names and lack any substantial reality.

Fools do not understand that the skillful teachings of the sages are merely provisional designations; consequently, through discrimination, false imagination, and conceptualization, they take the names, words, and phenomenal characteristics to be truly existent, thereby deluding their own consciousness.

O Son of the Buddha, a bodhisattva is able to know that the Tathāgata’s skillful means of verbal expression are beyond all calculation, transcending the sphere of activity accessible to the intellect, and are devoid of conceptual discrimination.

"The perception of water where there is no water arises from craving; ordinary fools perceive things in this way, but the noble ones do not. Because of craving, one falsely conceives the notion of water in a place where there is no water;

by analogy, because of ignorance and craving, ordinary fools falsely conceive notions of arising and ceasing, or existence and non-existence, in a place where there is neither arising nor ceasing, neither existence nor non-existence.
These four verses respond to the five types of objections provisionally raised by Mahāmati.
"The vision of the noble ones is pure; it arises from the three doors of liberation... and thus the fruit of the noble ones is produced."
It is said that the three liberations arise from the pure knowledge and vision of the noble ones.
For one who remains far removed from arising and ceasing and constantly dwells in the signless realm, there are no such dharmas as existence or non-existence, unity or difference, and so forth.
By means of this, one realizes the equality of existence and non-existence and awakens to the true nature of all phenomena; therefore, one is able to give rise to the fruits of the noble ones.
"What is the existence and non-existence of phenomena?
How does one achieve equality?"
"When the characteristics of disorder reach their limit, they then cease.
The Buddha himself then inquired:
"What is existence and non-existence? What is equanimity?"

This means that those deluded worldlings, failing to realize that all phenomena are illusory, cling to the notions of existence and non-existence, thereby becoming confused and disturbed both internally and externally.
If one can understand this, then existence and non-existence, as well as false conceptualization, are fundamentally equal, and the signs of confusion naturally vanish.

The preceding three and a half verses praise the Tathāgata’s response to the five kinds of objections, concluding that all phenomena possess a true intrinsic nature; that existence and non-existence are equal and can give rise to the fruits of sagehood; and therefore, one should rely solely on realization and correspondence, rather than engaging in false conceptualization.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reached the point where it says: "The non-arising of conceptual discrimination is called wisdom.
Mahāmati, based on what was said above, [asserted] that the three realms of existence are merely provisional names and lack any real substantial essence.
Furthermore, it is said: "All phenomena are unborn; the wise do not engage in conceptual discrimination.
Thus, he raises this wisdom—which cannot be divided into subject and object—as a question, saying:
"World-Honored One!"
For what reason is it said that this wisdom does not apprehend its object? It is because the meaning of identity or difference cannot be established; thus, it is said that it does not apprehend.
Is it like throwing a single grain of rice into a large quantity of rice, where they are so similar that they cannot be distinguished, and thus the wisdom does not apprehend?

"Is it because the various specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) of all phenomena are mutually concealed by their manifold differences that they cannot be apprehended?
Or is it like throwing a small amount of salt into a large volume of water, such that because the characteristic of taste is concealed, wisdom cannot apprehend it?"
"Is it because it is covered and obstructed by mountain crags, rocky walls, curtains, or screens that one cannot perceive it?
It is because there are objects outside such obstructions that cognition does not apprehend them.
“Is it because they are extremely distant, extremely near, or because they are old, young, blind, or lack their sense faculties that they do not perceive?
That which is extremely near is the eyelashes.
The preceding four sections establish the thesis; from this point onward, each [section] addresses an objection.
"If one does not understand the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena... up to: because they do not know despite having an objective domain."
"Because one is unable to discern and attain future phenomena, this must be ignorance.
However, if it is because the various self-characteristics and common characteristics of all phenomena are diverse and not unknown, [then it is not ignorance]."
It is not that there are no prior objective appearances; rather, when these appear in conjunction with cognition, they are termed "cognition.
This is because, in the case of mountains, cliffs, or stone walls, one does not know them as long as cognition is not fully developed.
Because one is unable to discern these various matters due to their existence, this too is a lack of wisdom.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati!..."
"This is truly wisdom; within it, there is ultimately nothing to be attained.
When the Tathāgata says "this is truly wisdom," he does not mean that it is called "non-wisdom" because it cannot apprehend an external object as you have described.

You claim that because external objects mutually obscure one another, wisdom cannot apprehend them; I, however, maintain that since objects are merely conventional designations lacking reality, that which does not apprehend them should indeed be wisdom—because it realizes that all phenomena are solely one's own mind, free from the nature of existence or non-existence, and thus within that realization, wisdom finds nothing at all to be attained.
"Because there is nothing to be attained, cognitive objects do not arise; one enters the three gates of liberation, and even the substance of wisdom is forgotten.
This means that because no phenomena are apprehended, wisdom does not arise toward objects, and one enters the three gates of liberation.
"If even the essence of wisdom is forgotten, how much more so other external phenomena?
It is not that ordinary people with conceptual thoughts do not know; rather, it is when they reach such a state that it is called 'not knowing'."

To know in such a way—as one who is not like a foolish person of deluded thoughts and false imaginings, whose beginningless habituation to vain and frivolous discursive proliferation leads them to cling to the forms and characteristics of phenomena as being either existent or non-existent—is what is called "not knowing."
"Because they do not understand that all phenomena are seen as manifestations of mind alone, their minds come to abide in the view of nihilism (uccheda-dṛṣṭi).

This means that those deluded persons do not realize that all phenomena are merely the measure of what is manifested by their own minds; they falsely conceive of "self" and "what belongs to self," and through the discrimination of objects and cognition, they take them to be substantially real. Because their faculties—whether obstructed, distant, or near—are incomplete, they do not know whether external phenomena exist or do not exist; this is called "lack of wisdom" and is termed the "view of nihilism."
"In order to cause one to abandon such conceptual discrimination, it is taught that all phenomena are established as mind-only.
To say that the myriad phenomena of the triple world are established as mind-only is the essential medicine for treating the ailments of sentient beings, as prescribed by all the Tathāgatas.

Thus, a verse states: "Knowing that all phenomena are mind-only, one abandons the appearances of external objects; through this, conceptual discrimination ceases, and one awakens to the equality of True Suchness.

This means that by merely departing from delusive conditions, one is the Buddha of Suchness (Tathatā); ordinary sentiments and the measures of the sages vanish of their own accord, without depending on the separate performance of contemplative practices.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"If there is one who, regarding objects of perception, does not perceive with wisdom, they lack both knowledge and non-knowledge; such a person is called a false conceptualizer."

Reciting the verse, one cannot observe, discern, or know the meaning of the self-characteristics and common characteristics of all phenomena that possess objects of cognition, nor the various matters of their objective spheres, nor the sense of identity and difference.

Even if one were able to know, it would not be wisdom; nor is it the case that not knowing constitutes a lack of wisdom. To claim that knowing or not knowing constitutes wisdom or non-wisdom is merely the conceptualization of deluded, ignorant people.
"Boundless, mutual concealment, obstruction, and distance—these are called false knowledge.
These two verses both cite the first three lines as the thesis and the final line as the refutation, as is clear from the text itself.
Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Six.
Commentary on the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra, Scroll Seven:
"Furthermore, Mahāmati! Foolish ordinary beings [do not understand] the pure, true reality that is free from the four extremes."

Based on the preceding verse which states, "That which is neither wisdom nor non-wisdom is called the false view," [the text] intends to clarify that foolish people do not understand the Tathāgata’s true doctrinal intent regarding phenomena and the teachings expressed in words;
thus, they are deluded by beginningless falsehood, evil perversity, and false conceptualization, and consequently are unable to realize that these are the false conceptualizations of their own minds.

Because the Bodhisattva knows these two kinds of dharmas, he is able to comprehend the false imaginings of his own mind; therefore, next, the dharma of the ultimate reality (*yathābhūta-artha*) and the dharma of verbal expression (*nirukti*) are elucidated.
Mahāmati said: “So it is! So it is!”
"I have taught for them various skillful means and instructions.

All the sūtras of the Tripitaka and the twelve divisions of the canon are the Tathāgata’s diverse teachings given through skillful means, in accordance with the differences in the minds of sentient beings.
When words and their ultimate meaning both vanish, it may be called the "penetration of the teaching through speech.
As for the "Dharma as it truly is," this refers to that which practitioners—and indeed all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas—should skillfully cultivate and study.

Regarding what is called the "Dharma of the Reality-Principle (yathābhūta-siddhānta)": it is the realm realized by the noble wisdom of self-awareness (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), wherein practitioners of cultivation do not engage in false discrimination regarding the manifestations of their own minds, do not fall into the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*), and transcend the mind and consciousness. It is free from the conditions of delusion and the corresponding views of subject and object (*grāhya-grāhaka*). Because it cannot be fathomed by the wisdom of non-Buddhists or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), it is therefore named the Dharma of the Reality-Principle.
Therefore, he concludes by exhorting all bodhisattvas that they should diligently cultivate and study these two dharmas.
Question:
Since the two meanings of "verbal expression" (*yanshuo*) and "doctrinal intent" (*zongqu*) have already been clarified in the preceding text, is this repetition not redundant?
Answer:
The former was based on the Three Vehicles, while this is based on the One Vehicle.

Furthermore, the former first presents the established doctrine and subsequently explains it, whereas this first provides the explanation and subsequently presents the doctrine; since the capacities and responses of the audience differ, these are not redundant.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"I teach two kinds of dharmas: the verbal instruction and the reality as it is. The verbal instruction is shown for the sake of ordinary people; the reality is for the practitioner."
The teaching is shown to ordinary people; one version reads "the speaker instructs the ignorant," meaning that the foolish and unknowing are like children.
Since the principle of the ultimate truth (yathābhūta-tattva) is not a verbal expression, it is for the practitioner.
Chapter Five: Lokāyata (7). At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva approached the World-Honored One and said: "World-Honored One!"
"For what reason was this said?
Mahāmati then addressed the Buddha on this basis: "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of dharmas:
namely, the dharma of verbal expression and the dharma of suchness."

Since this [teaching] involves verbal expression, one raises the question to the Tathāgata regarding the Buddha’s past statement that one should not associate with the spells, incantations, and treatises of the Lokāyata.
Since this teaching likewise involves verbal expression, why did that [other] teaching make such a statement?
"Lokāyata" has not yet been sought for a formal translation; it refers to the proponents of non-Buddhist (tīrthika) treatises.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati!..."
"Lokāyata leads one to wander through the various realms of saṃsāra without ever attaining liberation.

This means that all the doctrines and teachings of the non-Buddhists merely adorn their words and phrases to deceive and delude the world; they do not accord with reality nor conform to reason, cannot lead one to realize the Dharma as it truly is, and by destroying themselves and others, they never achieve liberation.

"Why is this? Because they do not understand that all phenomena are seen as being solely manifestations of the mind, [failing to realize this] up to the afflictions of birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, and grief.
The phrase "Why is this? is the Buddha's own inquiry.
The explanation follows below; the conclusion follows below, as can be understood from the text. "Mahāmati!
Śakra Devendra extensively explained various treatises up to the point that they can act as causes for the production of suffering."

It is said that although Śakra’s merit and wisdom are both preeminent, he was still confounded by the disciples of worldly discourse who manifested in the form of animals and deluded him with their rhetoric; how much more so, then, for ordinary humans?
"Therefore, one should not associate with them," because that worldly discourse (*lokāyata*) can serve as the cause for the suffering of birth and death.
"Mahāmati! Worldly discourse speaks only of the objects of bodily perception; it does not even know itself to be a delusive dharma."
Regarding the discourse of the Lokāyata, it speaks only of this body as an object of false perception—seen, heard, sensed, and known.

All its hundreds and thousands of words and phrases will, in the future final age, be divided into many schools; all shall originate from the Lokāyata, yet through their various causal characteristics, each shall fail to recognize that these are delusive worldly dharmas, instead clinging to them as superior understanding.
At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, does even the World-Honored One’s teaching accord with the teachings of the non-Buddhists?
This objection [arises because] the Tathāgata also speaks of the various expressions of the world, which fall into worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*) and are not the Dharma of self-realization.
"If that is so, is it not the same as the discourse of the non-Buddhists?
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati!
"I do not teach worldly discourse, for there is neither coming nor going; one attains liberation through this.

The Buddha replied, "I do not speak of worldly theories concerning the dharma of arising and ceasing. I am not like the non-Buddhists who fall into the midst of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Realizing that external phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are merely one's own mind, one remains free from the grasped and the grasper, does not give rise to false discrimination, enters the single mind and the three gates of liberation, and realizes the dharma as it truly is."
“Mahāmati! I recall that at one time, while dwelling in a certain place, I reached the eleventh generation of the Worldly Discourse (Lokāyata) teachers.
The Tathāgata recounted those past events in detail to clarify the Worldly Discourse, stating that all phenomena were created by Brahmā and others.”

Because he was asked first, he answered that there are "one" worldly doctrines; because he was asked again, he answered that there are "two" worldly doctrines; subsequently, by combining the latter four, they are clarified as six; furthermore, by taking the previous six and the subsequent five, they become eleven.
"Gautama" is the clan name of the Buddhas and patriarchs;
its meaning is as explained elsewhere. He further asked:
"Is everything determinate?
Up to your worldly discourse, it is not what I have taught.

Space, nirvāṇa, and cessation not through deliberation—these three are unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). The remaining meanings should be understood as all being the worldly discourse of non-Buddhists, and not the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata.
"O Brahmin! I teach that all things arise from beginningless conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*); how much more so can one speak of 'action' and 'non-action'?

The Buddha teaches that all phenomena arise from the grasping of karma and various evil habitual tendencies born of beginningless conceptual proliferation, which produce the three realms of existence. Fools do not realize that these are merely what is seen through the deluded imaginings of their own minds; they grasp at external phenomena, as well as the doctrines of non-Buddhists who claim that cognition arises from the conjunction of a self, the sense organs, and their objects."

The Buddha is not like this; because he knows that all phenomena are entirely illusory, he cannot speak of them as having causes or being causeless. They exist only through the provisional application of dependent origination based on the dualistic discrimination of deluded thought; they have no substantial reality from the beginning and cannot be realized by those who cling to a self.
Furthermore, even things such as *nirvāṇa* exist merely as three enumerations; how much more so when speaking of "action" and "non-action"?
"Mahāmati! At that time, the world-theorizing Brahmins [claim that] all analytical distinctions regarding external objects are merely world-theory."

"Because ignorance, craving, and karma serve as causes and conditions, one is born into the three realms; furthermore, that all dharmas enter into their own-characteristics and common-characteristics is the teaching of the Two Vehicles. Even until the subtle flow of mind-consciousness is not yet exhausted, it all belongs to worldly discourse."
“Mahāmati! At that time, that Brahmin arrived at what is consistent with the principles of meaning, not inconsistent.
The Brahmin said:

"Whatever discourses and treatises all non-Buddhists possess, with their various phrases and expressions adorned by causes and analogies, none do not emerge from within my own Dharma; they are all merely worldly theories."
"Is there perhaps anything further that is not worldly discourse?
The Buddha replied:
"There is a teaching that is not worldly discourse; because it does not belong to you, it is not what you accept, yet it is not something the world rejects."
"Although it transcends verbal discourse, it must nevertheless rely upon various phrases and sentences, adorned with causes and metaphors, for one to finally attain awakening.
Therefore, it is not that we do not speak various phrases; rather, their meanings and principles are mutually consistent, not inconsistent."
He asked again:
"Is there not a 'non-worldly discourse' (alokavāda) permitted by the world?
It culminates in that which is not yours."

Because they give rise to attachments through false discrimination regarding various unreal external phenomena, and fail to understand that all are merely manifestations of their own minds, they are unable to realize that this is not worldly discourse.

The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "All dharmas exist with their distinctions solely based upon deluded thought; if one is free from mental conceptualization, then there are no appearances of any objective realms."

Therefore, all phenomena from their very origin have been free from the characteristics of verbal expression, free from the characteristics of names and words, and free from the characteristics of mental objects; they are ultimately equal, without change or variation, and indestructible.
"It is because this is solely the one mind that it is called True Suchness (Tathatā).
Being able to abide in its own place, without giving rise to the deluded conceptualization of existence and non-existence, is the Dharma of the Tathāgata, not something possessed by non-Buddhists.
"Brahmin, to speak briefly, all of this is your worldly doctrine (loka-vāda) and not my Dharma.
This clarifies that the conceptual attachments of deluded consciousness to phenomena such as the past and future are all merely worldly doctrines.

“Mahāmati! As for the Lokāyatika brāhmaṇas, even when they reach the point where they should realize that such discrimination does not arise—if they pose questions as described above and receive answers as given by the Buddha, they still fail to gain even a slight awakening. Yet, considering themselves wise and enlightened, they do not take their leave, but instead harbor the thought that what the Tathāgata has said is incorrect.”
“Mahāmati! You now likewise ask me about this meaning [only] to obtain material gain and not the gain of the Dharma.
This cites the previous answer given to the Brahmin, concluding the response to Mahāmati’s request.
Mahāmati said:

"Regarding what was stated—that the pursuit of wealth and the Dharma leads to conceptual proliferation and discrimination between the two extremes of eternalism and nihilism—[it means that] the increase of material gain fosters craving, birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and affliction; therefore, one should not associate with them."
The Buddha Dharmamegha has conferred empowerment upon you, such that you have attained mastery over all phenomena; therefore, you should draw near to him, serve him, and make offerings to him.
"Mahāmati! The worldly treatises of the non-Buddhists cause ignorant people to fall into the two extremes; therefore, you should diligently investigate them."
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) conceive of the five aggregates as not arising from causes, and thus give rise to the view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
They conceive of the destruction of conditioned form (*saṃskṛta-rūpa*) as being unable to arise again, which they call the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

What the Tathāgata has taught is that [all things] are merely the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*); those who do not perceive arising, abiding, or ceasing [are established in the truth].
One should diligently observe these two distinctions and not fail to abandon them like the conceptual attachments of the non-Buddhists.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Subduing and gathering sentient beings, With precepts one overcomes all evils; With wisdom one extinguishes all views, And through liberation, growth is attained."
The Tathāgata, in taming and gathering sentient beings, constantly teaches the practice of the three definitive meanings:

namely, taking the collected mind as the precept (*śīla*), from the precept arises concentration (*samādhi*), and from concentration issues forth wisdom (*prajñā*); these are called the three untainted trainings (*anāsrava-śikṣā*).
By studying this Way, liberation increases and one is able to realize the true nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).

Now, ethical discipline (*śīla*) constitutes the substance of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), while wisdom (*prajñā*) constitutes its function; the verse is elliptical and abbreviated, yet it is not that these are not mentioned.
"The false teachings of the non-Buddhists are all merely worldly discourses; they recklessly speculate on the agent and the acted-upon, and thus cannot establish themselves.
They claim that Brahmā and others are the agents and that all phenomena are the acted-upon, falsely conceptualizing agent and object."
The Tathāgata’s dharmakāya is the true self-nature; that [position of yours] cannot be established.
"Only my own self-nature is free from attachment to subject and object; I teach it for the sake of my disciples to lead them away from worldly discourse."

It is said that the Tathāgata appears in the world solely for the sake of his own unique doctrine; since both subject and object are entirely non-existent, he teaches his disciples in order to lead them away from worldly discourse.
"The dharmas of grasper and grasped are merely mind; they do not exist at all—this is the discourse on worldly dharmas.
These four verses above briefly summarize the conceptual attachments of worldly treatises as set forth in the long prose; they may be understood according to the text.
Although there are ninety-six kinds of heterodox views among the non-Buddhists, none of them deviates from the five views and two causes.
As for the five views, they refer to the five sharp fetters (*tīkṣṇa-kleśa*) among the ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*).
As was briefly explained in the third fascicle, the "two causes" refer to the absence of cause (*ahetu*) and false causes (*mithyāhetu*).

Some reckon that the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) arise from primordial darkness (*prakṛti*) and so forth; some reckon that they arise from the conjunction of the six categories (*ṣaṭpadārtha*) and so forth; some claim they arise from Īśvara, Brahmā, and so forth; or they claim that the world is produced by atoms (*paramāṇu*), space (*ākāśa*), past karma (*pūrvakṛta*), and so forth.
Furthermore, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra* fundamentally subsumes all such reckonings within four views:

namely, the Sāṃkhya’s reckoning of identity, the Vaiśeṣika’s reckoning of difference, the Īśvara-kāraṇavādin’s reckoning of both identity and difference, and the Jaina’s reckoning of neither identity nor difference.
If one calculates that they are identical, it means that the effect exists within the cause;
if one calculates that they are different, it means that the effect does not exist within the cause;
and the third [position] is that it both exists and does not exist.
The fourth [alternative] is neither existent nor non-existent.
All other heterodox views do not transcend these [four].
Although they differ in many ways, when their fallacies are examined, they do not deviate from two causes:
This means that [the claim] it arises spontaneously from empty space is itself causeless;
all other [explanations] are false causes.

As for the two teachings of Confucianism and Daoism in this land, if one considers them in terms of ruler and subject, father and son, the Three Powers, the Five Constants, and so forth, they represent the ultimate transformation within the realm; indeed, they need not be further discussed.
Furthermore, the non-Buddhist outsiders of India clearly expound upon the three periods of time and believe in cause and effect; they know to weary of birth and death and joyfully seek nirvana.
Yet, because their understanding of the true source is slightly deficient, they remain at a vast distance from the Way—how much more so for those who specialize in such sectarian studies!

In the superior state of goodness, even if one has lifelong anxieties, there is no concern for future lives; though one may equate life and death and force a unity between prosperity and decline, one merely calculates according to spontaneity or attributes it to the mandate of Heaven, as it is said: "Man models himself on Earth; Earth models itself on Heaven; Heaven models itself on the Dao; and the Dao models itself on spontaneity."
If one holds that "nature" (svabhāva) is the cause capable of producing all things, this is a false cause.
If one claims that all things arise spontaneously—just as a crane is white and a crow is black—this is to be without a cause.

Furthermore, it is said that in the *Yi* there is the Supreme Ultimate (*taiji*), which gives rise to the two polarities (*liangyi*); the two polarities give rise to the four images (*sxiang*); the four images give rise to the eight trigrams (*bagua*); the eight trigrams determine good fortune and misfortune; and from good fortune and misfortune arise great undertakings.
If one reckons the Great Ultimate (Taiji) as the cause, this is a false cause.
If one claims that "the alternation of Yin and Yang is called the Way," and thus reckons that the transformations of Yin and Yang can produce the myriad things, this too is a false cause.
If one calculates that "one" is empty, non-existent, or spontaneous (*svabhāva*), then it likewise lacks a cause.
