However, to have no cause or a false cause constitutes a great error, for it would imply that things such as space or spontaneity arise [without cause], and thus they ought to arise eternally.

In the past, by explaining the causes and conditions of the Hīnayāna, one has already refuted the profound subtleties of external schools; thus we know that even the most superficial aspects of the Buddha-dharma are far superior to the deepest doctrines of the non-Buddhists.

Thus we know that those from distant lands and different regions all stem from delusion regarding the primary causes and conditions; their confused and divergent calculations prevent them from even knowing that the three realms arise from one’s own mind and that they flow and circulate without end due to ignorance and craving. How could they possibly understand the principle of the emptiness of nature, the gateway of wondrous existence, the manner in which True Suchness follows conditions, the non-obstruction between nature and characteristics, their perfect fusion and mutual reflection, or their profound interpenetration?

Those who claim that what is confused with or identical to Buddhist teachings are all remnants of the Buddha-dharma, are like the parable of the "stolen ox" in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: if one cannot properly extract [the essence], even adding water and gruel makes milk difficult to obtain; how much more so when one attempts to churn donkey's milk to obtain ghee?

Some possess shallow understanding and employ worldly wisdom in vain conjecture; others greedily pursue empty fame and cultivate the seeds of false views. Thus they plant the roots of suffering in hell and obstruct the profound causes for the wisdom of all modes (sarvajñajñāna). How tragic this is!

The various divergent views are explained in detail in the sixth fascicle of the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra*, the ninth and tenth fascicles of the *Prakaraṇāryavācā-śāstra*, the eleventh and twelfth fascicles of the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra*, and as set forth in the *Saptati-śāstra*; they are also extensively refuted in treatises such as the *Madhyamaka-śāstra* and the *Śata-śāstra*.

Chapter Six: On Nirvāṇa (7). Chapter Six: On Nirvāṇa. At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva approached [the Buddha] and said: "However, the various non-Buddhists engage in manifold conceptual discriminations."
Thereupon, an outsider asked:
"Are space, nirvāṇa, and non-analytical cessation produced,
or are they unproduced?"
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! Space, nirvāṇa, and cessation not through deliberation are fundamentally without intrinsic nature; they are merely designated as three by way of enumeration."
Therefore, the Tathāgata has raised the question of what dharma constitutes nirvāṇa, yet the various non-Buddhists each engage in false conceptualization, giving rise to views of nirvāṇa.
The Buddha said: "Mahāmati!
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, you non-Buddhists!
I shall explain it for you."
He said: "It is not that those non-Buddhists' falsely imagined nirvana can accord with true nirvana. Mahāmati!
There are some non-Buddhists who say that seeing the impermanence of phenomena up to the point where one does not see their destruction is called nirvana."
A non-Buddhist practitioner said:
"Because one practices contemplations such as impermanence, one does not crave sensory objects; because these contemplations are perfected, one attains meditative concentration (*samādhi*).

Consequently, neither material forms nor mental states and their concomitants manifest before the mind, nor does one take the objects of the three periods of time as a cognitive focus, for the causes of delusion, craving, and karma have been exhausted."
Just as a lamp is no longer bright when its oil is exhausted, just as a seed does not sprout again when it is rotten, and just as fire does not ignite again when the fuel is spent;
because the grasped and the grasper do not arise, false discrimination is not produced, and one conceives the notion of nirvana regarding this state, whether with remainder or without remainder.
This is the nirvana of the śrāvakas.
Because they attain nirvana only upon seeing the destruction of the segmented cycle of birth and death (*bhavāṅga-jarāmaraṇa*), it is also the same as that of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Some say that one attains nirvana only when reaching the ultimate limit, where the perception of objective realms ceases, just like the stilling of the wind.

The teacher Fanglun (Direction-Debater) maintains that humans arise from the directions and that humans are born within heaven and earth; after death, they return to the directions, asserting that the directions are eternal.
The teacher Fengxian (Wind-Sage) maintains that wind can produce and destroy all things, and that the nature of wind is likewise eternal; both claim that these constitute the attainment of nirvana.
"Some claim that not perceiving the perceiver and the perceived, and reaching the views of permanence and impermanence, is called attaining nirvana.
The Vedāntic masters reckon that Brahmā is able to produce all things and is thus the perceiver, while the myriad phenomena are the perceived.

The Īśvara masters maintain that all things arise from Īśvara; while objects are impermanent, he is eternal. They claim that when one no longer perceives subject and object and ceases to give rise to conceptual discrimination, this is called attaining nirvāṇa.
"Some may say that by discriminating various marks (*lakṣaṇa*), one eventually gives rise to deep affection and attachment, grasping them as *nirvāṇa*.
The Nirgrantha masters hold such a view, not realizing that these marks manifest from the mind."

Furthermore, it is said that there is a class of people who take the Heaven of Non-conception (*asaṃjñisattva*) as *nirvāṇa*, and others who take the four formless attainments (*ārūpyadhātu*) as *nirvāṇa*; all of them harbor such conceptualizations.
Some even claim that the realization of internal and external phenomena up to the indestructibility of their inherent nature constitutes the notion of *nirvāṇa*.
The Vaiśeṣika masters reckon that space and the nature of the four great elements are indestructible throughout the three periods of time.
Others reckon that the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, and all phenomena are without destruction or cessation, and they conceive of this as nirvana.
The eternalist teachers (śāśvatavādins) maintain that the self and all phenomena never undergo destruction.
Furthermore, there are non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who, lacking wisdom, regard the creation of all things as nirvana.

The female attendants and the masters of logic (tārkika) maintain that there exists a primal nature (svabhāva) and a person (puruṣa), which, through the transformation of their capacities, produce all things.
Or, some non-Buddhists (tīrthika) maintain that the exhaustion of merit and demerit constitutes the true agent, and this they consider to be nirvāṇa.
The ascetic non-Buddhists reckon that both demerit and merit are exhausted [to attain liberation];
the master Vimalanetra reckons that all afflictions are exhausted not through wisdom;
and the master Mādhava reckons that Maheśvara is the true creator of the birth and death of sentient beings.
"Some claim that sentient beings arise from one another in succession until, through a lack of understanding, they grasp this state as *nirvāṇa*.

The teachers of the Nirgrantha school calculate that at the beginning of the eon (*kalpa*), one male and one female were born; these two united and gave rise to all beings in succession. Failing to recognize that ignorance, craving, and karma are the root, they maintain that when all things cease and return to that [primordial source], it constitutes *nirvāṇa*."
"Or they calculate that by realizing the path of the truths, they attain nirvana through false conceptualization.

The Sāṃkhya masters calculate that the twenty-five principles arise from primordial darkness (*avyakta*) and possess four natural qualities; they claim this constitutes the realization of the true path of the truths.
"Some calculate that the qualities (*guṇa*) and the possessor of qualities (*guṇin*), whether they are conjoined or not conjoined, constitute *nirvāṇa*.

The Māheśvara masters maintain that Maheśvara, as a single entity consisting of three parts, possesses great functional power; when he enters into union with the possessors of that power, they fall into the views of the four alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*) and grasp this as *nirvāṇa*."
"Or, some calculate that all things arise from nature (*svabhāva*) and immediately cling to nature itself as *nirvāṇa*.
There are two types of calculations held by the proponents of the theory of nature:
if one holds that nature acts as the cause capable of producing the myriad things, this is a false cause."
If one claims that all things arise spontaneously, this is to say they are without cause.
Or, if one claims that by understanding the twenty-five principles (pañcaviṃśati-tattva) up to the protection of sentient beings, one attains nirvāṇa.

The master of logic, Kapila, holds that the clear realization of the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*) constitutes *nirvāṇa*. If one can embrace the doctrine of the six virtues (*ṣaḍguṇa*), it will bring peace and happiness to all people; this nature of peace and happiness is itself *nirvāṇa*.
"Some say that time gives birth to the world, and time itself is nirvāṇa.
The teacher Kālāmas maintains that the divisions of time are the cause capable of producing all phenomena of the world.
"Or they grasp at the existence of a thing and, regarding it as being no different from nirvāṇa, form the conception of it as nirvāṇa.
Or they take the nature of existence to be nirvāṇa, or the nature of non-existence to be nirvāṇa, or both the dharmas of existence and non-existence to be nirvāṇa."
Or, they may consider that while all phenomena are clamorous and active, nirvāṇa is quiescent; yet, because these two are non-different, they regard this as nirvāṇa.
Based on such various false conceptualizations, these non-Buddhists give rise to views regarding nirvāṇa.
The details of its characteristics are explained extensively in the treatises of Deva and others. "Mahāmati!
Furthermore, there are others who, unlike those aforementioned non-Buddhists, claim that one attains nirvāṇa through reaching [the limit] or by means of the mental consciousness."
This demonstrates the Tathāgata’s true *nirvāṇa*, so that having attained awakening, one may accordingly realize it, as clarified in the sūtra itself.

Therefore, the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra* (Cheng weishi lun), regarding persons of the three vehicles, distinguishes the meanings of *nirvāṇa* according to whether it is innate (*prakṛtistha*) or realized through cultivation (*bhāvanā-prabhāvita*). In total there are four types; all others are false views.

First is the *prakṛti-viśuddha-nirvāṇa* (nirvāṇa of intrinsic purity), which refers to the principle of *tathatā* (suchness) as the characteristic of all phenomena. Although it is defiled by adventitious stains, its original nature is pure; it possesses immeasurable and subtle merits, and being without arising or ceasing, it is as serene as empty space.

It is equally shared by all sentient beings; it is neither identical to nor different from all phenomena; it is free from all marks and all conceptual discrimination; it transcends the paths of intellectual inquiry and the tracks of names and words; it is realized only within the inner self of true sages; because its nature is fundamentally quiescent, it is called *nirvāṇa*.

Second is nirvana with remainder, which refers to suchness emerging from the obstacle of afflictions; although there remains a subtle suffering and its basis has not yet been extinguished, because the obstacles have been eternally stilled, it is called nirvana.

Third is nirvana without remainder, which refers to the emergence from the suffering of birth and death within suchness itself; since afflictions have been exhausted and the remaining substratum has also ceased, all sufferings are eternally stilled, and it is therefore called nirvana.

The Great Nirvana of the Four Non-abidings refers to True Suchness (tathatā) emerging from the cognitive obstructions (jñeyāvaraṇa), constantly supported by great compassion (mahākaruṇā) and wisdom (prajñā). Because of this, it does not abide in either saṃsāra or nirvāṇa, benefiting and bringing joy to sentient beings until the end of the future; being active yet eternally quiescent, it is therefore called nirvāṇa.

All sentient beings possess the first [kind of nirvāṇa]; those of the Two Vehicles who have attained the stage of no-more-learning may possess the first three; only the Buddha, the World-Honored One, can be said to possess all four.

The various divergent theories of the aforementioned non-Buddhists are precisely due to their delusion regarding this intrinsically pure nirvāṇa of original nature; having fallen into false views, they each give rise to conceptions of nirvāṇa through arbitrary discrimination.

By cultivating the contemplation of impermanence above, one does not dwell upon sensory objects; when the thought of nirvana arises—like the extinguishing of a lamp—this is precisely what constitutes nirvana with remainder and nirvana without remainder.

When one is able to thoroughly penetrate that all which appears is manifested by mind alone and enters the stage of Buddhahood, transcending the mind, thought, and consciousness—this is called attaining nirvāṇa.
This is precisely the great nirvāṇa of non-abiding. Regarding "nirvāṇa," ancient translations rendered it as "unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta) and also as "extinction and deliverance" (nirodha-mokṣa).
The Tang translation renders this as "perfect quiescence" (*parinirvāṇa*), meaning that there are no virtues not fully possessed and no obstructions not completely exhausted.
"Mahāmati! Those false conceptualizations of the various non-Buddhists—such as those you have mentioned and others—should be avoided by you and all bodhisattvas."

It is said that the various speculative theories of the non-Buddhists regarding what they conceive to be nirvāṇa contradict correct principle and ultimately achieve nothing; they only increase deluded consciousness, leading to restlessness and distraction, causing one to wander through birth and death without attaining liberation. Therefore, it is urged that Bodhisattvas should remain far removed from them.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"The views of nirvana held by the non-Buddhists are each distinguished differently; they are the deluded and false discriminations of the most ignorant.
This clarifies that the various non-Buddhists hold false views regarding nirvana; lacking the skillful means for liberation, they falsely conceive the notion of liberation.
Everyone possesses false understanding, each pursuing a different path; all are merely ignorant and deluded conceptualizations.
All foolish non-Buddhists falsely perceive a creator and a created, [claiming] this leads to the true cause for the cessation of suffering.
"Worldly discourse is said to be the root of birth and death within the three realms;
to be free from worldly discourse is called the true cause for the cessation of suffering.
It is like an image in a mirror: although it appears, it is not real, and upon analysis, it does not arise."

It is said that objects appear within the mirror of the deluded mind; because they lack reality, they cannot be said to be two. Fools do not understand this and thus perceive duality, but if one realizes that there is only mind, the delusions of grasper and grasped will not arise.
"The mind itself is manifold; it is far removed from the characterized and the characteristics, such that even the foolish and ignorant cannot perceive it.
This means that various objects arise from the deluded mind; since they arise from the deluded mind, there is neither a characteristic nor a characterized.
That which is seen and falsely discriminated by the ignorant is, despite being seen, a non-seeing.
It is the same with the three realms of existence; the ignorant are unable to awaken to this.
As it is said in sutra after sutra: "Discrimination is merely a different name; if one departs from language, its meaning cannot be apprehended."

To speak of the dharma of conceptual discrimination is merely verbal expression and lacks any real meaning; if one discards the signifier to realize the intended meaning, the objects of false discrimination cannot be found at all.
Chapter Seven: The Dharma-body (Dharmakāya). Chapter Seven, "The Dharma-body. At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati attained skillful means, awakening himself and awakening others.

Because Mahāmati had previously clarified that true nirvāṇa transcends mind, mentation, and consciousness, he now raises the question regarding the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body—the realization of the nature of self-awareness—which serves as the means for realizing nirvāṇa. He does so in order to enable us Bodhisattvas to attain this skillful means, whereby we may realize it ourselves and awaken others.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! Regarding what you have asked—whether [these] up to such [states] are different or not different—"
"You ask: Is the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma) or an unconditioned phenomenon (asaṃskṛta-dharma)?
Is it a fruit (phala)?"
Is it the cause?
Is it the characteristic?
Or is it that which is characterized?
Is it the speech?
Is it that which is spoken?
Or is it the one who perceives?
Is it that which is awakened?
Is there a Tathāgata’s dharma-body apart from these phrases?
Or are these very phrases themselves the Tathāgata’s dharma-body?
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! Why is it that the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha has attained [this state]?"
"Because both positions entail faults.

This clarifies that whether one asserts the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is conditioned (*kṛtaka*) or unconditioned (*akṛtaka*), both entail errors; therefore, the Buddha negates those errors by stating in general that it is "not so."
“Mahāmati! If the Tathāgata were something created, he would be impermanent, because he would then be established through non-created causes.
If the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata were something created, then that Dharma would be impermanent; this is something the Buddha does not accept.
If it were not produced through action, then phenomena would lack intrinsic nature and could not be established by causes; therefore, the Dharmakāya is neither produced nor unproduced.
"If it is neither cause nor fruit, then it is neither existent nor non-existent," extending thus to all the meanings of the Tathāgata’s phrases.

If it is neither produced nor unproduced, then it is neither cause nor effect; if it is neither cause nor effect, then it is neither characteristic nor that which is characterized; therefore, it is said to be neither existent nor non-existent.
If it is neither existent nor non-existent, then it is neither that which speaks nor that which is spoken; therefore, it is said to transcend the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*).
Now, that which falls into propositions is called the mundane world; thus, the so-called "four propositions" exist only as verbal expressions following the conventions of the world.
If that which transcends the four propositions consists of nothing but verbal expression, it is like the son of a barren woman.

The son of a barren woman exists only as a verbal expression and does not fall within the four propositions; because he does not fall within them, he cannot be measured, and thus he is neither the subject of cognition nor the object of cognition.

The wise should know that all the phrases and meanings of the Tathāgata are likewise; how could there be anything other than this? It is precisely these words and phrases that constitute the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata.
"Mahāmati! Just as I have taught that all phenomena are without self, you should know that the meaning of the Tathāgata’s words is likewise so.
This citation of past provisional teachings serves to clarify the present reality.

I have always taught through skillful means that all phenomena lack a self-nature; therefore, I speak of "no-self," but this does not mean that the dharmas of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases lack their own intrinsic nature.

If one wishes to compare the Dharma-body with the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas), there is no inherent nature of birth and death within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; yet it is not that the Dharma-body lacks its own eternally abiding nature. Therefore, it is said that the meaning of the Tathāgata’s phrases should be understood in the same way.
Therefore, the *Bodhisattvabhūmi-sūtra* elucidates two types of dharma-nature:
first, the nature of phenomena (*dharma-nature*), because its characteristics are differentiated;
second, the nature of reality (*tattva-nature*), because its essence is true.
The intrinsic nature of these dharmas—the aggregates, elements, and sense bases—is the conventional dharma-nature;
the eternally abiding intrinsic nature of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is the ultimate dharma-nature.
“Mahāmati! Just as a cow lacks the nature of a horse, so it is with all phenomena being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).

For example, when cows and horses are gathered in a herd, the cow does not have the nature of a horse, nor does the horse have the nature of a cow. One cannot say that the nature of a cow exists or does not exist upon the body of a horse; yet, it is not that the self-nature of the horse’s body is non-existent.”

This is used as an analogy for the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) conjoining with all phenomena—the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas). Regarding the Dharma-body, one cannot say that the nature of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases exists or does not exist; yet, it is not that the self-nature of the Dharma-body is non-existent. Therefore, it is said that all phenomena are likewise so: they have no self-characteristics, yet they are not non-existent, but rather are existent.
To say that it does not exist means that there is no self-nature (*svabhāva*) in any phenomena;
to say that it exists means that the *dharmakāya* has the nature of eternal abiding.
However, this can only be realized through direct correspondence with reality; it is not something that ordinary, deluded people are capable of knowing.
Why is it not known? It is because ordinary, deluded beings possess false conceptualization that they do not know.

When it is said that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and without self-nature, and that this applies to everything in the same way, it clarifies that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya possesses the emptiness of all phenomena, is unarisen, and lacks self-nature; it transcends existence and non-existence, abiding eternally in its own nature. Therefore, it is said that he knows them all to be likewise.
“Mahāmati! The Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates (skandhas), and this applies to all phenomena as well.
This clarifies that the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata and the five aggregates are free from the relationship of identity or difference; therefore, the horns of an ox are used as a metaphor.
As it is with the five aggregates, so it is with all phenomena, such as the elements and the sense bases.
This is as clearly revealed in the sūtra: "O Mahāmati!"
"The Tathāgata is described in terms of liberation, yet there is still a distinction; therefore, it is not that they are not different.

The preceding section clarified whether the Dharma-body is distinct or non-distinct from the phenomena of bondage—the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases; this section further clarifies whether it is distinct or non-distinct from the supramundane dharma of liberation.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is described by the name "liberation," and it is said that the Tathāgata and liberation are neither different nor not different.
If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, then he would be identical to material form (*rūpa*) and thus impermanent.

If the Tathāgata and liberation were one and the same, then there would be no distinction between the person and the dharma attained; the vision of practitioners would be without differentiation, yet there exists a distinction between the person who realizes and the dharma realized. Therefore, they are not one. Thus, the Tathāgata and liberation transcend both difference and non-difference.
"In this way, wisdom and the object of knowledge are neither different nor not different, up to the point that they do not undergo cessation; thus they are like space.
From here on below, the true *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is elucidated; "wisdom" refers to the *dharmakāya*.
That which is to be known consists of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*).

What is called the true *dharmakāya* knows that all objective realms are free from the false views of the four extremes—existence and non-existence, unity and difference, permanence and impermanence—and transcends seeing, perceiving, hearing, and knowing all mental objects (*cittamātra*). It is merely a matter of verbal expression; it is without arising or ceasing, just like empty space.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "If you wish to know the mind of the Buddhas, you should contemplate the wisdom of the Buddhas; the wisdom of the Buddhas has no place of dependence, just as space has nothing upon which it depends."
“Mahāmati! Space is neither created nor a creation, extending to the eternal transcendence of all sensory domains.

This reiterates the previous point to conclude the response to the question, clarifying that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, the Perfectly Enlightened One, eternally transcends all sensory domains and cannot be measured by the deluded consciousness of ordinary beings.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"Transcending the measure of all faculties, it is neither fruit nor cause; It is entirely free from such things as characteristics and the objects of characteristics."
The seven verses below praise the Dharma-body as being free from conceptual thought and transcending the two views; this collectively clarifies that it is entirely free from them.
"The aggregates, conditions, and perfect enlightenment— One cannot perceive them as either identical or different. Since there is no one who perceives, How could discrimination arise?"

The "conditions of the aggregates" refers to the aggregates, elements, and sense bases; the "Perfectly Awakened One" refers to the Dharma-body. This statement means that the Dharma-body is neither identical to nor different from the aggregates, elements, and sense bases.
If there were no one who perceives them, one could not differentiate between identity and difference.
"It is neither created nor created by another; it is neither cause nor non-cause; it is neither the aggregates nor not the aggregates; furthermore, it is not mixed with other things.
This states that the *dharmakāya* is free from the faults of the aforementioned phenomena.
"There is not a single dharma-substance as it is seen through false discrimination, nor is it non-existent; such is the nature of all dharmas.

This means that the Dharmakāya does not possess a single dharma-substance as it is falsely discriminated and perceived by those foolish worldlings; yet, although its nature is not what is seen by the foolish, it is also not non-existent.

That the nature of all phenomena (*dharmatā*) is thus means that the nature of all phenomena is likewise from the very beginning; it is free from existence and free from non-existence, and is ineffable.

Because non-existence is established in dependence upon existence, and existence is established in dependence upon non-existence, since non-existence cannot be grasped, existence likewise should not be spoken of.
Now, as for the teaching of existence and non-existence through skillful means, these arise through mutual dependence and relative contrast.
One speaks of "non-existence" in order to dispel the attachment to existence; one speaks of "existence" in order to dispel the fall into non-existence.
If one says that the Dharmakāya transcends all measures, then since non-existence cannot be grasped, how could existence be subject to verbal expression?
"Failing to understand self and non-self, they cling merely to words; they are submerged in the two extremes, destroying themselves and destroying the world."

"It is said that fools do not know that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is in essence free from existence and non-existence; they calculate in terms of self and non-self, cling to verbal expressions, and wallow in the faults of all dualistic extremes, thereby destroying themselves and others as they wander through birth and death."
"If one can see this Dharma, one will be free from all faults; this is called right contemplation, and one does not disparage the Great Teacher.
If one can see this Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata, one will be free from all faults and afflictions regarding existence and non-existence; therefore, it is called being able to contemplate correctly.
One does not disparage the essential teachings spoken by the Teacher.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva asked: "In what sense is it said that these are alternative names for the Tathāgata?

Mahāmati then stated that the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is without arising or cessation; furthermore, as the Buddha previously explained in the sūtras, he analytically grasped the concepts of non-arising and non-cessation, declaring that these are indeed alternative names for the Tathāgata.
However, that which is neither born nor extinguished is a non-existent dharma; how then can it be spoken of as another name for the Tathāgata?
Thus, Mahāmati raises this contradiction between these two teachings to request that the Tathāgata provide a reconciliation.
Is this the absence of intrinsic nature?
Or is it a synonym for the Tathāgata?
As the World-Honored One has spoken of all dharmas, I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain them to me.
If dharmas do not arise, then there is not even the slightest dharma to be grasped; who, then, would be the Tathāgata?
In that case, one falls into the view of non-existence (*nāstidṛṣṭi*).
If one says that the grasping of the unarisen and unceasing is another name for the Tathāgata, then since there is something to be grasped, one falls into the view of existence (*astidṛṣṭi*).
Therefore, I again request the World-Honored One to proclaim this for my sake, so that I may not fall into the two views.
The Buddha said:
"Listen attentively!"
"I shall explain this for you, yet even Bodhisattvas up to the seventh stage do not fully comprehend its meaning.

When he says, "I speak of another name for the Tathāgata called 'neither arising nor ceasing,' which is not a non-existent dharma," he is answering the previous question by stating, "This, then, is a non-existent dharma."
"Nor is it that which grasps the unarisen and undestroyed" answers the previous question by stating, "How is it said to be another name for the Tathāgata?
"Nor does it depend on conditions" answers [the objection] that [the Tathāgata] would fall into the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*).
"Nor is it without meaning" answers [the objection] that one would fall into the view of non-existence.

What I call "non-arising" is neither identical to nor separate from [reality]; it is precisely another designation for the Tathāgata’s awakening to the self-nature of phenomena, which is innate and co-emergent—the Dharma-body of mental formation.

However, this non-arising and non-ceasing is not the realm of the ignorant and heterodox, nor of the dull and inferior followers of the Two Vehicles, nor of Bodhisattvas on the seven stages whose mental objects have not yet been extinguished; they are all simply unable to comprehend it.
"Mahāmati! For example, Indra, the earth, and space—though they possess many names when encountered, they are not without a single essence.

This means that although the Buddha has various distinctions of names, there is ultimately no difference in essence presented separately; thus, from Indra down to hands and feet, although each individual thing has many names, its essence is one and only.
"Mahāmati! I am also like this:
though one has arrived [at the truth], one does not know that it is another name for the Tathāgata.
Here, the Tathāgata first responds to Mahāmati’s question by explaining it through the Dharma, then clarifies it by citing a simile, and now again unites the Dharma with the simile.
"Regarding the term 'asaṃkhyeya,' this is translated as 'innumerable'; the rest of the text may be understood accordingly.
Among them, there are some who know the Tathāgata to be like the moon in water—neither emerging nor entering."
As briefly cited above, there are fifty such names known by some, which serves as an illustration for the vast multitude.
Viṣṇu is translated here as "Great Power.
Kapila is the name of a city; because the Buddha was born in that city, he is consequently called the Sage Kapila.
Indra is here translated as "Venerable.
Kubera and Śūka have not yet been seen in their correct translations.
Although there are thus three hundred thousand such names and appellations, filling the incalculable [aeons], their designations differ while their essence is one alone, without increase or decrease.

In this world and other realms, those of sharp faculties are able to know that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body manifests in accordance with the minds of sentient beings, yet in reality there is no coming or going.
It is like the bright moon reflected in various waters; how could there be any entering or exiting?
"However, the minds of all ordinary, foolish beings are submerged in the two extremes, such that they do not even know these are the Buddha’s various names and titles.

This means that those deluded ones fall into views of the two extremes; although they may serve and make offerings, they do not understand the meaning of names and cling to mere verbal expressions. They are ignorant of the Tathāgata’s true *dharmakāya*, which in reality has no coming or going, and they claim that what is neither born nor extinguished is identical to non-existence. They do not realize that these are the Buddha manifesting various names according to the minds of sentient beings.
"Just as with Indra, Śakra, and others, the designations reach their respective meanings without any distinct ontological essence to those meanings.
*Śakra* means "the valiant" (*yǒngměng*).
The term "and others" (*děng*) includes the remaining [deities].

Indra, Śakra, and so forth are all alternative names for Śakra; yet, because they place blind faith in the terminology of the teachings while remaining ignorant of their actual substance, they grasp at the meaning of phenomena merely according to the words.

Those who are deluded speak thus: "The meaning is not distinct from the verbal expression; that is to say, the expression itself is the essence of the meaning, and neither exists. Such people do not understand that while verbal expressions arise and perish, the meaning does not arise or perish.
“Mahāmati! Because those people are deluded, they fail to realize the state that transcends both existence and non-existence, and the absence of arising and intrinsic nature.
This clarifies that all speech falls within the realm of names and designations, whereas the ultimate reality does not fall within names and designations.”
Because they are free from existence and non-existence, they have no rebirth and no bodily characteristics; therefore, they do not fall [into error]. "Mahāmati!
The Tathāgata does not speak of falling into dharmas of words, with the sole exception of those who do not fall into words."

The various dharmas taught by the Tathāgata in response to the capacities of sentient beings may fill the dragon palaces and pervade the entire dharma-realm, yet in reality they do not fall into the realm of written characters or verbal instruction.
This is because the intrinsic nature of words and language is transcendent; they serve only as skillful means to correctly manifest the ultimate meaning.
"Not falling into the realm of conventional teachings" means to penetrate the subtle intent behind the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma. "Mahāmati!
If a person preaches the Dharma while falling into words and letters, they have not yet reached the point where they do not engage in conceptual discrimination that fails to follow the meaning."
It is said that if a person does not preach the Dharma well and falls into mere words and verbal teachings, this is called false and deceptive speech.

The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time and all the Bodhisattvas have, in reality, never uttered so much as a single word in response, because the nature and characteristics of all dharmas are detached from such expression; yet it is not that they do not accord with the true meaning, for they employ provisional conceptualization and explanation merely to manifest it.
“Mahāmati! If it were not taught, the Dharma would be severed, failing to establish the state of the noble ones’ self-realization.

Thus, the Tathāgata, desiring to cause sentient beings to know the meaning, employs provisional verbal expressions to reveal that foolish people are attached to words and do not attain the true meaning.”
Upon hearing this, sentient beings think to themselves:
"For what reason does the Tathāgata not speak directly of the true meaning, but instead employs such discourse?
He causes sentient beings to become attached to [concepts] and fail to attain the true meaning."

Why is this? It is because, in order to eliminate this doubt, it is clarified that one cannot speak directly of the true reality of non-arising and non-ceasing; for if one were to do so, sentient beings would give rise to doubts regarding annihilationism and the view that the Three Vehicles and so forth are empty. Thus, one must correctly employ skillful means and speak by way of provisional words.
If one were not to employ skillful means (*upāya*) in teaching, the Dharma would be destroyed;
without the noble ones of the three vehicles, who would teach and for whom?

Therefore, a Bodhisattva should not cling to the literal letter but should preach the Dharma according to what is appropriate, clarifying the teachings of skillful means. These Tathāgatas expound the Dharma in accordance with the diverse inclinations and understandings of sentient beings, so that they may realize all phenomena are but manifestations of the mind alone, abandon internal and external discrimination, and turn back and extinguish deluded consciousness. This is not for the purpose of establishing the state realized by the Tathāgata’s own self-awakened noble wisdom (*svapratyātma-āryajñāna*).
“Mahāmati! A bodhisattva-mahāsattva should follow the meaning (artha) until it reaches a point where the mind can no longer achieve conceptual understanding.

This demonstrates that a bodhisattva should rely on the true meaning and not follow mere verbal expression; for if one relies on the literal words, one will ruin both oneself and others and fail to attain clear awakening.
"If one can skillfully know the characteristics of all phenomena, up to the point of not severing the lineage of the Buddha, one will attain a supreme and wondrous state.
To say that one "can know the true meaning" refers to the vast benefits described above.
The "excellent and sublime place" refers precisely to the state realized by the noble wisdom of self-awakening! "Mahāmati,
when Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas are born in this excellent and sublime place, they reach the true reality of phenomena because it is free from words and letters."

Having attained the supreme and wondrous state as a Bodhisattva in his final existence, one emerges from obscurations with perfect clarity and can continue until the end of the future; by means of the ten powers of mastery, one transforms sentient beings, leading them to realize the truth that is beyond words. Therefore, one should not give rise to attachments as described above.

Regarding the ten masteries (*vaśitā*), they are as follows: first, mastery over life, because one adapts the length of one's lifespan to suit sentient beings; the same applies to mastery over mind, wealth, karma, birth, vows, faith, suchness, wisdom, and the Dharma.
It is exactly as explained in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*: "Mahāmati!
It is like a person pointing at an object with a finger; one must not become attached to the words used, just as one would not look at the fingertip itself."
Fools cling to the finger of verbal expression and fail to grasp the actual meaning. There are two metaphors for this:

the first illustrates how one clings to the means of expression while forgetting the meaning; the second illustrates how one should realize the meaning and abandon the means of expression. Each has its corresponding application of the Dharma as clearly explained in the text. Therefore, I exhort you to diligently cultivate skillful means.
Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka* says: "If one wishes to seek the eradication of immeasurable faults and evils, one should, within the Buddha-dharma, be courageous and always diligent."
"Do not merely cling to names and teachings, for it is no different from looking at the tip of a finger.
Mahāmati! The true meaning is subtle and tranquil; those who are attached to written words should quickly abandon them."
This clarifies that by awakening to the true meaning (*tattvārtha*), one attains *nirvāṇa* through freedom from all conceptual constructions and distractions.

The true meaning is obtained from those who have heard much; "those who have heard much" refers to those who have properly reflected upon and cultivated the teachings in accordance with their meaning, rather than merely being skilled in verbal expression.
To prevent oneself and others from falling into the evil views of external paths is called "extensive learning.
Therefore, those who seek the true meaning should draw near to such [teachings], while one must be careful never to approach that which contradicts the true meaning.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, having reached the point regarding "and non-analytical cessation, which is neither arising nor ceasing," addressed the Buddha on this account:
"For the sake of the ignorant, it is not possible to speak directly of the true meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing; it is just as a nursing infant should not be given raw food."
Therefore, he asked again:
"Regarding that which the Tathāgata has taught as neither arising nor ceasing, there is no extraordinary time [in which this occurs]. Why is this so?"

All non-Buddhists also speak of a creator that is neither born nor extinguished; this is no different from the Buddha, the World-Honored One, who speaks of the three unconditioned dharmas as being neither born nor extinguished.
"The non-Buddhists also speak of a creator as the cause and conditions; thus, there is no difference between their teachings and those of the non-Buddhists.

Previously it was stated that the Buddha and the non-Buddhists alike teach the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing; here it is further stated that they likewise teach that all worlds arise through causes and conditions, and therefore there is likewise no distinction between them.
"The non-Buddhists (tīrthika) say that the subtle atoms (paramāṇu), whether supreme and wondrous, existent, or non-existent, are all unattainable.
This expresses the non-Buddhist doctrine of neither-arising-nor-ceasing, which consists of nine substantial entities:
first, time;...
Second, the two directions;
third, space;
fourth, atoms.
Fifth, the four great elements;
sixth, the Brahmā deities;
seventh, the Śubhakṛtsna deities.
The eight great sovereign deities;
and the ninth, the Lord of Sentient Beings, which is the *ātman*.

These various non-Buddhists reckon these nine entities as neither arising nor perishing, capable of acting as the cause for all phenomena of birth and death; they are collectively termed "agents. This is no different from the Mahāyāna teaching of the Buddha, which states that all phenomena are fundamentally neither arising nor perishing, and that whether they exist or do not exist, they are entirely unapprehendable.
“World-Honored One!
The great elements do not perish because they possess their own specific characteristics; therefore, as previously stated, they must exist.
Among the nine substances, he raises one great element to formulate this objection against the Tathāgata, using it as an analogy for the others.

It is said that the four great elements are likewise neither destroyed nor disintegrated; they circulate through the seven realms of existence, their self-nature is eternally abiding, and they are neither born nor extinguished.

Although the various dharmas explained by the Tathāgata through his analytical discernment differ slightly from these, in reality there is nothing that has not already been taught by the non-Buddhists. If there are points of difference, I pray you explain the reason for them; if there is no distinct meaning, then all non-Buddhists are themselves the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One has always taught that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system;
yet, as you have just stated, this would indeed be the case, because what you have said is no different from that of the Tathāgata.
The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati! That which I have taught regarding all dharmas is that they are neither existent nor non-existent."
The meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing as taught by the Tathāgata is not the same as that of the non-Buddhists; therefore, he does not propound a theory of impermanent arising and ceasing.
The non-Buddhists falsely cling to the notion that all phenomena possess a real intrinsic nature and characteristics, and thus they conceive of "non-arising and non-ceasing."
Because the Tathāgata does not fall into the categories of existence or non-existence, all the teachings he expounds are free from existence, non-existence, arising, and ceasing.
How are they free from existence and non-existence?

Like the forms in a dream or an illusion, while one is actually dreaming, one cannot say those forms do not exist; yet, because those phenomenal forms are not truly existent, one cannot say they do exist. Since both the subject that perceives and the object perceived are unobtainable, it is said that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished, being free from existence and free from non-existence.
"If one realizes that [all things] are seen only as manifestations of one's own mind, this pertains to the affairs of ordinary fools and not to those of the noble ones.

For one who can realize that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, they abide in the true nature of the Dharmakāya, free from deluded discrimination; thus, all worldly activities and the affairs of birth and death are utterly stilled.
To engage in activities based on false conceptualization is not the way of the noble ones. "Mahāmati!
To differentiate unreal objects with a deluded mind, leading to the arising of views of birth and cessation, is not the way of the noble ones."

This is like leading a small child to see a city of Gandharvas or illusory conjurations, with merchants coming and going; the child thinks they truly exist. In the same way, fools falsely give rise to notions of arising and ceasing or non-arising and non-ceasing, and whether things exist or do not exist.
In truth, illusory persons neither emerge nor enter; all phenomena are likewise, being free from arising and free from cessation.
It is only through the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings that various divergent views arise; this is not the case for the noble ones.
"To speak of what is false and illusory as being not in accordance with the *dharmatā*—that which reaches the state of neither arising nor ceasing—is *nirvāṇa*.
To speak thus is to say that the true *dharmatā* taught by the Tathāgata possesses something extraordinary."

Because those who harbor false imaginings do not realize the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) as it truly is, they give rise to various inverted views; by grasping at all phenomena as having real intrinsic nature and characteristics, and failing to perceive their original state of quiescence, they are unable to abandon deluded discrimination.

Therefore, those who perceive the signless are superior because they take it as the cause for nirvāṇa; this is not like perceiving signs and reckoning that which is neither born nor extinguished as the cause for rebirth. To realize the absence of intrinsic nature and characteristics, wherein there is no deluded conception of arising, abiding, changing, or ceasing, and which is quiescent, wondrous, and eternal—that is nirvāṇa.
Mahāmati said:
"Nirvāṇa is the vision of the state as it truly is.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
"To eliminate the attachment to existence, the meaning of non-arising is established," up to the words, "How could it be for me to speak?

This statement that non-arising is without cause means that it is not like the falsely imagined creator posited by the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who serves as the cause for the arising of all phenomena.
Therefore, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "Delusion originally has no cause; it is within deluded thought that the nature of causes and conditions is established.
All of these are the conceptual calculations of the deluded minds of sentient beings.
"Separated from all conditions of conjunction, wisdom cannot perceive them; for this reason, I say they are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
Because there is no one capable of seeing them apart from all delusive conditions, I therefore say they are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
"Each and every condition, through their conjunction, appears though it does not exist; all phenomena are like this.

That which is produced by the conjunction of false conditions is fundamentally without intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); although it appears and can be seen, it is not truly existent. Therefore, the treatise asks:
"If all phenomena are not truly existent, how is it that they are clearly visible before us?"
The answer was:
"Reflections in a mirror, the moon in water, a city of the Gandharvas, dream-visions, illusory phenomena, and a second moon—these are clearly visible; how could they possess any reality?"

The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* also states: "It is perceived as being like a dream; that which sees and that which is seen do not coexist. At the time of seeing, there is no conceptual discrimination. How, then, can one say it is 'perceived as present'?"
"The wild horse is but a mirage and wandering vapors.
[The text] "Subduing the proponents of causality and expounding the principle of non-arising,
so that all non-Buddhists are struck with terror," means that when the non-Buddhists hear it taught that there is neither cause nor arising, they immediately give rise to the fear of annihilationism.
At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse:
"What is it? By what cause? And for what reason does it arise?"
"In what place do they conjoin,
such that one propounds the theory of causelessness?
As for the phrase "how so," there was once a Great Being who spoke to the non-Buddhists as follows:
"How does this phenomenon that has arisen arise?
Does it arise from a cause,
or does it arise without a cause?"
He replied:
"It arises from causes.
As for the question "What are its causes?"—since it has arisen from causes, one asks what those causes are.
He replied:
"They arise from causes such as atoms, primordial nature (*prakṛti*), and the four great elements.
Regarding the statement, "For what further reason do they arise?", it means he asked again: for what reason do those great elements and so forth arise?
He replied: "The four great elements and so forth arise without cause.

When asked, "In what place do they combine to establish this doctrine of causelessness? he said: "If the four great elements and so forth were without cause, then being without cause, they would not exist as phenomena (*dharma*). If they do not exist as phenomena, there is no location. If there is no location, there is no combination. If there is no combination, there is no arising. How, then, can you establish the doctrine that the four great elements arise without cause to produce all worlds?"
Mahāmati raised this point and earnestly requested the Buddha for a definitive resolution.
At that time, the World-Honored One replied with a verse:
"Observing conditioned phenomena, they are neither caused nor causeless; thus the views of those who debate arising and ceasing are extinguished."

The Buddha said: "One should contemplate all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as neither arising from a cause nor arising without a cause; therefore, they are said to be 'unborn' (*anutpanna*), thereby extinguishing the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of arising and ceasing held by the non-Buddhists."
Question: We directly perceive that all phenomena arise and cease; why do you say they do not exist? Answer:
All phenomena arise through dependent origination and lack intrinsic nature; therefore, no self-substance of arising or ceasing can be found.
Arising is non-arising, and ceasing is non-ceasing, just as the water of a mirage is fundamentally dry from the start.

Therefore, the *Vajrasamādhi Sūtra* states: "The meaning of that which is produced by causes and conditions is the cessation of meaning, not its production; the cessation of all meanings of arising and ceasing is the production of meaning, not its cessation."
As in the nine verses above, the calculations of the non-Buddhists that [things] arise from false causes are refuted; therefore, it is said that there is no arising.
At that time, Mahāmati spoke in verse, asking:
"Is it because they do not exist that there is no arising?"
Is it dependent upon various conditions?
Or does it have a name but no actual meaning?
I pray that you will explain this for me.
Is it because of non-existence that there is no arising?
Or is it because of dependence upon various conditions that there is no arising?
Since the designation "non-arising" exists, the meaning of this non-arising cannot be non-existent; it is merely explained through conceptual differentiation.
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied in verse:
"It is not that non-existent things do not arise, nor is it by waiting for conditions; reaching this point is the characteristic of non-arising.
Thus the Tathāgata answered.
All of these are incorrect.
This is the body born of mind (manomayakāya), designated as "unborn" (anutpāda); it is not within the realm of externalists, followers of the two vehicles, or Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage.
"Detached from all causes and conditions, and with no agent whatsoever—this is what I call 'non-arising'.
To be "detached from the two natures" means to be detached from the two natures of the internal and the external.
The remaining text may be understood.
"External objects exist or do not exist, yet the mind takes nothing therein because it has reached non-arising; therefore, it is called 'empty'.
It is not empty like the great void or the emptiness of annihilation; rather, it is called "empty" because the *dharmakāya* is non-arising.
The eight lines of verse above explain that the Tathāgata’s mind-born Dharma-body is non-arising.
"Because causes and conditions assemble together, there is thus arising and ceasing; this applies likewise up to the point where both are negated."

If, apart from false conditions, there were another distinct dharma such that one could speak of cause and effect as being either identical or different in nature, this would be the deluded conceptualization of the various non-Buddhists and the ignorant.
The same applies to the four propositions of existence, non-existence, both, and neither, which do not arise.
"Except for the convergence of various conditions, within which one perceives arising and ceasing, the meaning of 'arising' cannot be found.

Ordinary beings cannot comprehend these delusive conditions; therefore, throughout long kalpas, they are hooked and worn away like an unbroken chain. Thus, the causal conditions are termed a "hooked chain" (*guoluo*).
"If one is separated from delusive conditions, there is no distinct dharma that arises.
This final verse states: "I say it is merely a chain; because arising does not exist, there is no arising, up to the point where there would be something distinct among dharmas.

This concluding verse refutes the externalist's defense establishing that the dharma of arising exists prior [to conditions], yet must depend on causes and conditions to arise—just as an object existing beforehand in the dark must wait for the illumination of a lamp before it can be seen; therefore, it says, "If the manifestation of the chain were thus..."
This means that phenomena arising through causes and conditions are like a lamp illuminating objects in the darkness.
The Buddha said:
"If one argues in this manner, it would imply that there is a phenomenon of arising existing separately and apart from causes and conditions."
"Non-arising means the absence of intrinsic nature; when its essence is like empty space, one has reached the stage of the patience toward non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

Because there is no arising of those four characteristics—momentary birth, abiding, change, and cessation—it may be called 'non-arising'; this is what is named the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena."
"In all worlds, there is nothing that is not a causal chain; to say otherwise would contradict the principles of the teaching.
This statement regarding ignorance (*avidyā*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), and karma refers to three of the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*).

To speak in full detail: ignorance conditions volitional formations; volitional formations condition consciousness; consciousness conditions name-and-form; name-and-form conditions the six sense bases; the six sense bases condition contact; contact conditions feeling; feeling conditions craving; craving conditions clinging; clinging conditions becoming; becoming conditions birth; and birth conditions old age, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair. This elucidates the law of the false causes and effects of the three periods of time.
This means that in the past there are two causal factors:
first, ignorance; second, volitional formations.
In the present there are five resultant factors:
First, consciousness; second, name-and-form; third, the six sense bases; fourth, contact; fifth, sensation.
In the present, there are three causal factors:
first, craving; second, clinging; third, becoming.
In the future, there are two resultant branches:
first, birth; second, old age and death.

It is said that all sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been bound by the long-term chain of the twelve links of dependent origination rooted in ignorance, wandering within the prison of the triple world without any means of escape.

The wise person realizes this and, by severing it through the cultivation of the path, immediately attains liberation; therefore it is said that with the cessation of ignorance, volitional formations cease, and so on until with the cessation of birth, old age and death cease. One should know that because these delusive causes and conditions must be extinguished, one must cultivate the path.
Question:
What is the cultivation of the path?
Answer:

When one investigates the root of the twelve links of dependent origination, it is found to be ignorance (*avidyā*). Because of ignorance, afflictions and karma arise; because of karma, retribution arises, resulting in all manner of suffering. Thus, ignorance is the fundamental cause of them all.
Just as one who fells a tree must first sever its roots.
Question:
What is this ignorance?
Answer: It is because one does not realize that the mind is [the source].

Due to this non-realization, false discrimination arises, and one perceives phenomena as existing outside the mind—claiming they exist or do not exist, that they are so or are not so, that they are gained or lost. Thus, one undergoes all manner of retributive fruits, such as the sufferings of body and mind, all of which stem from ignorance (*avidyā*).
Now, wishing to sever ignorance, I must first awaken to the source of my own mind; all delusive thoughts that arise according to the mind originate from the unawakened mind.
One must know that the nature of one's own mind is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, and without coming or going.
How is this known?
All deluded thoughts arise suddenly; once they are awakened to, they do not arise.
What is meant by "awakening"?
When greed, hatred, and delusion arise, one uses one's own mind to observe and investigate these greed, hatred, and delusion: what is their shape?
Are they blue or yellow, red or white? Are they future, past, or present? Do they exist internally, externally, or in between?

When one investigates greed, hatred, and delusion, they are found to have no form whatsoever. If they had existed from the very beginning, they should also be visible at the time of present awakening;
since they are not perceived upon awakening, we know that they suddenly arise through non-awakening and do not arise when there is awakening. Therefore, awakening is the antidote to ignorance.

Because this present ignorance cannot be apprehended and the mind is devoid of ignorance, all delusive thoughts and afflictions do not arise. Because afflictions do not arise, karma does not arise; thus, there are no two causes of the past.
Because these two causes are absent, the five fruits of the present do not arise. Because the five fruits do not arise, the three causes of craving, grasping, and becoming do not arise.
Because these three causes of the present are absent, the two fruits of retribution in the future do not arise; this is called severing the chain of the twelve links of dependent origination.
This twelvefold dependent origination, when it is without location, is called nirvāṇa;
this self-realized noble wisdom is called bodhi.
Based on this twelvefold dependent origination, there are generally three types of practitioners who observe and cultivate:
Those with superior wisdom who contemplate this attain the bodhi of a Buddha;
those with middling wisdom who contemplate it attain the bodhi of a pratyekabuddha;
and those with inferior wisdom who contemplate it attain the bodhi of a śrāvaka.

Therefore, the *Zhao lun* states: "The contemplation of dharmas by the three vehicles is no different; it is only that the mind has degrees of magnitude and smallness that constitutes the distinction.
[Furthermore: "If produced dharmas were not existent, for whom would they serve as causes and conditions?"
"Arising through successive succession—this is the meaning of dependent origination.
[The opponent asks: "If produced phenomena (*jātidharma*) do not truly exist, for what would those causes and conditions (*hetupratyaya*) serve as causes and conditions?"
These two phrases cite the calculations of the non-Buddhists.
Because they arise from one another in succession, one correctly understands that there is the principle of causes and conditions, and that there is no separate nature of arising.
"Solidity, moisture, warmth, motion, and so forth, are the conceptual constructions of the ignorant, up to the eightfold path of coolness.
These differences are spoken of because of the diversity of persons, not because there is any difference in the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*);
the treatments differ according to the specific ailments, but there is no distinction in *tathatā*.
Therefore, it is said that there is only the One Mahāyāna, the eightfold path of coolness.
This eightfold path is the cause capable of producing the fruit-dharmas of the One Vehicle.
The one is the eight, and the eight are the one; they are perfectly interfused and mutually reflected, without duality or distinction.
To hold that only one [of the aggregates] exists and not the others is a biased view.

Chapter 8: On Impermanence (VIII). Chapter Eight on Impermanence.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati asked: "Furthermore, how many kinds of impermanence are there?"
Because ordinary worldlings give rise to views of arising and ceasing based on delusion, this is not the case for the noble ones.
That is to say, because non-Buddhist worldlings fail to attain reality as it is, they give rise to false views of impermanence, arising, and ceasing; therefore, [the teaching] speaks of impermanence.
The Sage has attained the principle of reality as it is; he should not give rise to the deluded view of impermanence and arising-and-ceasing.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you also say that "all conditioned phenomena are impermanent and are dharmas of arising and ceasing"?
It is not yet known which of these explanations is erroneous and which is correct;
furthermore, how many kinds of impermanence are there?
The Buddha said:
“Mahāmati! The non-Buddhists assert that there is a state of impermanence characterized by ‘having reached birth and then not being born.

There are non-Buddhists who say that the nature of the four great elements creates form and other phenomena from beginningless time; once they have been created, they are abandoned, and they thus reckon these created phenomena to be impermanent.”

"Some say that the transformation and disintegration of shape and location is what is called impermanence, [extending] up to the fact that the intrinsic nature of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) is fundamentally non-arisen.
From this point downward, the text restates, explains, and extensively refutes these seven types of false conceptions regarding impermanence.
This first section restates and refutes the sixth [view] regarding impermanence.
The phrase "Among these, neither entity nor non-entity is impermanent" restates the opponent's position.
The various subsequent sentences beginning with "That which is the creator" constitute the refutation.

Regarding the statement that the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derivative phenomena (*bhautika*) they produce are false and unreal, their characteristics being subject to destruction: since the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the primary elements cannot be apprehended, they are fundamentally unarisen.
Because they are unarisen, they do not cease. How, then, could there be any real phenomenon—whether primary or derivative—to which one could apply the term "impermanent"?
"Regarding 'non-arising impermanence,' this means that if permanence and impermanence were to coincide, one would fall into the non-Buddhist (tīrthika) doctrine of arising impermanence.
Next, the seventh type of impermanence is restated, explained, and refuted.

It is said: "All phenomena are originally quiescent; it is not the cessation of what has arisen that is called impermanence. Those who do not realize this reckon that non-arising is itself the arising of phenomena, and that their cessation is what is called impermanence.
"If there were a thing that is impermanent, it would mean that while it has reached non-eternality, it does not itself perish; this case is also like that.
This third restatement explains and refutes the fifth [type of] impermanence.

Regarding the statement, "In the state that is neither eternal nor non-eternal, the non-Buddhists do not understand it and instead conceive of it as non-eternal," this is their own self-arising delusion.
As for the passage beginning with "What is its meaning? and following, it interrogates and explains the meaning of that false conception through analogies, as is clearly evident in the sutra itself.
"Mahāmati! It is because impermanence is directly perceived in all phenomena, leading to the realization that all phenomena are ultimately non-existent.
Below this, the Tathāgata correctly refutes that [erroneous] conception.

This means that since the observed impermanence of things is not of a different essence from the various phenomena produced, it is said that there is no distinction between the agent and the object produced.

Since it is stated that "this is the impermanence of things" and "this is the produced phenomenon," and because there is no difference between them, both the agent and the object produced should necessarily be eternal.
Why is this? Because one does not perceive any entity that, having impermanence as its cause, is able to destroy all conditioned phenomena and bring them to non-existence.
"Mahāmati!..."
"The destruction and disintegration of all phenomena (*dharma*) indeed have causes, yet they cannot be understood by the ignorant and foolish.

Because non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) calculate that the impermanence of things occurs without cause, and that there is no one who can bring about the transformation, existence, or non-existence of humans and devas, the Buddha therefore said: "The dependent and primary phenomena of humans and devas—all such phenomena—arise and perish; they indeed have causes, yet they cannot be understood by the ignorant and foolish."

That is to say, a single moment of deluded thought is the cause of arising and destruction; because the non-Buddhists do not understand this, they take the impermanence of external objects as the cause.
"Mahāmati!..."
"A different cause should not produce a different effect... how then can a different cause produce a different effect?
From this point downward, the Tathāgata refutes the counter-argument.

Above, it was stated that there is no distinction; this refuted the calculation that things are impermanent yet do not themselves perish or disintegrate, but rather that they are capable of destroying other phenomena—this is what is meant by "having a distinction."
Furthermore, to refute the further claim that [different causes] can produce various phenomena, it is said that a different cause should not produce a different effect;
if they were truly able to produce one another, then all distinct phenomena would necessarily produce one another.

Just as millet seeds produce hemp and bean seeds produce wheat, if the sentient were to produce the insentient and the insentient were to produce the sentient, then there would be no distinction between those phenomena and these phenomena, or between the producer and the produced;
yet we clearly perceive in the world that all phenomena are distinct. How then can you falsely speculate that a different cause produces a different effect?
“Mahāmati! If the nature of impermanence were an existent entity (*bhāva*), then all things that are impermanent would necessarily be permanent.

If one reckons the nature of impermanence of things as a productive cause (*janaka-hetu*) that is an existent entity, it should be identical to its effects; thus its nature would not be ultimate, and it itself would be impermanent.”
Since impermanence itself is [itself] impermanent, how could it destroy or cause the arising of various phenomena?
All phenomena that are impermanent would consequently have to be permanent. Why is this so?
Since they are identical in their activity and are reckoned as eternally abiding and indestructible, all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) are therefore eternal. "Mahāmati!
If the nature of impermanence were to abide within all phenomena, then because it would reach them, its own self-nature would likewise not undergo destruction."

If one reckons that the nature of things is impermanent, yet it abides eternally within all dharmas and is capable of producing and destroying all dharmas, then since it abides within those dharmas, it should likewise fall into the three periods of time and perish along with them.
If their own substance does not exist, how could they cause things to be impermanent?
All non-Buddhists falsely reckon that the essential nature of the great elements is indestructible, while claiming that derived matter is destroyed.

"Form arises from the combination of the differentiation of the great elements; because it is neither distinct nor non-distinct [from them], the intrinsic nature of that form likewise does not perish. Mahāmati!"
"Within the three realms of existence, can that which creates and that which is created continue until the production of things without ceasing?
This concludes the refutation of the view that things are eternal, as can be understood from the text.
The refutation of the impermanence of destroyed objects is complete.

Regarding "the impermanence of discarding immediately upon creation," one should know that this does not refer to the primary elements (*mahābhūta*), but rather to the impermanence of what is not created from the beginning.
4. The fourth section provides an exposition refuting the first [position]: that what is created at the very beginning is immediately abandoned, which is impermanent.
This refers to the calculations of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), which do not go beyond the three [possibilities] of mutual, self-originated, or co-arisen causes as the creators.

Regarding the statement, "The primary elements do not mutually produce one another because they are distinct," this means that solidity, moisture, and so forth lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) from the outset; since their functions are mutually contradictory, they cannot serve as the basis for producing form (*rūpa*) for one another. Therefore, it is refuted by stating, "because they are distinct."
As the verse says: "The great elements have no intrinsic nature," and it further states: "Since the great elements are mutually contradictory, how could they produce form?
Regarding the statement, "It is not produced by its own characteristic, because there is no difference," the word "self" (sva) means "alone" or "unique."
This means that the great elements (mahābhūta), being by nature originally unarisen, cannot arise independently to produce form; therefore, it is refuted by stating "because there is no difference.
As the following verse says: "The great elements are originally unarisen; therefore, there is no produced form."
Regarding the statement, "They do not create together because they are discordant," "together" (saha) carries the meaning of harmony.

This means that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) are by their very nature discordant and mutually suppress one another—just as water cannot contain fire—and how, then, could they ever act in concert to produce form (*rūpa*)?
Therefore, it is refuted by stating that they are mutually exclusive.
As the following verse says: "Fire burns form, water causes it to decay, and wind can cause it to disperse and perish; how, then, could form arise?"
One should know that "it is not something newly created" refutes [the notion of] impermanence as a product.
As for "impermanence as the destruction of form," this cannot be a creative agent; by inference, it falls within the Sāṃkhya school.
5. Fifth, the exposition refuting the second [view of] impermanence:

To reckon that one merely perceives the cessation of forms such as length and shortness, while not perceiving the cessation of the essence of the created and the creator—this view falls within the Sāṃkhya school.
"Form is itself impermanent" means that this very form is impermanent in its shape, up to the point where it is nothing more than mere verbal designation.
This is the sixth [point], which restates and refutes the third [position] on impermanence.
If one reckons that the great elements (*mahābhūta*) are eternally abiding and indestructible, yet [the self] who acts as the agent is also impermanent, then there would be no worldly affairs.

Such a reckoning falls into the Lokāyata view of the non-Buddhists, for according to their false views, all phenomena arise from their own characteristics; they possess only verbal designations and lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
"Regarding 'impermanence through transformation,' it means that while the physical form undergoes change, the gold itself remains unaltered; this case is likewise so.
(7) This restates and refutes the fourth type of impermanence.
The transformation of the qualities of form is what is called impermanence; it is not that the substance of the primary elements (mahābhūta) itself is called impermanent.
Therefore, the analogy of gold fashioned into ornaments is used: while the ornaments undergo transformation and are thus called impermanent, the gold itself remains unchanged and is not impermanent.
The impermanence resulting from the transformation of the substance of these material phenomena (*rūpadharma*) is likewise thus. "Mahāmati!
In this way, for all such various non-Buddhists, up to the primary elements and their derivatives, there is total annihilation."

This summarizes the aforementioned seven kinds of impermanence, as well as the views on the nature of impermanence held by other externalists through their false conceptualizations and discriminations.
For instance, they calculate that when fire burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), it cannot burn the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of those elements themselves.

As for the statement that "if they can be burned," the primary elements (mahābhūta) and their derivatives would subsequently be subject to cessation; however, because they are seen not to cease, one reckons the nature of the great elements to be permanent.
"Mahāmati! [he said].
"When I say that all dharmas are neither permanent nor impermanent, it is because upon reaching [this realization], one no longer discriminates between the agent and the object of action.
This clarifies the true dharma realized through the Tathāgata’s own self-awakened noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
Whatever is taught and shown is spoken in accordance with realization, differing from the eternalist and nihilist views of the non-Buddhists. Why is this so?

It is because one understands that external phenomena are illusory and unreal, and thus remains free from grasping; furthermore, being free from the views of existence and non-existence, one does not falsely discriminate between the agent and the object of action.
There are ten meanings that, when explained, establish the correct principle; these may be understood from the text itself. "Mahāmati!
The mundane, the supramundane, and even that which transcends them are not capable of being known by ordinary, ignorant people."

It is said that all phenomena—those of the mundane world, those of the supramundane, and those that are most excellent and supreme among the supramundane—are solely mind and lack any external dharmas; they are neither eternal nor impermanent. If one cannot realize this, one falls into false views.
Based on their own deluded imaginings, they calculate and discourse upon permanence and impermanence.
All such skillful means, verbal expressions, and conceptual discriminations regarding these three types of phenomena are likewise beyond the capacity of the foolish and ignorant to perceive.
At that time, the World-Honored One spoke again in verse:
