Therefore, the treatise states: "Those who compete in grasping at right and wrong are contentious; those who have attained realization have no disputes.
Regarding the Buddha, there are thirty-six [aspects], each further having ten types, extending from the ālayavijñāna to the life-faculty (jīvitendriya).

The seeds of the fundamental consciousness (mūlavijñāna) are called "life-span" (*āyus*), because they are able to sustain the consciousnesses; these seeds can cause form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) to remain uninterrupted, and are also termed the "vital faculty" (*jīvitendriya*).

The objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) of this consciousness—namely, the material phenomena and the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*)—is termed "warmth" (*uṣman*); the manifesting consciousnesses are termed "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).
"The mind (*manas*) and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) are both distinct names for discernment; this is the sphere of practice for all the noble ones (*ārya*).

This means that all noble ones cultivate the true contemplation of suchness (*tathatā*) as well as the contemplation of mind-only consciousness (*vijñaptimātra*), just as one proceeds toward the Mahāyāna through skillful means.
The Sūtra states: "If one cultivates faith and understanding regarding the single reality of the objective realm, one should practice and study two kinds of contemplative paths:
first, the contemplation of mind-only consciousness; second, the contemplation of the true nature of suchness."

One who practices the contemplation of mind-only consciousness should, at all times and in all places, observe every action performed by body, speech, and mind, and recognize that these are nothing but the mind.

Furthermore, regarding all objects of experience, if the mind turns toward them in thought, one should examine and know them all; do not allow the mind to wander aimlessly toward indeterminate objects (avyākṛta) without self-awareness.
In every moment of thought, one should observe everything; according to whatever objects the mind contemplates, one should cause the mind to follow those thoughts, so that the mind knows itself.
Having known this, one naturally gives rise to conceptualizations within the inner mind; it is not that all objective realms possess thought or discrimination.

What is meant is that the inner mind itself naturally gives rise to views such as long and short, good and evil, right and wrong, gain and loss, decline and profit, existence and non-existence, as well as immeasurable other conceptions;
yet all objective realms have never possessed these conceptions, which arise from discrimination.

One should know that because all objective realms are inherently devoid of conceptual discrimination, they are themselves neither long nor short, neither good nor evil, and so forth, up to being neither existent nor non-existent, transcending all marks.
Observing in this way, one sees that all phenomena arise solely from the mind’s perception.
Were it otherwise, apart from the mind, not a single phenomenon or characteristic could manifest its own distinct differences.

As for the true contemplation of suchness: one contemplates that the nature of the mind alone is without arising or ceasing; it does not abide in seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and is forever free from all conceptualizations of discrimination.
Therefore it is said: "True Suchness and Consciousness-Only are the sphere of activity for all the Sages.
Only when one practices both principle and conduct as described above can it be called the contemplation of the Dharma.
Thus Yongjia said: "To cross the sea, one must first board a ship; without a ship, there is no means to cross."
Cultivating the mind must involve entering meditative observation (*vipaśyanā*); without observation, there is no means to clarify the mind.
If the mind has not yet been clarified, when will realization be attained?
If one could attain *bodhi* without such cultivation, then even cats, rabbits, and the like would surely realize it.
"This existence is said to be non-existence; that is not to understand my Dharma, which extends from the Truth of Suffering to the Truth of the Path, all of which are fully complete.
Regarding this meaning of the Four Noble Truths, Tiantai, based on the "Chapter on the Holy Conduct" (*Śrī-mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra*), opens them up into four kinds of Four Noble Truths:
namely, the Truths of Arising and Ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*), Non-arising and Non-ceasing (*anutpāda-ananirodha*), the Immeasurable (*apramāṇa*), and the Unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Regarding arising and ceasing: suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are the causes and effects of the mundane world, while cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are the causes and effects of the supramundane.

That which is oppressive is called suffering; thus, it is subject to the transition of the three characteristics. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "The birth of sentient beings and the bases upon which they are born are both termed the Truth of Suffering."

"Growth" is called "origination" (*samudaya*); it refers to the movement of the four mental aggregates. The *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "All afflictions (*kleśa*) and the various karmas produced under the dominant influence of afflictions are collectively termed the Truth of Origination (*samudaya-satya*)."
To define the Path as the removal of afflictions makes it susceptible to being overturned by its opposites;
to define Cessation as tranquility implies that existence is extinguished and returns to non-existence.
This causes sentient beings to know suffering and sever its origin, to rejoice in cessation and cultivate the path.

Although both mundane and supramundane phenomena are subject to transformation, they are therefore called the Four Truths of Arising and Cessation (*utpāda-nirodha-satya*). "Truth" (*satya*) has two meanings:
first, it means reality (*tattva*); second, it means thorough investigation (*parīkṣā*).
If one realizes that the Four Truths are empty because they arise from conditions, one transcends the means [of expression] to awaken to the ultimate meaning and thereby achieves wisdom.
This means: understanding that suffering is without suffering is called the Noble Truth of Suffering;
understanding that accumulation is without combination is called the Noble Truth of Accumulation.
Understanding that cessation is without cessation is called the Noble Truth of Cessation;
understanding that the path is without a path is called the Noble Truth of the Path; therefore, these are termed the Four Truths of Non-arising.
The *Mahāparinirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Suffering has immeasurable characteristics, which are not known by Śrāvakas or Pratyekabuddhas."
"The same applies to the truths of origination, cessation, and the path.
This refers to the four noble truths of immeasurable scope.
If one realizes that the aggregates (*skandha*) and sense bases (*āyatana*) are all suchness (*tathatā*), there is no suffering to be abandoned;
Ignorance and afflictions are themselves bodhi; there is no accumulation to be severed.
Birth and death are themselves nirvana; there is no cessation to be realized.
Extremes and deviance are all the Middle Way; there is no path to be cultivated.
Because there is no suffering and no origination, there is no mundane world;
because there is no cessation and no path, there is no supramundane world.
All phenomena are the true mark (*dharmatā*); outside of the true mark, there are no other dharmas. This is the unconditioned Four Noble Truths.
Therefore, the *Xuanyi* states: "Because of delusion regarding the principle, bodhi becomes affliction and is termed the Truth of Accumulation;
nirvana becomes birth-and-death and is termed the Truth of Suffering.
Because of the ability to understand, afflictions are immediately bodhi and are termed the Truth of the Path."
Birth-and-death is itself nirvana; this is called the Truth of Cessation.
To accord with reality within phenomena, there is no thought and no recollection, and no one who acts; therefore, it is called "unconditioned" (anabhisamskāra).
It is also called the Single Truth of Reality.

Thus, when the eight thousand śrāvakas at the assembly of the Lotus Sūtra beheld the Tathāgata-nature, it was like the harvest of autumn followed by the storage of winter; there was nothing further to be done, for having realized the fundamental source, things are naturally so.

Those who have not yet personally realized this must not complacently fold their hands and imitate non-action and non-cultivation; they must instead wait for the water to reach the channel so that it flows spontaneously and effortlessly.
By means of these Four Truths, they firmly confront the various lands, wherein there is increase and decrease.
There are four [levels] in the Land of Common Residence, three in the Land of Expedient Means, two in the Land of True Reward, and only one in the Land of Tranquil Light.
Furthermore, these are collectively called the Four Noble Truths, while individually they are called the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination:
suffering consists of the seven links of consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, birth, and aging-and-death;
origination consists of the five links of ignorance, volitional formations, craving, grasping, and becoming.
The Path is the skillful means of the causal conditions for counteraction;
Cessation is the cessation of ignorance, the cessation of volitional formations, and so on, up to the cessation of old age and death.
Therefore, the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* elucidates the four sets of the Four Noble Truths and also elucidates the forty-two links of dependent origination.
Those of inferior wisdom contemplate it and attain the enlightenment of a śrāvaka;
those of middling wisdom contemplate it and attain the enlightenment of a pratyekabuddha;
those of superior wisdom contemplate it and attain the enlightenment of a bodhisattva.
When observed by those of the highest, highest wisdom, one attains the bodhi of all Buddhas.
Thus, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions" refers to arising and ceasing;
"that which I say is emptiness" refers to the absence of arising and ceasing.
"To be called 'provisional designation' refers to the immeasurable;
to be called 'the meaning of the Middle Way' refers to the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*).

Furthermore, it is said that 'conditions are themselves origination (*samudaya*), that which is produced is itself suffering (*duḥkha*); the means for extinguishing origination is the path (*mārga*), and the exhaustion of the accumulation of suffering is cessation (*nirodha*')."
Question:
Since the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is not even a single phenomenon, how can one investigate it by means of the numbers one, two, three, and four?
Answer:
The *dharmatā* (the nature of phenomena) is that which is deluded by, while suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*) are that which deludes.
Regarding the deluding subject, there are degrees of lightness and heaviness; regarding the object of delusion, there is both identity and separation.
When distinguished according to the internal and external realms, there are thus four kinds of suffering and its origin.
According to the faculties, natures, and realizations of principle, there are differences of one, two, three, or four types.
If those within the realm are dull-witted, their delusion regarding the truth is heavy, and their suffering and its origin are likewise heavy;
if they are sharp-witted, their delusion regarding the truth is light, and their suffering and its origin are likewise light.
The same applies to those outside the realm regarding their sharpness or dullness, and the lightness or gravity [of their faculties].
The *dharmatā* (nature of phenomena) is that which is to be understood; cessation (*nirodha*) and the path (*mārga*) are that by which it is understood.
Regarding what is to be understood, there is both attachment and detachment; regarding that by which it is understood, there is both skill and clumsiness.
Within the realm, what is understood by those of dull faculties is characterized by separation, and their ability to understand is clumsy;
what is understood by those of sharp faculties is characterized by immediacy, and their ability to understand is skillful.
Beyond the realm, immediacy and separation, as well as skillfulness and clumsiness, are likewise so.
Question:
Since there are four [truths] regarding origination (*samudaya*), why are there only two regarding the fruit of suffering (*duḥkhaphala*)?
Answer:
Delusion follows understanding, and thus there are four types of accumulation;
understanding follows delusion, yet it only brings about two kinds of death.
For example, in the Lesser Vehicle, delusion follows understanding, resulting in the afflictions of the path of seeing and the path of cultivation.
If one understands that [birth] follows from the afflictions, it is merely a case of the分段生死 (segmental birth-and-death).
Question:
While suffering (duḥkha) and its origin (samudaya) may indeed be phenomena produced by causes and conditions, why is this the case for cessation (nirodha) and the path (mārga)?
Answer:
Suffering (duḥkha) and its origin (samudaya) are that which is to be destroyed; cessation (nirodha) and the path (mārga) are that which destroys.
The destroyer derives its name from that which is destroyed; both are phenomena produced by causes and conditions (pratītyasamutpanna-dharma).
Therefore, the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* states: "By extinguishing ignorance, one immediately attains the blazing lamp of *sambodhi*.
This, too, is a matter of causes and conditions.
Question:
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is that which is deluded about;
why is it two? Why is it four?
Answer:
The nature of phenomena (dharmatā) follows the provisional and the ultimate; therefore, there are two.
The nature of phenomena follows the faculties and conditions; therefore, there are four.
If one penetrates this principle, then when applying the fourfold analysis to seeing forms, hearing sounds, and so forth, there will be no confusion or error.
Thus we know that the one mind and the four truths encompass horizontally and penetrate vertically;
there is no principle that is not exhausted, and no dharma that is not complete.
"Ordinary beings engage in false discrimination because they grasp at the three natures; therefore, through their total eradication, all become pure."

Regarding the phrase "afflictions of both seeing and cultivation": these refer to the afflictions of conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) abandoned through the path of seeing (*darśanamārga*), as well as the innate afflictions (*sahaja*) abandoned through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*).
Regarding the explanation according to the three vehicles, there are briefly ten types:

first, greed; second, hatred; third, delusion (also called ignorance); fourth, pride; fifth, doubt; sixth, the view of a self-identity; seventh, the view of extremes; eighth, false views; ninth, the grasping at views; and tenth, the grasping at precepts and observances.

Thus, among these ten afflictions, both collectively and individually, four types—doubt, wrong view, and the two types of grasping—arise solely through discrimination; these are the afflictions abandoned by insight (*darśana-heya*).
The remaining six, beginning with greed, are both discriminative and innate;
they are abandoned by both means, namely, by insight and by cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*).

Among the eight consciousnesses, the first five can give rise to both the initial three [types of afflictions]—namely, those arising from discrimination (*vikalpita*) and those that are innate (*sahaja*).

Within the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), because it is induced by the three causes of false teachers, false teachings, and false reflection, there is the occurrence of afflictions arising from discrimination.
The sixth consciousness possesses all ten [afflictions] in total; four are exclusively discriminative (*vikalpita*), while six are both discriminative and innate (*sahaja*).

The seventh manas-consciousness possesses only the four innate ones—namely, self-delusion, self-view, self-pride, and self-love—because this consciousness is of the nature of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*).
The eighth consciousness, in its entirety, does not arise; it merely contains their seeds, as it is exclusively of an unobscured-neutral nature (*anivṛtāvyākṛta*).
Both the discriminative and innate [afflictions] pervade all three realms, whereas only the single type of anger exists solely within the desire realm.
The afflictions of both the form realm (*rūpadhātu*) and the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) are all subsumed under the category of obscured-unspecified (*nivṛtāvyākṛta*) nature.
Within the Four Noble Truths of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), there are ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*) for each, totaling forty.

In the two upper realms, anger is excluded from each of the four truths, resulting in nine for each; thus, there are seventy-two. Together with those of the desire realm, there are one hundred and twelve in total.

Regarding those that arise simultaneously (*sahaja*), the desire realm possesses all six, while the two upper realms exclude anger, possessing only five each; these together total sixteen. When combined with the previously mentioned analytical afflictions (*vikalpa*), there are one hundred and twenty-eight afflictions in all.

If they are of the capacity of the Two Vehicles, they sever the afflictions of conceptual discrimination regarding the Four Truths of the Three Realms by means of the eight patiences and eight knowledges, thereby attaining the fruit of Stream-enterer; subsequently, they cultivate the nine paths of uninterrupted transition and the nine paths of liberation to sever the innate afflictions of the Three Realms, thereby attaining the remaining three fruits.

Regarding those who have pacified the various realms of existence through the obstacles to knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), these are severed upon entering the state of *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*. As for all other [obstacles], some are severed while others are not; thus, they differ from those of the "foolish Dharma" (the Śrāvakas).

Because the latter sever only the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), when those of the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) turn their minds toward enlightenment, they become identical to Bodhisattvas who have turned their minds. They differ from the Śrāvakas of the foolish Dharma in that they partially sever the obstacle to knowledge, whereas those of the foolish Dharma sever only the obstacle of afflictions. As for the Bodhisattvas who advance directly, they sever both obstacles. Within the obstacle of afflictions, the Bodhisattvas who have turned their minds differ from the two vehicles in terms of their realms and stages; yet, in the severing of the obstacle of afflictions, they may be similar to the two vehicles.

Regarding those [afflictions] among the two obstructions that arise from conceptualization: their active manifestations are suppressed prior to the stages (bhūmi), and at the time of the True Path of Seeing (darśanamārga) in the first stage, their seeds are suddenly severed in a single moment.
Regarding the innate afflictions (*sahaja-kleśa*), from the first bhūmi onward they can be severed at will; however, because their seeds are retained, they are not completely eliminated.

Why is this? It is for the sake of moistening birth and gathering in sentient beings, so as not to fall into the two vehicles, in order to sever the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and to attain great enlightenment (*mahābodhi*).
The afflictions of that seventh consciousness do not, by their nature, moisten rebirth; therefore, they are not what is retained.
Because its mode of activity (*ākāra*) is subtle, it occasionally manifests even from the seventh stage onward, as the wisdom of contemplation is intermittent.
Therefore, one should know that the seeds of the afflictive hindrances persist until the stage of the diamond-like concentration;

however, because the aspects of the cognitive hindrances are subtle and they directly obstruct the Bodhisattva path, they are severed portion by portion throughout each stage (*bhūmi*), and are only exhausted without remainder upon reaching the stage of Buddhahood.
For this reason, it is said that both obstacles and the afflictions to be abandoned through cultivation persist until the stage of Buddhahood.

Thus, the *Abhidharmasamuccaya* states: "Furthermore, throughout the ten stages of the bodhisattvas, they cultivate only the path that serves as the antidote to the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), not for the purpose of abandoning the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*)."
"When attaining bodhi, one suddenly severs both the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstructions (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
According to the definitive teaching (*nītārtha*), the various śrāvakas are only able to suppress the afflictive obstructions; how much less could they possibly sever the cognitive obstructions?

Regarding these Bodhisattvas, within the two obstacles, there is no distinction between the innate (*sahaja*) and the discriminative (*vikalpita*); there are only the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) and their residual impressions (*vāsanā*). Before the stages (*bhūmi*), the active afflictions are suppressed; at the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), the seeds of the active afflictions are severed; from the subsequent stages onward, the residual impressions are eliminated; and at the Buddha-stage, ultimate purity is attained.
Regarding the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) herein: immediately after the seeds of the active afflictions (*paryavasthāna*) are severed, there remain residual habitual tendencies.

If one distinguishes them according to their association with the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*) across the six, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses, there are two interpretations: first, that within the eight consciousnesses, there are only habitual tendencies; within the *manas* (seventh consciousness), there are only seeds; and within the six consciousnesses, there are only active manifestations (*samudācāra*).
Alternatively, it is said that the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses all encompass habitual tendencies, seeds, and active manifestations.

However, these two obstacles both obstruct wisdom and are collectively termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*), as they constitute the fundamental and derivative forms of ignorance. As stated in the *Awakening of Faith*:

"The two obstacles are explained according to the gate of mutual dependence between the fundamental and the derivative. The six defiled mental states arising from ignorance are called the 'obstacle of afflictions' (*kleśāvaraṇa*), which refers to the afflictions of the four stages of abiding. The fundamental ignorance that gives rise to these defiled mental states is called the 'obstacle to wisdom' (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), which is the stage of nameless abiding."
That obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) is also called the "branch-end ignorance" (*mūlānta-avidyā*) and is also termed the "obstacle to the knowable" (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Why is this?
Because from the perspective of its capacity to defile the object (*ālambana*), it is called an "affliction."
Because it functions as an obstruction to the domain of wisdom, it is also termed "ignorance" (*avidyā*).
Thus, the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* states: "There are two types of ignorance: that which is associated with craving and the like is called 'associated ignorance,' which is a secondary branch;
that which is not associated with craving and the like is called 'independent ignorance,' which is the root, for it is the primary factor."
The *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi* further states: "There are two types of non-common ignorance (*asādhāraṇa-avidyā*):
first, the ever-active non-common [ignorance], which exists only in the manas and constitutes its derivative branches;
second, the independent non-common [ignorance], which does not exist in the manas and constitutes its fundamental root."

Therefore, Tiantai holds that the "cessation of realizing reality" (tǐzhēn zhǐ)—the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional—in conjunction with the wisdom of emptiness, is able to destroy the delusions of views and thoughts (jiàn-sī huò) and the afflictions of the four abodes (sìzhù fánnǎo), thereby perfecting the wisdom-eye and all-encompassing knowledge (yīqiè zhì). Through this wisdom, one attains the essence; one attains the true essence.

By means of skillful means, one follows conditions to cease [discursive thought] and enters the contemplation of entering the conventional from emptiness (*śūnyatā-praveśa-kuśala-darśana*). One discriminates various dharma-gates regarding medicines and illnesses, thereby destroying the ignorance that deludes and the secondary branches of nescience (*avidyā*). Thus, one perfects the Dharma-eye and the knowledge of the modes of the path (*mārgajñatā*). Through this wisdom, one attains the essence—that is, one attains the essence of the conventional.

By employing the cessation that is free from the dualistic discrimination of the two extremes and the two higher forms of contemplation as skillful means, one enters the contemplation of the Middle Way. Therein, one destroys fundamental ignorance and attains the Buddha-eye and the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*). Through this wisdom, one realizes the essence and attains the essence of the ultimate truth of the Middle Way; this is what is termed the meaning of the sequence of skillful deliverance.

If we speak in terms of the perfect and sudden *śamatha-vipaśyanā* (calming and insight) of the single mind: the quiescence of the dharma-nature is called *śamatha*, while its constant illumination within that quiescence is called *vipaśyanā*. When *śamatha* takes the truths as its object, one truth is the three truths;
when the truths are bound to *śamatha*, one *śamatha* is the three *śamathas*.
For example, just as the three characteristics exist within a single moment of mind, and though it is a single moment of mind, it possesses these three characteristics;
so too is the truth of cessation (*nirodha-satya*).
The phenomena that are ceased, though one, are three; the mind that effects the cessation, though three, is one.
When one uses contemplation to observe an object, then a single object becomes three objects;
when an object gives rise to contemplation, then a single contemplation becomes three contemplations.
It is like the three eyes on the face of Maheśvara: although there are three eyes, they constitute a single face.

Contemplating the objects is also like this: contemplating the three is to realize the one, and manifesting the one is to realize the three. This is inconceivable; it is neither mundane nor supramundane, neither provisional nor real, neither superior nor inferior, neither prior nor posterior, neither simultaneous nor distinct, and neither large nor small.
Therefore, the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "Phenomena produced through causes and conditions are emptiness, they are the provisional, and they are the middle.
Thus we know that for destroying all delusions, nothing is better than emptiness; there is no provisional nor middle that is not empty.
For establishing all phenomena, nothing is better than the provisional; there is no emptiness nor middle that is not provisional.
In the ultimate realization of all natures, nothing surpasses the Middle Way; there is nothing that is neither provisional nor empty that is not the Middle.

These are all established as skillful means to counteract the mental illnesses of sentient beings—ignorance and afflictions—and within the School of Worthy Head (Xianshou zong), they still belong to the meaning of the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao).
The ignorance and afflictions refuted above are also termed the two obstacles of principle and phenomena (*li-shi-er-zhang*) in the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment*.
According to the Sudden Teaching (*dun-jiao*), because both the nature of delusion and the nature of wisdom are fundamentally pure, it cannot be said whether they are severed or not severed.
Even if one were to say that there are afflictions to be severed, they are not severed gradually according to the stages and positions [of the path].
As the *Awakening of Faith* states: "If one is free from deluded thoughts, then there are no appearances of any objective realms. This is precisely what is meant.

In the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), one further does not distinguish between the outflows (*āsrava*), habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), seeds (*bīja*), or manifest states. This means that the essential nature of all afflictions is ineffable; thus, they are entirely delusive and entirely true, being nothing other than the inexhaustible, multi-layered Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Within the minds of the Buddhas are sentient beings, and within the minds of sentient beings are the Buddhas, interpenetrating one another. Therefore, when one hindrance is present, all are present; when one is severed, all are severed.

However, for one who practices contemplation, it is necessary to realize that the subject which cuts off is devoid of intrinsic nature and that the object which is cut off is fundamentally empty; only the cutting off of "no-cutting-off" constitutes correct cutting off.
If one clings to the notion that things definitely exist, one falls into eternalism, for what exists cannot be cut off;
if one clings to the notion that things definitely do not exist, one falls into nihilism, thereby losing noble wisdom.
Therefore, the former masters said:
"The Buddha-nature is originally present yet must be diligently cultivated; delusions are fundamentally non-existent yet must be severed.
"The intrinsically pure mind of one's own nature is that which sentient beings are deluded about; even the most wise should not speak of it [as an object]."

That is to say, if one practices according to reality based on the Tathāgata’s authoritative sacred teachings and the correct principles they expound, severing delusions and realizing the Truth, then there will be no fruitless waste;
to abandon this and seek instead to extinguish afflictions is entirely the teaching of Māra.

Therefore, Master Xuanshu, employing the correct principles of the Buddha’s holy teachings to elucidate the essential tenets and other matters, skillfully adapted them to the capacities of sentient beings and divided each into five sections, as seen in his *Huayan jiaozhang* and the *Qixin lun shu*.
Furthermore, the holy teachings are fivefold:

first, the Hīnayāna teachings. Because they accord with the capacities of beings and follow the words of others, they teach that all phenomena are categorically distinct; this is for the purpose of distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox, differentiating between ordinary beings and sages, allocating between what is to be rejoiced in and what is to be loathed, and clarifying cause and effect.

However, the principles explained therein merely reveal the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*) and do not clarify the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*); they establish the roots of defilement and purity solely based on the six consciousnesses and the three poisons, without exhausting the source of all phenomena, and thus give rise to much dispute and contention.

Second is the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna, also called the Partial Teaching (*bhinna-śāsana*). This refers to the view that those of fixed nature among the two vehicles (*dviyāna*) and those of no-nature (*abhavya*), such as the icchantikas, will both fail to attain Buddhahood.

Since this does not yet exhaust the principles of the Mahāyāna Dharma, it is established as the first stage; because there are those who do not attain Buddhahood, it is termed "partial. It extensively explains the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) and explains the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) only slightly.

The nature of the dharmas taught herein corresponds to the categories of dharma-characteristics; because they are definitively resolved and clearly distinguished, there is little room for dispute. Third is the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao), also called the True Teaching (Shijiao).

It teaches that the *tathāgatagarbha* follows conditions to become the *ālayavijñāna*, and that all phenomena arising through conditions are devoid of intrinsic nature and are entirely suchness (*tathatā*). It maintains that those with fixed natures as well as those without natures shall all attain Buddhahood. This constitutes the ultimate discourse of the Mahāyāna; therefore, it is established as "Final" (*zhong*), and it is called "True" (*shi*) because it accords with the true principle.

It teaches the characteristics of phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*) sparingly and the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) extensively; even the characteristics taught ultimately converge back into that nature, and thus there is no room for dispute.
These two aforementioned teachings both rely on the gradual cultivation through the successive stages (*bhūmi*), and are collectively termed "gradual" (*anupūrva*).
However, this single gate differs from those preceding and following it.

It is merely that the teachings differ in having distinctions of beginning, end, sudden, and gradual; the Dharma itself possesses no differences of superiority or inferiority, nor of shallowness or depth.

Fourth is the Sudden Teaching (Dun-jiao). It asserts that the mere non-arising of a single thought is itself called Buddhahood; it does not rely on stages or gradual progression in its exposition, and is therefore termed "Sudden.
It makes no general discussion of phenomenal characteristics, but addresses only the true nature (bhūtatathatā).

All that exists is merely delusive thought; the entire dharma-realm is beyond words. The five dharmas and the three natures are all empty; the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness are both discarded. One censures teachings to encourage detachment and destroys appearances to extinguish the mind: the arising of the mind is itself delusion, while its non-arising is the Buddha.

The fifth is the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle, which clarifies that one stage is all stages and all stages are one stage; therefore, the fulfillment of the mind of the ten faiths immediately encompasses the five stages and the attainment of perfect enlightenment.
Because it is fully endowed with both the primary and the auxiliary, it is called the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

What is taught here is exclusively the inexhaustible Dharma-realm, wherein the ocean of nature is perfectly interfused and dependent origination is unimpeded, like the pearls of Indra’s net, infinitely layered and inexhaustible. If one were to manifest this sutra within the five teachings, it properly belongs to the Sudden Teaching while also encompassing the Final Teaching.
However, in the doctrinal treatises, the term "One Vehicle" (Ekayāna) is used specifically within the context of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao), wherein there are two types:
first, the One Vehicle of the Common Teaching, so called because it is common to both the Sudden and the Real;
second, the One Vehicle of the Distinct Teaching, so called because it alone possesses perfect fusion and complete virtue.
That is to say, the Separate Teaching (biejiao) is entirely distinct from all other teachings, while the Common Teaching (tongjiao) universally subsumes them all.
Among the doctrinal judgments made by the various masters of past and present, none are more excellent than this.

However, as the five teachings of the various vehicles have not yet been clarified—since each possesses its own common and distinct, as well as shared and unshared aspects—I shall now continue [the discussion] to complete this exposition.

First, regarding the Hīnayāna teaching: it takes the common vehicle of humans and devas as its "teaching of the same" (tóngjiào), and its exclusive revelation of the Four Truths and Four Fruits as its "uncommon and distinct teaching" (bùgòng biéjiào). Thus, the *Prakaraṇapāda-śāstra* (Pinzú lùn), fascicle 6, states: "There are dharmas shared with ordinary beings (pṛthagjana) and dharmas not shared with ordinary beings."
What is meant by "shared"?
It refers to meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and rebirth (*upapatti*).
Furthermore, what are these?
This refers to such concentrations and such births, which can both occur for ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and noble ones (*ārya*).
How, then, are they "unshared"?
It refers to the four paths of practice (*pratipad*), the four kinds of intrepid confidence (*vaiśāradya*), the four fruits of the ascetic life (*śrāmaṇyaphala*), and so forth.

Second, regarding the Initial Teaching of the Mahāyāna: it is considered "common" because it consists of teachings for those of the Two Vehicles who have turned their minds toward the Mahāyāna; it is considered "distinct" because it consists of teachings for those of the Two Vehicles who proceed directly [to the Mahāyāna] without such a turning of the mind. This is as explained in the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* (Treatise on Wisdom) in the chapter on the common and distinct Prajñā teachings, which clarifies these two teachings of turning the mind and proceeding directly.
Regarding the Final Teaching of the Three Great Vehicles, it is considered "common" insofar as it shares commonalities with the preceding three vehicles.

The *Lotus Sūtra* states: "Within the single Buddha-vehicle, I have differentiated and taught three; all that you practice is the path of the bodhisattva. It is considered "distinct," however, because it does not share [the teachings] with the three vehicles but is exclusively the One Vehicle.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "In the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, there is only the One Vehicle; there is neither a second nor a third.
This alone is the true reality; the other two are not real."
Thus we know that both the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* and the *Mahāparinirvāṇa-sūtra* reveal the One Vehicle (Ekayāna) by means of responding to those of provisional capacity and the Śrāvakas.

Regarding the four Mahāyāna sudden teachings (tunjiao), they are considered "common" insofar as they share the same beginning and end with the Śrāvaka vehicle, and "distinct" insofar as they do not share the preceding three [gradual teachings] but are exclusively sudden.
As the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states: "This sūtra is called the Mahāyāna of Sudden Teaching; sentient beings with sudden faculties attain awakening through it.
This refers to those of the direct-advancing capacity according to the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).
It further states: "It also encompasses all classes of beings who practice through gradual cultivation.
This refers to those with the potential for conversion according to the Shared Teaching (tóngjiào).
Regarding the fifth, the Perfect Teaching of the One Vehicle (yīshèng yuánjiào), it is as described in the text of the preceding chapter on the Distinct Teaching (biéjiào).
Among these five teachings, if categorized by the contrast between the Small and the Great, the first is Small and the latter four are Great;
if categorized by the contrast between the Provisional and the Real, the first two are Provisional and the latter three are Real;
if categorized by the contrast between the Sudden and the Gradual, the first three are all Gradual and the latter two are Sudden.
If we contrast the partial and the perfect, the first four are all partial and the last one is perfect.

However, while each preceding stage does not encompass the succeeding stages, each succeeding stage necessarily includes all preceding ones; this is explained according to the Shared Teaching (*tongjiao*).
If, however, we speak according to the Distinct Teaching (*biejiao*), then each succeeding stage refutes each preceding one.

Therefore, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "The true and eternal nature of phenomena transcends mental conceptions; even those of the Two Vehicles can attain this. It is not for this reason that one is called the World-Honored One, but rather because of profound and unimpeded wisdom. This is the sudden meaning of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*).
This sutra states: "The first stage is itself the eighth; even regarding the signless, what sequence could there be? Sudden destruction culminates in gradual [realization].
The *Lotus Sutra* states: "There is neither two nor three," thereby ultimately subverting the Initial Teaching.

In the *Brahmajāla Sūtra*, the Two Vehicles are rebuked as holding false views; this is a provisional refutation intended to cure those of inferior teachings, serving merely to eliminate their "illness" rather than their "Dharma.

Nevertheless, although the intermediate three teachings within the *Tongjiao* (Teaching of Commonality) are identical to the preceding ones, they may also partially share in the nature of the subsequent teachings.

For instance, the *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* contains the three contemplations of the perfectly taught Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*), while works such as the *Mahāyānasaṃgraha* contain the practical aspects of the truly taught [teachings].
Yet, while there is that which they share, there is nothing that distinguishes them;
there is the meaning, but not the explicit teaching.
This establishes only the meaning within the forthcoming teachings.

Because various sūtras and śāstras contain such dharma-gates—whether identical or distinct, common or uncommon—that emerge and subside while interpenetrating one another, the five distinct teachings are provisionally established.
Question:

It is already known that each of the five teachings has its own commonalities and distinctions, which run through all the various expositions. By means of this, it is clarified that the temporal teachings of a single lifetime contain no further hidden depths.
How is it that the single mind, when applied to these various teachings, possesses such diverse meanings?
Answer:
There are two meanings to this, and thus this statement was made.

First, regarding the comprehensive inclusion of phenomena: it means that because this profound dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) possesses five aspects within a single mind, the Noble Ones accordingly employ one gate or another to guide and transform sentient beings.
First, the gate of subsuming meaning through names, as explained in the Hīnayāna teachings;
second, the gate of subsuming principle through phenomena, as explained in the Initial Teaching;
third, the gate of the non-obstruction between principle and phenomena, as explained in the Final Teaching.
The fourth is the gate of the exhaustive principle of the four matters, as taught in the Sudden Teaching;
the fifth is the gate of the ocean of the five natures possessing all virtues, as taught in the Perfect Teaching.
Thus, one does not move from the fundamental while remaining at the derivative, nor does one destroy the derivative while remaining at the fundamental.
The five meanings are mutually integrated as the single mind alone.

Second, regarding the differentiation of the teachings received according to the capacities of sentient beings, their faculties and dispositions differ; that is to say, some may receive the name but not the meaning, as in the Hīnayāna teachings;
others may receive both the name and a portion of the meaning, as in the Initial Teaching (Śākyamuni’s first turning of the wheel).
In some cases, one obtains both the name and the full meaning, as in the Final Teaching (Zhongjiao);
in some cases, one obtains the meaning while the name does not exist, as in the Sudden Teaching (Dunjiao);
and in some cases, both name and meaning are inexhaustible, as in the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao).

Thus we know that although the holy teachings differ in ten thousand ways, they are essentially comprised of these five alone. The first is clearly distinct and non-overlapping, while the latter completely encompasses one another.
This harmonious integration into a single flavor and the cessation of all doubts are entirely the Tathāgata’s great skillful means for gathering in and transforming sentient beings.
The other thematic categories are explained at length as stated therein.
"First, one must definitively understand the self (*ātman*), and analyze the various appropriations up to the fifth, the 'inexpressible' (*avaktavya*).

Regarding the statement "the three times and the non-temporal constitute the fifth, the inexpressible," this refers to the Vātsīputrīya school of India, which takes the coexistence of the self and phenomena (*dharma*) as its tenet. They establish five categories of phenomena (*pañca-dharmaskandha*): the three times constitute three; the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) constitutes the fourth, which is the non-temporal; and the fifth is the inexpressible category (*avaktavya-skandha*). The self is contained within this [fifth category], being inexpressible as either conditioned or unconditioned.
Therefore, this school was collectively rejected by all other schools and labeled as a non-Buddhist sect that merely clings to the Buddha's teachings.
"That which is known by all Buddhas: regarding the abiding of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*), do not engage in further conceptual discrimination."
This final verse concerns the entrustment for circulation according to the meaning.
"Teaching" (jiao) refers to the trace; it is the mind as the means of expression.
"Principle" (li) refers to the source; it is that which is expressed by the mind.
Without the fundamental, there would be no way to manifest the traces; without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the fundamental.

If one can seek the fundamental through the traces, one will naturally sever the traces and return to the source. Thus it is said: "The teaching is established because of the principle; the principle is revealed because of the teaching."
This teaching is the definitive, ultimate teaching within the Mahāyāna;
this principle refers to the profoundly deep, ultimate truth of dependent origination and the single mind.

Therefore, I exhort the disciples of the four assemblies to have faith, to understand, to practice, and to cultivate, so that they may realize and enter [this truth] according to reality and never sever the lineage of the Tathāgata.
Thus it is said: "One should rely upon this teaching and principle; do not engage in further conceptual discrimination."
The śramaṇa Huiwei, who carved the woodblocks through the solicitation of alms, re-examined and corrected [this text].
